Just about everything has been mentioned regarding the gameplay except for full moon events and New Game +. Every month of the game there's a full moon. The game will give you a indication of when the next one is going to begin and you'll have a certain amount of days to prepare for it. When a full moon day comes, there's always a boss fight that's usually harder then most in the game coming. Not just that, but you usually have to go through a minor dungeon in order to reach the full moon bosses as well. Aside from full moon events, there's one last feature in Persona 3 that's good. New Game +. Once you beat the game you can select New Game + using your cleared game save data. In New Game +, you carry certain things over and unlock a few more optional things in the game. So, re-playability is definitely high due to this. It makes future playthroughs be easier and different, but also offers more optional content for you to do as well. Definitely good to see New Game + in Persona 3. Overall though, the gameplay of Persona 3 despite it's shortcomings is quite good. Game is a lot of fun and quite linear. It has a unique take on the RPG genre and plays out quite differently then most. There is indeed dungeon crawling and Tartarus can get repetitive, but it's still a enjoyable experience the whole way through. Battle system is unique and has a lot of depth, but the forced A.I. is definitely not a feature to be happy about. All-together, I give the gameplay a 8.4/10. For the third section, it's going to be on storyline which I consider the third most important aspect of a game. Storyline:8.2/10 :In Persona 3, you play the role of a silent protagonist who's a high school student. He's moved into a dorm occupied by several other students after the death of his parents and begins experiencing extremely odd events. As time goes on, it's discovered he has the ability to summon Persona's who are magical beings that are really powerful. Not only that, but he's extremely proficient at it too. It turns out that the dorm he's moved into really serves as a organization known as SEES.The group's purpose is to eliminate the shadows whenever the Dark Hour happens. Between midnight and 1AM the Dark Hour occurs to a few. Most who are effected during it, experience what's called Apathy Syndrome. A extremely bad effect that puts it's victim into a comatose state and possibly even kills them if they are unlucky. At this time too, shadows which are evil creatures wander around aimlessly killing whatever they find. If that's not bad enough, the school which all the characters attend turns into a gigantic tower known as Tartarus during this time. It's assumed that Tartarus is the origin of where all the shadows are coming from. So, it's up to you and SEES to eliminate them and save everyone from them. Like most RPG's, it eventually turns into a journey to save the world. However, Persona 3 does do it in a interesting way. Game takes place in a modern setting. You play the role of a silent protagonist whom mainly just chooses choices during conversations and has other characters do all of the talking in the game. However, the game does a good job of keeping you immersed in the role of that silent protagonist. All of the other characters are quite interesting too, but if I had one issue it's that they aren't dynamic personality wise. Some of them are quite straightforward and predictable when it comes to their behavior patterns. Not only that, but some of their backstories are generic too. For example, one of your party members failed to save someone in the past and has a hard time looking past it despite there being nothing he could have done. That's a backstory that's quite frequently used in stories nowadays. However, despite that, the character interactions are interesting and the dialogue is pretty well written. Each of the characters are well developed too. You learn their motivations and backstories etc. Aside from the lack of dynamic personality shown in characters, and generic backstories there's also one other major gripe. Antagonists in Persona 3. Oh boy, does Persona 3 have some horrible antagonists. The main antagonist group Strega has got to be one of the least interesting villain groups I've ever seen before. Their personalities are extremely bland and they have poor motivations for what they do. This is essentially their motivation:Life is too painful for us and death alleviates that problem. So, we're trying to kill everyone so they no longer have to deal with the pain. Fortunately, the final boss/final main antagonist of the game is quite well done and ties in to the whole plot and Strega well. As for Persona 3's main plot it's decent. For the most part, the plot is pretty simple. However, later on it becomes more intricate, but it's still quite easily understandable. Yet, it is well done and all ties in well together towards the end. In addition, the ending of the game is pretty good and the final events were handled pretty well. Overall, the Storyline receives a 8.2/10. Main plot is decent, but I don't really care for main plots much. Characters are what makes or breaks a storyline for me. For the most part, the game succeeds, but the lack of dynamic personalities in characters and generic backstories brings them down. Not only that, but it takes a while for the ball to get rolling in the storyline. Once it does get good too, it's only for a short while then dies down a little. Compared to Persona 2 Innocent Sin, which took a while to get going too, but had a amazing plot once it got good. Fortunately, for more character development you can also do Social Links with other characters in the game to learn more about them and gain additional EXP for fusing Persona's in the Velvet room. Last, is the Music. Which I consider the second most important thing in a game. Music:9.4/10 :Shoji Meguro did a extremely good job with the music. The OST(Official Soundtrack) of Persona 3 comes close to being one of the best out there, but falls just barely short. To say the least, voice acting and sound effects are great. Soundtrack mainly consists of J-Pop and rock/jazz music. The rock songs are more light and not really heavy metal or anything like that. Most of the rock songs which is only a few, are the boss songs. Personally, my main gripe with the OST is Tartarus's music. It's about a 6-8 second loop and gets extremely repetitive to hear after a while. Aside from that though, the music, sound effects and voice acting is great. Music obtains a 9.4/10 for it's score. With the last category reviewed, what do I think of Persona 3 overall? Overall: 8/10 - Great Pros: +Extremely fun game. +Deep innovative battle system that's not complicated to get the grasp of. +Really good soundtrack and voice acting. +Storyline is great, but does have some problems. +Good character/enemy designs. Lots of creativeness. +Insane amount of customization. +Extremely unique and refreshing approach to the JRPG genre. +New Game + for more re playability. Cons: -Forced A.I. -Lack of dynamic attitudes in the characters. Extremely one dimensional characters. -Generic back stories for some of the characters. -Horribly uninteresting antagonists aside from the final antagonist of the game. -Plot takes a while to get going, but doesn't become nearly as good as Persona 2 Innocent Sin's plot which took a while to get good too, but was so much more incredible then Persona 3's storyline when it did. -Game doesn't feel too epic. Feels really broad in scope aside from maybe the end and one or two events. Shin Megami Tensei Persona 3 is definitely worth a purchase. It's a great game all-together, but does have some flaws that prevent it from being a nearly perfect masterpiece. Graphics are good, but not really high quality and relies on style. However, I don't care for Graphics unless it negatively intervenes with the gameplay or anything else so I won't count it. Gameplay is ridiculously fun, but the forced A.I. is annoying and dungeon crawling in Tartarus can get repetitive. Storyline is pretty good too, but there's a lack of dynamic attitudes in the character and the antagonists are terrible for the most part. The story takes a while to get good and the scope of the storyline just isn't that epic. Last, but not least the Music is really good, but falls short just barely of being a excellent soundtrack. Voice acting is well done though. If someone was trying to get into the Persona series or SMT in general, and asked Persona 3/4 I would personally suggest 4 first. Yes, 3 is a great game, but 4 completely improves over it and is more accessible. If you do have the patience...Wait until the PSP port/remake of sorts comes out which removes the forced A.I. and improves the game more comes out. Overall, Persona 3 FES receives a 8/10 from me. Great game in my opinion, but doesn't hold a candle to Persona 4 or 2 Innocent Sin.

author: Melee_Ace
review_title: Bang for your buck, and I'm not just talking about the evokers.
review_text: Persona 3: a game that sadly flew under my radar for a good many years, and I suspect did the same for many other people. Released back in 2006/2007 for the PlayStation 2, Persona 3 was ignored by many game players due to the arrival of the next generation of consoles. However, the game managed to have enough followers to create a buzz. Being a long-time JRPG fan, I had kept up with the genre enough over the years to hear the Persona series mentioned a few times, but unfortunately never got to experience it as I had misplaced my PS2. When browsing through the PSN store recently, however, I had come across Persona 3 FES for the price of $9.99, and so I decided to buy the game and try it out. I don't regret this decision one single bit. Persona 3 excels in that it offers solid traditional RPG mechanics along with the unique Social Link system, which sets the Persona series apart from virtually any other RPG series to date. Simple yet deep, Persona 3 manages to offer an easy-to-follow narrative and gameplay style but appeal to experienced RPG fans with intricate plot details and complex gameplay mechanics. Persona 3 FES is a special edition of the original Persona 3, with added features and tweakings (such as social links, items, events). Most prominently, an extra episode called “The Answer” was added to supplement the main story, dubbed “The Journey”. While focusing mostly on The Journey, I will also address The Answer when appropriate. Without further ado, here's my breakdown of P3F. Story: You begin the game as a high school student transferring to Gekkoukan High School in the fictional city of Iwatodai, Japan. As you're walking to your dormitory, electrical appliances suddenly shut off, the sky and surroundings take on an eerie green hue, and people are shockingly transmogrified into upright coffins. Upon entering the dorm, you find a couple of girls who, like you, have been spared from the mysterious transformation and welcome you to the dorm, shrugging off any abnormalities. A few nights later, the dorm is attacked by dark, monstrous beings, and you're forced into a confrontation with them. Through a turn of events, you then unexpectedly discover the ability to destroy the enemies: by summoning a supernatural being from the depths of your mind, which leaves you exhausted to the point of passing out. After recovering at the hospital, your fellow dorm residents invite you to a discussion about the events that transpired. You are told by your dormmates that the monsters are called Shadows, which attack humans by feeding on their psyches, rendering them members of “the Lost”, humans unable to speak, interact, or otherwise care for themselves. Shadows only appear during the Dark Hour, a 25th hour which occurs every night at midnight, during which the aforementioned environmental changes occur. The Shadows mostly take residence in a large tower named Tartarus, which also only appears during the Dark Hour. Your dormmates then tell you that they are members of SEES, a team dedicated to fighting Shadows and eliminating the Dark Hour. They explain that they have the ability to summon beings known as personas, manifestations of their psyches, by firing a customized piece of equipment shaped like a gun at their heads, called evokers. Since you yourself have exhibited the unique ability to wield multiple personas, they urge you to join their cause, as only persona-users can defeat Shadows. The game is set in motion as you accept their request, making regular ventures to Tartarus from then on in the hopes of discovering clues to the elimination of Shadows and the Dark Hour. The main plot is great in that it's simple yet engrossing. Most of the game's progression has you living a normal high school life, while also making ventures to Tartarus and taking on rogue Shadows during particular events. Roughly every in-game month, a story-related event will take place to freshen things up, and usually offer more insight into the narrative and the nature of Shadows and the Dark Hour. Sometimes, a plot twist will come up, which keeps the story interesting and adds more depth to it. New characters are introduced and added to your team at regular intervals, which not only offers a new cast member to become familiar with but also affects your older characters through their interactions with the newcomer. However, the story can sometimes feel slow-paced, as major events often take an in-game month to transpire. As such, you'll often find yourself twiddling your thumbs as you go through the days going to school and Tartarus, waiting for the next big moment. The characters are perhaps the area where the game truly shines. The members of SEES are diverse and unique, spawning several archetypes, and are all fully explored and developed throughout the course of the story. The starting members of SEES include Yukari, a popular and bright junior girl driven by a past similar to yours, Junpei, a junior class clown who's excited to use his persona for good, Akihiko, a senior boxing champion and long-time field leader of SEES, and Mitsuru, preppy senior and de-facto leader of SEES. All of your teammates are very likeable, which I find to be a rare quality in a game, even if some of them rub you the wrong way sometimes and some initially seem like joke characters. Their interactions with you and each other are very rich, and serve as one of the highlights of the game. Some get along better with others and certain hostilities may be present, and yet the team believably comes together and puts their differences aside for the sake of achieving their goal. Another set of characters that are well-developed is the social links, non-playable characters that you interact with in order to boost your stats (further explained in the gameplay section). These characters include classmates, after-school club members, and people you meet outside of school. Your interactions with each social link character forms a sub-plot, usually one involving supporting your friend in his or her struggle with a personal problem and helping him or her grow as a person. For instance, your classmate Kenji confides in you about his fascination with a teacher, and the social link has you supporting him and giving advice. Most of the social link stories are engaging and well-told, although you'll occasionally encounter annoying ones. The main character of Persona 3 is worth noting. You are prompted to name him at the very beginning of the game, with no official name provided. He has little back-story, other than he was orphaned roughly 10 years ago and that he has just moved back to his hometown of Iwatodai. He, like many of his peers in the genre, is a silent protagonist, only speaking when you, the player, are presented with a dialogue option. While I normally find silent protagonists to be unappealing and boring, I find this one to be very well-done and enjoyable to play as. The game is presented in such a way that it has you personally involved, and so the main character is supposed to be your avatar, perhaps the reason the developers haven't given him an official name. For all sakes and purposes, he's supposed to be you. You're presented with plenty of dialogue options and opportunities for social links that you feel like you're shaping your character, and the stoic and simplistic “every-man” design of the protagonist supports this structure. You'd truly be hard-pressed to find a better silent protagonist than this one. The Answer takes place 1-2 months after the end of The Journey. For the sake of avoiding spoilers, I won't mention any details. However, I will say that it offers some back-story for the members of SEES, and addresses a few questions left by the ending of The Journey. While not as involving or refined as The Journey, The Answer can still be interesting and entertaining. Score: 9/10 Gameplay: I should probably start this section by discussing what makes the Persona series unique among RPGs: the Social Link system. During most days, you'll spend time going to school and listening to lectures. After school, you're given the option to socialize with particular people, often classmates, club members, or acquaintances from outside of school. By talking to one of these characters, you'll spend time with him or her, during which he or she will discuss a problem of theirs and ask for your input. You're then prompted with dialogue choices, which affect the reaction of your friend and potentially earn you points towards your social link. If you earn enough points, your social link will level up. However, if you offend someone, your social link will reverse or break, thus making you need to patch things up before the social link will get back on track. The system is fairly similar to a dating simulator, for lack of a better comparison. However, instead of feeling out-of-place in an RPG, it offers a nice change in pace from combat. Some of the more entertaining aspects of the game is attempting to read the social links' characters and judge what to do or say. The purpose of working on social links is that it directly affects the growth and abilities of your personas. Each social link represents an arcana, a class of which personas that are divided into based on their stats, attributes, and abilities. Leveling up a particular social link will raise the effectiveness of the personas of the respective arcana, by offering additional experience points upon creating such a persona via fusion. For example, fellow club member Chihiro corresponds to the Justice arcana, which contains light-specialized personas. As you spend time with Chihiro and level up her social link, you'll notice that the Justice personas you create by fusion gain increasingly more EXP, allowing them to level up and learn new abilities. In addition, maxing out a social link will allow you to fuse the ultimate persona of the respective arcana. So while initially the social link system seems like a filler element and amusing diversion, it actually has a big impact on the combat aspect of the game and should not be neglected. My one gripe with social links is that they can become rather formulaic. While you may by tempted to answer questions honestly or give the most amusing answer, there is very often a “best” answer that you “should” choose if you want to level the social link up quickly. While this is understandable and makes reading your characters more engaging, there are some social links that can throw you off and are very unpredictable. The monk character is a good example, as misbehaving towards him by saying “None of your business.” actually gives more points than “I was with my friends.” As such, leveling up your social links can sometimes be marred by unexpected reactions or deviations from their normal personalities. Your character also has social stats, separate from his social link and battle stats. These are divided into three categories: Academics, Charm, and Courage. These stats are also raised after school or during the evenings, and mostly affect what social links you're able to access. To offer some examples, Academics can be raised by listening to a lecture rather than falling asleep or by studying at night, Charm is boosted by answering a question correctly during class or by drinking pheromone coffee at the mall, and Courage rises when watching particular movies at the theater or entering the horror house at the arcade. These aspects are fun to manage and offer a little more depth to the sometimes straightforward social links. Most nights, you can choose to visit Tartarus, which is where the traditional RPG side of the game takes place. Tartarus is essentially a very large dungeon, with floors that generate randomly each time you visit them. Each regular floor consists of Shadows, treasure chests, an access point which returns you to the first floor, and a staircase which takes you up to the next floor. Shadows will attack you if they see you in range, leading to a separate battle screen. Roughly every 10-15 floors, you'll happen upon a boss floor, which contains a checkpoint which can be accessed from the first floor and a boss awaiting you. Battles are turn-based, with your character always receiving the first turn. The actions you may perform are attack, use a skill from the currently equipped persona, switch personas (once per turn), use an item, assign tactics, wait, and escape. You only have full control over your character, and your party members are controlled via AI. You can issue commands to them such as “Act Freely”, “Heal/Support”, or “Stand By”, and generally they do a good job following orders. However, sometimes the AI can “misbehave”, for lack of a better word, healing only one ally when most of your party is down and you could use a cure-all spell. Another unfortunate feature of the game is that the game ends if the protagonist is knocked out, which erases all progress, personas, and rare items earned since your last save, which can be very frustrating. Magic is split into the elements of fire, ice, electricity, wind, light, and dark. Most enemies and personas have weaknesses that can be exploited to deal extra damage. Elements are not necessarily opposed in the traditional way that you'd imagine, such as a persona being weak against fire being strong against ice. An interesting feature is that physical attacks also have “elements”, as the three types of physical attacks are slash, strike, and pierce. Enemies and personas can also be weak or strong against specific types of these attacks. What makes Persona 3's battles especially interesting is the way that the weakness system works. Using an element that an enemy is weak against, or happening to land a critical hit, deals extra damage, as expected in many RPGs. However, doing so also knocks an enemy down, which leaves it unable to dodge, less resistant to damage, and unable to act on its next turn due to having to get back up. More interestingly, you are also granted one more turn which you can use to perform another action, including exploiting another weakness to get yet another turn. When all enemies are knocked down, you and any other available party members are able to perform an all-out attack, which deals a very large amount of damage to all enemies, often ending the battle. As such, the objective of your battles is almost always setting up an all-out attack, which is a fun and creative way to do battle. Managing personas plays a large part in your effectiveness during battle. Personas can sometimes be acquired after battles, but the main way of obtaining useful personas is through persona fusion. By selecting two or more personas, you can receive another with some of the previous abilities carried over. If you've leveled up a corresponding social link, your fused persona will gain experience points which it can use to level up, learning a good portion of its abilities. Since personas have different strengths and weaknesses, making sure you have a collection of personas that suits your needs is a must, especially against bosses. Bosses are generally overcome using an appropriate persona and some strategy as opposed to having high levels and grinding, which makes persona management necessary. Most bosses can be very rewarding, as they can be initially hard they are then found to be relatively easy using a good persona and smart use of tactics. What can be problematic is figuring out the abilities a boss uses and what elements its attacks fall under, and you may also not know how to fuse a persona that voids its major attacks. This can unfortunately make you dependent on online guides, persona lists, or bestiaries to prepare for battle. The Answer's gameplay consists of mostly dungeon crawling, with bosses appearing every few floors as in the main game. Sadly, a good number of features that were present in the main game are missing here, including social links, leveling up personas through fusion, special fusion options, and more. Thus, The Answer really just has you tediously fighting through battles to watch a simple scene, which is usually more difficult to do due to personas being harder to come by. On the other hand, there are some bosses which can be challenging, and may be worth the time invested for some dedicated fans. As such, I might recommend skipping The Answer altogether (since you can watch the scenes online), depending on the person. Score: 9/10 Visuals: From a technical standpoint, Persona 3 is decent. At first you may be put off by the character or environmental models, as they look very much like they came from an old version of The Sims or an online Flash game. This becomes especially obvious during victory poses after battle. For a late-end PS2 game, it's reasonable to assume it would have offered slightly better models. However, the models' appearances don't detract from the game at all, and do their job just fine. On the contrary; there's something about the graphics that actually make them look fine and natural on an HDTV, something few PS2 games are able to achieve. Occasionally, you'll be treated to an anime-style cutscene. While the characters look somewhat different in these, the scenes are interesting in that they offers more cinematic viewing angles and dramatize certain events. What you'll be spending much more time looking at are the character portraits, which are superb. While hardly animated compared to similarly-styled games such as the Ace Attorney series, there's barely any need for animation, as the portraits will change between text boxes to reflect changes in mood. Aside from looking great, the portraits do an excellent job of exhibiting the characters' demeanors and expressions. The more extroverted characters such as Yukari and Junpei have a wide range of portraits, while more reserved characters like Mitsuru and Akihiko have a relative few. However, each character has enough to portray their character perfectly, and each characters portraits all seem appropriate and fitting. The game also features a wide array of outfits for each character, and so each character has roughly 5-10 outfits to wear as opposed to the 1-2 usually given to RPG characters. These will differ depending on the day of the week, season, special occasion, or whether in Tartarus. The outfits serve to not only freshen things up visually, but give a sense of the passage of time and the significance of certain events. The environments in the game are diverse and well designed. Among the venues to explore are your high school, a mall, a few monorail stations, a strip mall, a shrine, and your dorm. Most places are simple, but believable and adequately detailed. Many of the restaurants and attractions draw from Japanese culture and give the game an interesting vibe. Unfortunately, though you have many areas to visit, you'll find yourself seeing the same places over and over throughout the game, which gets a little repetitive. Many of the outdoor locations will change with the passage of time, such as leaves changing with the passing of the seasons, so the repetitiveness is somewhat combated. The far greater offender in this category is Tartarus. Tartarus is split into several blocks, roughly containing 30-50 blocks each, each having its own theme and design. Each block features rooms and halls of usually a single color, often with blood-colored liquid running on the floor. Understandably, since the rooms are randomly generated, the floors all end up very two-dimensional, even with the addition of a few modifications such as staircases and raised sections. By far the worst visual element of the game is Tartarus's fifth block, which not only camouflages Shadows at times but also happens to be a complete eyesore. On the whole though, I would say the repetitiveness of Tartarus is tolerable, if regrettable. The hundreds of personas that you can acquire are all very well-presented. Aside from make brief appearances as 3D models during battle, you'll mostly see portraits of them in menus or during fusion. The names and looks of the personas draw from many varied mythological figures, including Ancient Greek, Egyptian, Hindu, and more. The representations are fairly accurate to lore and are interesting to behold. Score: 8/10 Audio: The sound effects in the game do their job and are fairly good. Door knocking and sliding doors sound accurate, fire spells sound like fire, and electricity spells have a distinct buzz or thunderous boom. The sounds certainly aren't the most realistic ones you've heard, but they fit in well with the game's visual theme and graphical style. The voice acting in the game is mostly great. There are some well-known actors in this game, such as Yuri Lowenthal, Michelle Ruff, and Vic Mignogna, and they all do excellent jobs as their respective characters. However, there are a few characters that aren't as well-done, such as that of your support character. Even then though, the voice acting is passable and shouldn't be too annoying. Voices will appear to narrate story-related text boxes, during anime-style cutscenes, or during battle, with most day-to-day banter left unnarrated. Voices thus serve to punctuate important parts of the story and add more emotion to them, fulfilling their purpose well. The music is very good, for the most part. Many of the background tracks you'll be hearing throughout the city consist of J-pop, J-rock, J-rap, and techno tracks. Lots of these are very catchy and ones you might find stuck in your head after a while, in a good way. Unfortunately, there are a couple of tracks that are very cringe-worthy and will have you reaching for the mute button. The tracks also sadly don't switch up very often, as you'll hear the same song at the dorm or at the mall for most of the game, though the school's theme does switch up every semester. The biggest offender is again Tartarus, which has the same theme for almost all of its floors, though it is remixed slightly for each block. Thankfully though, you're given the option roughly 20% through the game to change the Tartarus music to one of a few preset tracks. Score: 8/10 Value: My first time through The Journey took me approximately 90 hours, including times when I lost progress through game overs in Tartarus. You're then given the ability to play on a new game plus, retaining your character's level, persona compendium, equipment, and more. There's also the inclusion of extra difficulty modes which can easily tempt you to put in another playthrough. Other incentives to play again are to attempt to max out all social links and complete all sidequests, including one which unlocks on a new game plus. The Answer consumed about 30 hours of my time, thus bringing my total first playthrough time to roughly 120 hours. Aside from feeling that the story lags sometimes, The Journey is gripping and exciting and won't leave you impatiently waiting to get done with it. The Answer is best reserved for fans who genuinely liked the battle system, or would rather not watch the story segments online. However, when seen as an expansion or an analog to the present's DLC, The Answer is certainly much more worthy of your time then most of what you can find today. With a price tag of $10, this game is an absolute steal, considering the sheer amount of content and time for a first playthrough and its high replayability. The only game I've ever bought at that price that can even compare to the excellence of Persona 3 is Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. Score: 10/10 Summary: Pros: + Simple yet engaging story. + Excellent cast of characters. + Fun, fresh social link system. + Thrilling, unique battle system. + Wonderful character portraits. + Catchy soundtrack. + Enormous value. Cons: - Slow pace. - Main character getting knocked out can be frustrating. - Repetitive environments and music. Overall, I would fully recommend this game to any JRPG fan with an itch for either something traditional or a different take on the genre. For such a low price, I would even recommend the game to someone curious as to what the hype for the genre is all about. I rank this game among the top JRPGs I've ever played, and now fully look forward to playing the sequel: Persona 4 Golden. Don't overlook Persona 3 FES simply it was on a last-generation console; you owe that to yourself.

author: Exodist
review_title: A classic modern JRPG.
review_text: In a time when JRPGs were starting to become somewhat stale (with a few exceptions of course) comes the Persona series. A spin-off of the popular Shin Megami Tensei series (in Japan at least), Persona started with two games in the 90s then disappeared for a few years. Persona 3 made its way into Japan in 2006 and subsequently the West also with the updated edition, FES, which includes a bonus expansion to the game in order to finish up the story, featuring a more bare bones offering of what the full game has. Persona 3 is certainly very unique when it comes to JRPGs and has definitely shaken things up, along with setting a new standard for the modern JRPG. From the get go, with its long introduction and cut-scenes, Persona 3 is a game about delivering a great, dark and mature storyline. The game has plenty of exposition in order to set things up: who you are, why you're here, and what exactly is going on. The game, although taking a while to actually get into the full swing of things, doesn't take long to start the story up. You play as a nameless protagonist (its up to you) who transfers to a school in a modern city atop an artificial island. You reach your dorm where you find things aren't quite what they seem. As it turns out, the city falls under the curse of the dark hour, an hour between days where everyone turns into a coffin. Everyone except a select few, including you of course. During this time shadows – evil creatures – wander the streets, and prey on those not lucky enough to turn into the coffins, leaving them in a catatonic state in the real world. This is dubbed as 'apathy syndrome' and its up to SEES, a group of teenagers who live at the same dorm as you to explore Tartarus, a strange tower that appears at Gekkoukan High during the dark hour, find the source of the shadows, and save the people of the city. To do this, you fight physically, and also with Persona, manifestations of your personal being that can be controlled to fight. The story, although sometimes sparse, is entertaining and intriguing during the entire game. The game is split into actual days and weeks where you must schedule your life. Every Full Moon SEES perform an operation to fight a large shadow (ie the bosses of the game). Its on these nights that the story usually advances, however this isn't always the case. Although the game has plenty of other events and cut-scenes featuring the characters, the game can sometimes go for months and barely advance the actual story line of the game. It can be frustrating at times, however usually each time the story does progress it ends up being worth it, however don't expect new plot lines to be developing constantly. Its a bit of a slow game in that sense, although the aforementioned character cut-scenes are usually good and help build the characters and just provide general humour for the game. The ending was particularly surprising in that the whole thing was set up really well. The last boss fight is very cliched and is the same as Persona 4, and I imagine, will continue to be the same. Despite that, its only a minor flaw in a game which provides a dark and mature story full of surprising moments, great characters and character development at the expense of being a little slow at times. As mentioned, the game features an actual calender as you live out the average life of the Japanese teenager. From this, the game essentially has two major gameplay components: social simulator, and dungeon crawler. The social aspect of the game is probably what makes the game even better, although it can often depend upon the player. Persona is all about relationships. Its about people and their interactions with other people, what people mean to them, and what people can achieve together, be it by simply spending time together talking, solving each others problems, and venturing into a tower to fight evil shadows. The game lets you play every day as you wake up, go to school, then have time to do what you want for the afternoon. Your character has three primary stats: Courage, Knowledge, and Charm, each allowing you to do different things during social links (more on these soon) which can be improved by spending time doing things. You can go to the karaoke bar at night time to increase your courage, studying at night at the expense of sleeping early improves your knowledge, whilst drinking coffee in a shop increases charm. There are multiple ways of actually increasing these stats, and doing so spends your time, for example after school going to the library to study moves to night time. At night time you can visit the mall and do a few limited activities, or you can visit Tartarus. But without going into that, a major feature of the game are social links. After school you can choose to spend time with a number of NPCs found around the school and city. These social links are side stories in themselves, where you usually learn much more about this person as you spend time with them, eventually helping them overcome their troubles. These stories can range from interesting to not, however they don't take up a huge amount of time so even the bad stories won't feel like a huge waste of time. The more you hang out with these people, the more the social link levels up, going from 1-10 where upon you finish their story and can't see them again. You can go out with multiple people and ignore them for ages with no consequences, although 'dating' multiple girls can possibly be problematic. So you ask, this is all well and good, but what's the point of these social links? This is where the persona system comes in. Each of your party members have their own persona, they level up, learn spells automatically and thats it, you have no control and can't choose their spells, elements and so on. However, for the protagonist, you can equip any persona you find. A trademark of the Shin Megami Tensei series, you can own multiple persona and equip them on the fly in battle. Each persona is unique and will feature their own spells, weaknesses and strengths. What this means is that you can have multiple types of fighter on the same character, for example, you may have a fire persona, an ice one, a healing persona, a melee persona and so on. You can get persona by finding them after fights in a card shuffle (basically cards are shuffled, select the right one and get a persona). You can also visit the Velvet Room, a place where you can take side-quests, but more importantly, fuse persona. Two or more persona can be fused together in order to create a stronger persona, and this will be your main method of obtaining stronger persona through the game. Each persona has an affiliation to an arcana, which social links also do. If you fuse a persona, and its arcana is the same as a social link you have, the higher level social link you have, the more bonus EXP you receive upon fusion. This is practically essential in levelling some persona up later on as it can take quite a while to grind the EXP necessary for persona to level up just from battling. This means more often or not you'll want to get a good bonus for persona you fuse as you'll usually gain a lot of useful spells upon fusion. Its a fun system that is totally necessary to completion of the game; you HAVE to fuse persona otherwise you're gonna find life pretty tough. Despite this, even if you hit a dead end for a short while, as long as you have a good selection of spells, you won't be punished either for not having the absolute best persona at the time. Leading on from this is the dungeon crawling aspect of Persona 3. Tartarus is the only dungeon in the game featuring around 260 different floors. The tower is split into 6 different blocks, and within those blocks are smaller sections. When you visit Tartarus at night (you can visit on pretty much any night, although some characters are sometimes unavailable for certain points) you select your party and head in. The floors are randomly generated each time you visit. Floors consist of different rooms, corridors, mobs and treasure. You explore the floor, find the stairs, and move on. You can't go back down, and the only way to get back is via teleports that are scattered through the tower. When you get so high into the tower you will meet a road block, quite literally, meaning you can't go higher. When you get this far, you have to wait until you beat the next boss of the game in which case more floors will be unlocked. During the way you will find mini-bosses which provides a way of teleporting between the entrance and higher floors of the tower, and as, well, bosses to fight during your climb. The amount of floors between the next boss and blockage are usually completely manageable, meaning you have plenty of time to explore Tartarus and develop your characters. The main problem here though is that its not particularly interesting. Each block has its own aesthetic design, but due to the random nature of the floors, they all look completely bland and there isn't really anything to do. The dungeon crawling isn't the most interesting or original part of the game, but its well made. What does make the game fun however is the interesting and challenging battle system. There are a few major gripes with the system however: you get game over if your main character dies (an alarmingly common occurrence in JRPGs these days) and you cannot control your party members. The system is turn based, you make your turn, then sit and wait until all your allies and enemies have taken turns. The setup is pretty standard, you can attack, use a spell, item, run or change your persona. However you can also set tactics for your allies, ranging from conserving SP (Persona's MP), attacking all out or being a healer and support. This said, the AI for your party members is generally very good. During battle, you can scan your enemy for free by pressing L1 and selecting them. When you do this, you learn their strengths and weaknesses after a few turns. Once this is done, your allies will know too meaning the AI will exploit weaknesses or act accordingly. This said, its frustrating when you know what an enemies weakness is prior to the fight but you haven't 'officially' learnt it, meaning your allies end up healing them (for example second tries on bosses). Your allies will also learn through experimentation, if they use fire on an enemy and it absorbs it, they know not to use it again. Sometimes they will screw you over (one character, Koromaru, never did what I wanted so I ditched him) but for the most part it works. The elements are a major point of winning battles in Persona. Where as in a lot of RPGs the enemies have weaknesses and you do extra damage, its never really a core system like it is here. If you strike an enemy with their weakness they will fall down, also granting you an extra turn. If every enemy in the fight is knocked down, you get to rush them, dealing huge damage. This is essential to clearing fights and lasting longer in Tartarus by winning fights faster and efficiently. This means you can exploit enemy weakness one by one on each enemy, or use a multi target spell in order to get a rush. The flip side is, your characters also have weaknesses. Your characters can also be knocked down, meaning they miss a turn, and the enemies also gain an extra turn. It makes bosses challenging not only in their attacks but by protecting your characters and taking the right ones along. Fortunately, the game does not require you to level everyone as through the whole game apart from a few select instances, you have complete control over who you use. Unless you want to spend a huge amount of time grinding, I recommend using the same few characters. You can equip their gear (which is incredibly tedious, you have to talk to them individually to do this, you can't see their status through the normal menu) and thats pretty much it, apart from that, you're using them for your spells. In the end, the battle system, whilst again not original, is extremely well made and the most fun aspect of the game. Fights can be challenging and interesting, and the dynamic of your persona selection makes it more interesting. Fortunately in Persona 4, issues were fixed where you can control your party members, and your party members will also take death blows for you and so on, making your time easier. The FES portion of the game, also titled 'The Answer' is unlocked immediately from the beginning, but takes place after the main game is finished. This scenario however is much more bare bones and shorter, consisting entirely of dungeon crawling and story and no social links or day to day activities. It's a fun extension to the game, although the story ends pretty well on the base game so playing this extra scenario for a continuation of the story isn't absolutely necessary. However, for those yearning for more gameplay after finishing the game, it's all here. The graphics of the game consist of the typical Japanese anime style seen in a lot of JRPGs, and it works wonderfully. The characters all look fairly realistic, whilst at the same time totally being anime like. The game presents these characters through anime style portraits, whilst a few of the games cut-scenes are actually animated. The setting itself is also completely Japanese and gives a certain air of authenticity to the game, which also has to do with the excellent translation job. Persona 3 is set in Japan and they haven't changed this: no changes to setting, to the names or the holidays featured in the game. The voice acting in the game ranges from decent to annoying, for example Ken's voice is absolutely grating and Fuuka can be a little annoying. Characters like Junpei and Yukari have great voice work though, along with Aigis, one of my personal favourite characters. The music is one of the best soundtracks I have heard in a game for a long time. Composed by Shoji Meguro, listening to this and the Persona 4 sound track, I'm convinced this guy is a genius. Consisting of a huge mix of tunes, the game features a pretty stylish soundtrack with loads of vocal work, something not particularly common for a game. Its extremely pop orientated, however most people seem to love the music to these games and its easy to see why. It may not be for everyone, but those who do enjoy it will agree its one of the best around at the moment. Persona 3 is a game packed full of content and plenty of different mechanics. Taking around 70 hours to finish, the game has great characters and character developing, an interesting if not slow plot, a great social simulator, good dungeon crawling, a great battle system and excellent production values. If you don't like JRPGs, this probably still isn't for you. The RPG mechanics are pretty purist and although nothing original, are done to near perfection offering a game that will be familiar to fans of the genre, but also so different in many ways, it will be a complete breath of fresh air to those who haven't experienced the Persona series. For those who are looking at quite possibly the best JRPG series available right now, Persona 3 or even better, Persona 4, are the best choices right now.

author: Bkstunt_31
review_title: Don't be afraid to pull the trigger...
review_text: While there are a ton of games that have you saving the world from demons, not many games have you doing it while still in high school. But than there is Atlus's famous Shin Megami Tensei, where even students seem to be able to control demons in battle. Persona 3 is no exception, and while it's now been out for quite awhile, I only recently got a chance to play through it. But since it has been out for awhile, there's a good chance you may see it while rummaging around your favorite game store's bargain bin. Well, is it worth buying? Here's what I thought of Persona 3: Story: 8/10 You star as a nameless, silent protagonist, who has transferred to Gekkoukan High School. Early in the game, you learn of the Dark Hour, a time of day that starts at midnight where most of the city's citizens become encased in coffins, unable to act or do anything. This Dark Hour is home to monsters known collectively as shadows. However, not everyone is disabled during the Dark Hour, specifically people who have learned how to control their Persona's. A Persona is oftentimes described as a person's other self, buried deep inside their soul. To protect themselves from the shadows, Persona users summon their Persona's by using an evoker, a device that looks like a gun and is used by firing it at your head. Shadows prey on people during the Dark Hour, leaving them in a zombie-like state after-wards. The protagonist soon discovers his ability and joins a team of other students with similar abilities soon after-wards to look for a way to stop the attacks. As you may already tell with the evokers, the game has many, many dark undertones and overtones. Persona 3 isn't afraid to shy away from any issue, and you can explore several interesting issues and characters in the game's many side-stories (which they call Social Links, more on that later). These side stories are fleshed out extraordinarily well, and often require that you spend time with certain individuals throughout the school year. The game's main story is paced throughout the school year as well, and slowly reveals the cause and consequence of the shadows, as well as a nice chunk of each characters back-stories and motivation for fighting. Overall, the story is entertaining, but due to the pacing, the main and side-stories may or may not become stagnant depending on how you play. Game play: 7/10 The game is a mixture between the players high school life and fighting against the shadows, making it essentially a simulator/RPG hybrid. During the day you'll go to school and have the chance to interact with several acquaintances, forming social links that you can level up from 1 through 10. Each social link has its own side story and is associated with their own arcana (from the tarot deck). You get to choose your own replies when you talk to people which can either progress your relationships (level up) or hurt them. You'll also be able to work on your own personal traits during or after school, such as courage, charm, and intelligence. In fact, many social links can only start once you reach a certain stat personally. Just to give you an idea of how the game plays, you'll go through an entire school year, day by day, with many different pre-scripted events taking place on certain days. You'll get a chance almost every day to work on your social links and personal traits, as well as go to town and shop. Each thing you do (besides shopping) will take up your afternoon or late-night time, at which point you'll go to bed and repeat the cycle. However, you'll also have to fight against the shadows. During the Dark Hour a giant tower-like structure called Tartarus will appear where Gekkoukan High School is, filled to the brim with shadows. During the course of any day, you can choose to go explore Tartarus with your team members (exploring the tower takes up the rest of the night). In the tower, you view all of your team members in a third person perspective as you explore a randomly generated floor in the tower. On the floor you can find treasure, a device to take you back to the bottom, a staircase to the next floor, and of course, monsters! The monsters wander around aimlessly (they all look like blob-like shadows), so if you can try to hit them from behind you'll get in a preemptive attack. Fighting is fairly simple, for starters you will only control your main character, as your teammates are controlled by the game's AI. You can assign them different tasks, though, such as focus on healing or focus on this particular target. since you have multiple allies you'll have to choose which of them joins you in exploring, and since each of them has their own strengths and weaknesses you'll have to choose wisely. Of course, the shadows each have different weaknesses, such as a certain type of magic or physical attack that they are weak to. You can find out their weaknesses by scanning them and than even your AI teammates will exploit them. Each of your allies will also use their Persona's, usually when they fell like it or when they know they can do an attack the enemy is weak against, but the main character is special. You see, you can control multiple Persona's with your main character and switch between them on each one of your turns. So essentially, you can use every special Persona attack in the game. You can also cover every weakness in the game as well, since Persona's are very similar to the shadows in that they each have their own strengths and weaknesses. Attacking the shadow's weakness results in a "once more" attack, which is a free attack for whoever attacked the weakness. Plus, the shadow will fall down and will have to wait a turn to get back up. If you manage to get all the shadows to fall down, you can than do a massive group attack on the enemy. Often times the same enemy is grouped together, so you could cast bufu (an ice spell) on each enemy, knock them all down, and than attack them all for a quick win. Winning will result in experience and will randomly let you play a shuffle game where you can win weapons, money, boosted experience, or a new Persona. Near the beginning of the game, due to your special ability to control multiple Persona's, you'll gamin access to the velvet room, a special place between dreams and reality where a mysterious man named Igor will assist you in your new skill. Here you can join different Persona's together and create new Persona's. These new Persona's will also learn skills from their "parents", giving you some control in customizing your Persona's. You can also record old Persona's in a database and recall them for use later (for a fee). Also, to give your outside life more weight, when you fuse a new Persona, it will gain power based upon your social links. For example, if you fuse a Persona whose arcana is the magician, it will gain additional experience based upon your friendship with Kenji, a kid in your class. Persona fused like this are able to be a higher level than the main character even, resulting in some powerful combination's. Overall, the game play is rather unique. The social elements are addicting and even useful, and the amount of Persona's you can control is impressive. The game falters, though, at the repetition it presents while climbing Tartarus. After playing around in Tartarus for a few hours, you will have seen about all the game has to offer in its combat system. In fact once you learn what spells are what (because of the unique names, such as bufu=ice), the entire key to winning is scanning the enemy and hitting their weaknesses. Boss fights scattered throughout the School year and Tartarus give a nice strategical break, but the repetition is definitely noticeable. Nonetheless, thanks to the myriad of awards and different Persona's to obtain, I greatly enjoyed my time with Persona 3, even while climbing Tartarus. Graphics: 7/10 The graphics in the game are quite good, taking on a distinctive anime look. The backdrop of the game is, primarily, centered around Gekkoukan High School and the dorms, but you can go visit a few train stations, the mall, and a local shrine as well, all of which do their best to look like a typical medium-sized Japanese city (I've never been to Japan, but it looks rather convincing to me). Where you can explore is rather limited, though, since you travel between these places from a world map and absolutely no other places open up. Character designs were extraordinarily well done; I enjoyed all of the different character designs as well as the enemies. Common enemy designs fall into the dreaded trap of the infamous palate swap, though, often including the same weaknesses and strengths even (lame). Animations were well done, even though they are rather limited in the amount of actual 3D animations and make great use of text boxes combined with portraits. In short, the game features a limited amount of well done locales and characters with an anime feel. Music/Sound effects: 8/10 "Unique" is the first word I would say about the music throughout the game. The opening cut scene starts off with a bang, featuring fresh jazz beats mixed with fast-paced rap. After you hit the main menu, you'll be treated to one of the best piano-only music pieces I've heard in a video game. Yes, you really go between rapping and piano solos that fast. Unique. The rest of the game mixes in more rapping with mood pieces and other catchy unique beats. Most of these pieces play whenever you're in a certain area, whether it is around town or in Tartarus. In fact as a bonus, while you're in Tartarus you can ask one of your teammates to change the background music (you can choose between four different tracks, make sure to listen to number 2 for awhile, it's fantastic). Sound effects are also well done. The game features quite a bit of voice acting, mostly restricted to your team mates in the game's various cut scenes and in battle. I particularly enjoyed the various comments your team mates would make in battle, but since they only have one or two comments for each special thing they do, you'll quickly be listening to the same things over and over. In fact, that's the theme to Persona's music is how repetitive it is. While that is generally not a desirable trait, at least the music is awesome. Re-playability: 8/10 First off, let me say that this is a review for Persona 3:FES. That "FES" part on there differentiates between the regular Persona 3 game and this new updated version, which features a whole new sequel to Persona 3. FES divides the game into "The Journey" which is an updated version of Persona 3, and "The Answer", which is the add-on game. So when you get the FES version, you're also getting an entirely new sequel as well as Persona 3. Let's go over the re-playability option of Persona 3 first. Once you beat "The Journey", you'll have the choice to start a "New game +". If you noticed from the game play section, your time with Persona 3 is limited to one school year, so you may not accomplish everything you wanted to. When you start a new game, you will first of all keep all of your personal development (such as courage, charm, etc.). You will lose all of your social links, but you will get to keep the items you get from them when you max them. You'll also get to keep your Persona compendium and most of your equipment and items. You will start over at level one, though. It's tempting to start a new game this way because you'll have a lot more free time to focus on maxing every social link and you'll already have access to your old Persona's once you can afford them. "The Answer" provides a more fleshed out epilogue to the main story. In it you control the team (and one new team member) as they explore a Tartarus like area under the dorm. For the most part, that's all "The Answer" is about. There are no more simulation parts to the game, it's just one big dungeon filled with tougher enemies that you have to fight through with story scattered in between. There is a lot to come back to in Persona 3: FES, if you're willing to put the time into it. Playing a new game is definitely the best way to complete the harder quests and acquire the best Persona's though (the rewards and abilities you'll get are awesome). I wasn't too impressed by "The Answer" as I was looking for a bit more than just more battles and the follow-on story just wasn't able to hook me. Overall: 8/10 Persona, as a series, definitely isn't for everyone (it's more for us RPG fans). But if you're looking for a new RPG to play through, it's hard to go wrong with Persona. The battles can get repetitive and stale, but the Persona fusion systems and the social simulations are very addictive. The game is definitely worth a buy, as I have recently seen the FES version in the bargain bin at a local game store for under ten dollars. Have fun and keep playing.

author: Indignation211
review_title: A must-have game for any hardcore JRPG fan at an unbeatable price!
review_text: Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 3 is the third installment of the Persona series, a sub-series of the Megami Tensei series. This review covers the “FES” version of Persona 3. This version of the game includes the entire original game, known as “The Journey”, with enhanced features, as well as a new chapter called “The Answer”. This review will primarily cover “The Journey” and will have a separate section for “The Answer” near the end. Story The story centers around the Main Character (who you can name whatever you want), a transfer student to the prestigious Gekkoukan High School in Japan. Soon after his arrival in the city of Iwatodai, he experiences a hidden period of time known as the Dark Hour, a time when normal people turn into coffins, blood appears everywhere, everything electronic shuts off, and monsters known as Shadows feed off of the minds of humans. Plus, his school turns into a monstrous tower! In order to survive and solve the mystery of the Dark Hour, he joins a secret school club known as the Specialized Extracirricular Execution Squad and unleashes his hidden power: Persona. During the day, the members of SEES live the life of ordinary high school students. But when the Dark Hour comes, they are heroes with supernatural powers dedicated to defeating the Dark Hour. The story is pretty interesting, though it (like the rest of the game) becomes kinda boring by the late-middle part of the game. However, soon after it becomes boring it picks up again and hooks you until the end. The social links are also interesting and do a fairly good job of tiding you over until the next main story development. Gameplay When you first start the journey you asked to decide on what difficulty you would like to play the game. Your choices are Normal, Easy, and Hard. Normal is the standard difficulty setting. Easy is like Normal except you get up to ten “continues”. Hard is exclusive to the FES version and causes the enemy’s attacks to deal more damage, making battles more challenging than Normal. In addition, If you have a save file from the original version of Persona 3, you can import certain data from that file into your new game. This is especially helpful for those who want the benefits of New Game + without having the challenge sucked out from being overleveled. Of course, you can only do this if you owned the original version. The Journey is comprised of two different but connected gameplay types – a day-to-day dating sim and a dungeon-crawling RPG. The very first thing the game tells you is that you have one year to save the world. From your first day of school in April, you will live the day-to-day life of a high school student . Each day is divided into several time periods, though most of your activity will take place during the Daytime (or After School on school days) and Evening. During the day, you can explore the various places surrounding your Dorm and Gekkoukan High. When you do a significant activity such as eating at a restaurant or participating in a club the time will advance to Evening. Your options are more limited in the Evening but there is still plenty to do. After the Evening ends you will have the option to study before going to bed and starting the next day. There are two primary things to do during each day: improving your social stats and your social links. The Main Character has three social stats: Charm, Courage, and Academics, which improve when you do certain things. Staying awake during lectures increases Academics while watching a scary movie increases your Courage. When you perform enough actions toward a social stat its rank will increase, until it is maxed at rank 6. As you talk to different people you will become friends with some of them, establishing a “Social Link”. As you hang out with these people, the Social Links will improve as your relationship with those people grows (some might even become your girlfriend!), until the Link is maxed and you have forged an unbreakable bond with that person. Some Links will improve automatically at certain points in the game, but most require you to hang out with a specific person. Each person has their own story and issues, and you will often be prompted to say something to them. If the person favors your response, you will have an easier time reaching the next level of the link. On the other hand, if you do something to make that person angry at you, the link will Reverse or even Break, and you will have to make up with him or her later to repair the link. As you improve your social links you will discover more potential links, some of which require you to have a certain rank in one of your social stats before you can start it. There are twenty-two potential Social Links in the FES version, and it is possible to max out all of them on your first playthrough, but doing so requires following a strict schedule that kinda takes some of the fun out of the game. Now, becoming the most popular guy at school is great and all, but don’t forget that its your job to save the world, and to do that you have to battle Shadows during the Dark Hour. During the Evening, instead of going out at night, you can choose to go to Tartarus, a massive tower crawling with Shadows. Your goal on each floor in Tartarus is to find a staircase that will take you to the next floor. Along the way you will fight Shadows and collect treasure. You can initiate a battle by attacking a wandering shadow: attacking it before it notices you grants you Player Advantage (you get one full turn before the enemy), while being attacked by a Shadow gives Enemy Advantage (enemies move before you do). However, if you spend too much time on a single floor, you will be attacked by an incredibly powerful Shadow called “The Reaper”. In addition, after every few floors you clear you will reach a Boss floor, where you will have to defeat the Boss to proceed further into Tartarus. Each Boss floor also acts as a “checkpoint” from where you can start your next run. In addition to the Bosses, there are barriers at specific points in Tartarus that prevent you from going any higher until you have reached a specific date on the calendar, so don’t expect to clear this monstrosity of a tower on the first day. Also, after fighting a certain number of battles in one day, your characters will become tired, reducing their combat effectiveness, and your allies will automatically leave upon returning to the entrance of Tartarus if they’re tired (unless it’s the night before a full moon). The number of battles you can fight before becoming tired increases as you level up, so while it is annoying in the early game, it is rarely an issue in the late game. In order to get through the game you will need to devote a small number of evenings to Tartarus but not too much that you exhaust yourself so much that you can’t work on your social life. However, you also need to make sure that you do spend enough time leveling up in Tartarus. When you look at the calendar you will notice it not only tracks the date but also the number of days until the next full moon. This is important because you will automatically fight a boss on the night of every full moon, and you must defeat it in order to advance the calendar and the story. Fortunately, the full moon bosses are generally less challenging than their Tartarus counterparts, so if you keep up with Tartarus you should do fine during the full moons. Battles in Persona 3 are turn-based and are similar to most other turn-based RPGs. Each character’s life is measured in HP (Hit Points), and if their HP is reduced to zero, they are unable to fight. However, if the Main Character’s HP is ever reduced to zero, its GAME OVER! To fight your enemies, you can use a basic attack or consume your character’s SP (Spirit Points) to use a skill, or you can use items. However, there are plenty of differences in Persona’s system that set it apart from, say, Final Fantasy. First, you do not directly control your allies. Instead, you give them general orders like “Heal/Support” or “Full Assault” and their AI acts accordingly. Second, while the Main Character’s max HP and SP is based on his level, his other stats as well as the skills he can use are based on his equipped Persona. The Main Character can have several Personas with him at any given time, and can switch his equipped Persona mid-battle to meet the situation. This also makes the Main Character more powerful than his allies, who only have one persona each and thus only one skill set. Every offensive attack in the game is tied to one of ten attributes: Slash, Strike, Pierce, Fire, Ice, Elec, Wind, Light, Dark, and Almighty. The key to victory in Persona 3 is to exploit your enemy’s weaknesses. If you hit an enemy with an attack that it is weak against or score a critical hit, it will be knocked down, causing it to lose its next turn while at the same time granting the attacker an extra action. If the attacker then knocks down another enemy, he will gain yet another action and can keep this up as long as he keeps knocking down enemies. However, exploiting an enemy who is already down will not grant an extra action. In fact, attacking an enemy that’s already down causes it to get back up and regain its next turn. The catch is that this works both ways, enemies can also exploit your weaknesses, knock you down, and gain extra actions as well. However, the player has a special advantage, since if you knock down all enemies, you will be able to unleash an “All-Out Attack” which deals heavy damage to all enemies. Of course, in order to effectively exploit your enemy’s weaknesses you have to know what they are first. Fortunately, you can scan your enemies to learn their strengths and weaknesses so you can plan your attack accordingly. Scanning enemies also causes your allies to stop using attacks that the enemy is resistant to. The first time you scan an enemy it will take several actions before the results are displayed, but after that it is instantaneous. Scanning also does not take up an action, so its important to do it often. The catch is that when you scan most bosses, you will NOT be able to see their weaknesses or resistances, but your allies will and will act accordingly, so if you scan a boss and Yukari stops casting Wind spells, chances are that boss is resistant to wind. At the end of battle your characters gain experience and may Level Up, increasing their stats. Note that only the Main Character’s HP and SP increase when he levels up. Also, you might be presented with a mini-game called Shuffle Time! In this mini-game you are presented with several cards, each of which represents a specific type of reward. The cards then flip face-down and shuffle across the screen. You then pick a card and gain its reward. Rewards range from money to bonus experience to new Personas. There are some twists to it, like Double Up, which allows you to pick a second reward at the risk of not getting any reward at all, and cursed cards, which causes the Reaper to come after you much sooner than normal. Of course, this game is called “Persona” for a reason, and that reason is that you must acquire as many Personas as possible to succeed in your quest. There are 170 Personas in the FES version, each with different stats, elemental affinities, and skills. While you can acquire some Personas as rewards after battle, your main method of getting new personas is by fusing your existing personas together in the “Velvet Room”. The fusion system is pretty deep and there is much you can do with it, but you don’t need to go too deep into it to get through the game. The primary restriction to fusion is that you can only create personas whose base level is equal to or lower than the Main Character’s level. As your characters gain EXP, so does your equipped Persona, and if it gains enough it will level up, which causes one or more of its stats to increase and possibly learn a new skill. Persona fusion is also where the day-to-day aspect of the game meets the battle aspect. Each persona is tied to one of twenty-two groups, called “Arcana”. In addition, each Social Link is also tied to one of those same Arcana. When you create a persona of an Arcana in which you have established the corresponding Social Link, the new persona will immediately gain experience and level up upon creation. Also, the highest-level Persona of each Arcana can only be created once you have maxed the corresponding Social Link, so it is important to spend plenty of time on your Social Links during your day-to-day activities to power up your Persona. Thankfully, you can never permanently lose a Persona, as every Persona you acquire is recorded in the “Persona compendium”, from which you can summon any Persona you previously possessed… for a price. It should be noted that, on Hard mode, the price for summoning Personas out of the compendium is 4x that of Normal mode. Difficulty The battle aspect of the game, in my opinion, isn’t that difficult (most of the time). As long as the enemy has some type of weakness, its pretty easy. Most normal battles will be as follows: Player Advantage => Knock Down all enemies => All Out Attack => Shuffle Time, whereas bosses that have weaknesses can be very easy by just keeping them knocked down. Bosses that don’t have weaknesses are a different story, and there are several such bosses that have proven to be ‘headaches’ for many players. And of course, The Reaper, the final boss, and the ultimate boss are all plenty challenging. Perhaps the most diffucult aspect of the battles is making sure the Main Character never gets killed. There are plenty of ways to keep his HP up, but if an enemy manages to knock him down and follow up with another powerful attack, you could very well get a Game Over. Of course, it gets more difficult in Hard mode. Especially if you follow the formula above, there really isnt much change to the normal battles. Bosses, however, become significantly more challenging, since their attacks become near-lethal at best and all it takes is one unlucky critical hit on the Main Character to force a Game Over. Graphics The graphics in the game, while not spectacular, are good and they get the job done. The game is entirely 3-D. All of the character models look decent. The environments are pretty good but the interior of Tartarus, while not bad, is kinda lazy, though this could be necessary for a dungeon that’s entirely random. There are also CG portraits of all of the important characters which show whenever they are talking, and they are all well drawn and look good. In addition, there are several anime cutscenes which play during very important story sequences, these cutscenes are well animated and do a good job of spicing up the presentation of the story. Sound The sound overall is pretty good. The English voice acting does a good job and fits each character well. Unfortunately, the game does not include Japanese audio on the same disk (I understand an undub version was also sold for the original game, though this might not be true for the FES version) but the English voices satisfied me. Also I really like the music, especially the battle themes. Granted, the normal battle theme is a bit unusual, but I love all of the others. The first school music and last Tartarus tracks are also on my playlist of favorites. And of course, there’s “Burn My Dread” and “Kimi no Kioku”, the game’s opening and ending songs. I would buy the Persona 3 OST and the Burn My Dread: Reincarnation soundtracks just for these. Play Time/Replayability The box is not kidding when it says 70+ hours. This game is LONG! The drawback to this is that, separately, the day-to-day and Tartarus aspects of the game are quite repetitive. Fortunately, the fact that you alternate between them does break up and refresh the game a bit, but this doesn’t stop the game from becoming a bit boring around the late-middle part of the game. The good news is, once you reach this point, that very soon the story will pick up and renew your interest and keep you hooked through the end. Once you finally conquer your first playthrough, you have the option of New Game +, which starts the game over but carries over your social stats, persona compendium, items, and max S.Link items (which allow you to fuse those ultimate Personas). You can try maxing the remaining S.Links or perhaps even all of them (which is easier to do on New Game + since your social stats carry over). However, the fact that your level and compendium carries over sucks the challenge out of the new playthrough. The secret “ultimate boss” can only be fought on a New Game +, however, so you will need those Uber Personas to have any chance at winning that battle. If you seriously want to play this game again, I would recommend starting fresh, especially if you want to genuinely experience it on Hard mode. The Answer All of the above primarily pertains to “The Journey”. This section will specifically cover “The Answer”, the new chapter of the game that adds about 30 more hours of playtime. In The Answer, the day-to-day aspect of the game has been stripped away, meaning no school and no Social Links. The Answer is pure dungeon crawling with more challenging battles. Persona fusion is also more difficult since you cannot access the Persona Compendium at all during The Answer. Also, no Social Links mean no bonus levels for your Personas. The upside to this is that all personas learn one of their skills each time they level up, and there is no special requirement to create the “Max S.Link” Personas from The Journey. The story takes place after the events of The Journey and, as such, anything I mention about it would be a spoiler. What I can say is that The Answer features a new playable character that did not appear in The Journey. I mentioned earlier that alone, the Tartarus aspect of the game was very repetitive. However, I did not feel so strongly about that in The Answer, perhaps because of the greater variety of the battles. However, much of the increased challenge comes from the fact that most bosses have “Evade X” abilities for their weaknesses.
