In a game where exploiting weaknesses is key, making attacks that exploit those weaknesses miss 2/3 of the time turns your success into a matter of luck and essentially punishes the player for playing smart. Personally, I feel it was a cheap way to add fake difficulty to those battles. Fortunately, it doesn’t break the game. Overall, The Answer is a decent addition to this already great game. ESRB Rating: M (Mature 17+) Since this game is rated M for mature I have devoted a special section discussing why it got this rating. Suffice it to say the game well deserves this rating. The box mentions Blood, Language, Partial Nudity, Suggestive Themes, and Violence. The blood isn’t a big deal in my opinion, since you rarely see it come out of someone’s body. Language, there are a few instances of the big S and a bit more of some lesser words but its far from “constant cussing”. Partial Nudity, some of the In-game artwork for the personas shows some… excess skin but nothing too graphic. None of it is visible in any of the 3-D models. Suggestive themes is exactly that, suggestive and nothing more. Now Violence, yeah it’s a no brainer but one thing does bear special mentioning: the characters summon their personas using a device called an evoker, which looks exactly like a gun. The standard method for using it is for the character to put it to their head and pull the trigger. No, they aren’t commiting suicide, but it sure looks that way at first. Plus, they do this every time they use a skill in battle, which accounts for 90% of actions during battle, which means you are shown this image constantly during battles. If you are a parent and are worried that your teen might be influenced by this, then you probably shouldn’t buy this for him/her. In my opinion, this is the single greatest reason for the M rating. Another thing not mentioned on the case is the game’s overall occult theme. It has been an issue in other Megami Tensei games but I don’t personally think it is that big of a deal in Persona 3. Every one of the game’s 170 personas is inspired by a mythological figure from various mythologies. Many of these personas are based on demons or devils from these mythologies (one of them is actually named Satan). To balance it out, the game has its share of Angel-type beings as well. There are no “satanic rituals” or other active acts of devil worship portrayed in this game. In fact, much of the story and Social Links are lighthearted and humorous. However, the concept of Death plays a significant role in the story. To say more would be to give spoilers, so I will leave it at that. Final Word A good story, solid gameplay, good presentation, over 100 hours of playtime (albeit a bit repetitive), and you get all that for just $30, this game is a must for any hardcore RPG fan. Even if you already have the original Persona 3 the additional cost is reasonable enough for the new content and The Answer.

author: KrayzieJay
review_title: Quite simply one of the best JRPG's to ever grace the PS2...
review_text: Shin Megami Tensei, a series you've probably never heard of. Belive it or not the Tensei series have been around for over 10 years with the first Persona having it's release back in 1996 on the first Playstation. In fact the Tensei name is also responsible for releasing a number of other RPGs to glorify the PS2, some of which include the Digital Devil series and Lucifer's Call. Whilst they may not exactly be household names in comparison to to the ever popular Final Fantasy franchise, they still undoubtebly captured the hearts of role playing fanactics and also received generally positive feedback, averaing around an 82% and 84% reviews over the internet and gaming magazines. Now after a 8 year hiatus, Shin Megami Tensei have revived Persona back into the gaming scene, and unlike the previous two, Persona 3 has actually hit European shores, so this will be a first time experience of the series for many, and what better way to start… To cut things short and without spoiling too much; you play as an unnamed silent protagonist (similar to the RPG Suikoden V in which you play as that silent metrosexual), who so happens to be a new transfer student at Gekkoukan High, which is set in the game's fictional island city; Port Island. However upon arrival things do not seem entirely normal, what with the deep green coloured sky and bloody coffins in exchange of people all over the place. Our airheaded hero simply ignores these out of the ordinary obstacles and proceeds to his allocated dorm. Here we are introduced to two of the main female protagonists; Yukari and Mitsuru, but your warm welcome is soon cut short as one of the other dorm mates; Akihiko, suddenly staggers his way into the room; clearly injured and exasperated, shutting the door behind him to which he claims that a "shadow" is coming. You are at once forced to escape by Yukari in which you head to the rooftops, however this move appears to backfire as you are instantly surrounded by a horde of midget sized looking beings. What follows next is is the shock value that makes Persona oh so unique to any other RPG; the evoker to the head… No they're not trying to blow their brains out, the main characters in the game all possess an inner summon within them called "Persona". Our characters use these summons to aid them in battle, each equiped their own unique set of attacks and skills, but calling them out could be seen as one of the most controversial abilities to ever feature in a role playing game. It's simply not done by magic as found in most RPG's, e.g Final Fantasy X, but being different isn't a bad thing in Persona's case. Who wouldn't find the sight of teens pointing guns to their head somewhat extraodinary in a video game? Too frightened to release her Persona, your character, after a slight hesitation grabs the evoker off Yukari, points to it to their head, and fires, releasing his new found Persona named; Orpheus. An act of destiny described by your counterpart. Your character easily makes haste of these shadows with his new found power and is later congratulated and given a quick sum up of the events by your fellow dorm mate Mitsuru. The monsters refered to as "shadows" which you had previously fended off only appear during the "dark hour". A time that occurs at the stroke of midnight and before the dawn of a new day thus making a 25th hour to captivate the day. During this time the world is eclipsed and transformed into a ghastly looking wreck wher'e shadows are free to roam. Normal people never experience this time of day as they are transmogrified into coffins, but because you and your dorm mates bare the power of Persona, you have the ability to stay awake throughout. This is where your role in the game comes in. Mitsuru offers you a place in the dorm's secret group; SEES, an anti shadow group that works during the dark hour. From here on out you are now committed to helping out the SEES members in their mission to wipe out the shadows from existence. New comrades will join you as you progress through the strory, each possessing their own unique Persona. In fact the character's in Persona bring so much life into to the game as you'll find they are all extremely likeable and relateable to in their own unique way. You can literally find yourself being attatched to one of the character's featured in the game as they all have profound personalities to get acustomed with. Simply engaging in a conversation with one of the caracter's brings out their personality that almost feels life like. In comparisson to Final Fantasy XII, as great an RPG it was, the characters simply never felt "real" to me as they always sounded too monotone. You could just never feel a "warmth" from them. This could be due to the voice acting featured in both games. The voice actors in Persona sound like your typical anime character; vibrant, cheesey and fun, which is what everyone expects to hear in JRPG's, which is essentially why the cast is so loveable. The voice acting in Final Fantasy XII, although done very well always appears too serious, meaning you could never feel any real emotion illuminate from any of the characters. The battle gameplay in Persona is the turn based system you'd come to expect in any other RPG. However what makes Persona so different is it's many other features that bear within. The meat of the RPG element focuses on you exploring "Tartarus" a huge tower where your team battles shadows and is also where the games main theme of "dungeon crawling" takes place. You may only take up to three other SEES members with you at once leaving the rest on standby to wait on the ground floor, doing so means they'll not be able to gain any experience points which risks them falling behind your other party members, so you'll have to balance your team carefully. There are over 200 floors in the tower and they are split into five different sections, each section having different and stronger shadows as you progress. RPG's always tend to have random encounter battles, its almost an necessity as it's found in many great RPG titles such as; Dragon Quest VIII, Final Fantasy X & XII, Suikoden V etc. In Persona however you'll actually get to see your enemies wondering around each floor, and if you strike them first with the tap of the X button you'll engage into battle with an advantage, e.g; attack first. You'll have the choice to attack with your primary equiped weapon, or have the other command to use your Persona's battle skills. Your team mates however have a mind of their own and will attack using their own A.I. It surprisingly works very well and your team will react to changes occurred in battle such as healing wounded party members, cure status abnormalities and even react to exposed enemy weaknesses. Before you enter a new section within the tower you'll have to defeat a boss shadow that blocks you from progressing any further. You'll find many enemy shadows present on each floor in which they'll vary in weaknesses which you can easily identify through their masks. A certain colour such as green indicates that they are prone agaisnt electricity attacks. However if you are unsure about a shadow's weakness you can always choose the analyse option command which takes up a whole action turn for a character. Defeating shadows goes into random card picking mini game in which you can possibly earn EXP points to level up your characters, money or a brand new weapon or Persona. I honestly find it unecessary and rather annyoing actually, especially when you happen to pick the shattered card; earning you absolutely nothing! Thanks for rubbing salt on my wounds, greatly appreciated Atlus! In truth, leveling your character up does not make you stronger at all; it only furthers your ability to equip Personas of the same level or lower. In fact your strength comes from your equipped Persona with your stats such as speed, defence etc all focused on them. Your Persona's will also gain experience points at the aftermath of battles and as they level up you'll find yourself getting stronger too. They'll also learn new abilities and attacks to use in battle, some will serve as a huge asset in forthcoming missions. Leveling up monsters, doesn't that bring the Pokemon games to mind? Whilst indeed there are a large roster of Persona's to aquire, they're aren't quite up to par with the huge amount of pocket monsters found in the latest Pokemon games. We can still applaud Persona 3 for their versatility though. Persona's come in different shapes and sizes, some may look cute and cuddley such as; Jack Frost, whilst others may look grim and menacing, such as the Ghost Rider rip off; Hell Biker. You'll have access to Tartarus everyday after school in the evening as you'll be needing it to bulk up your characters for incoming missions on the calander. Yes, the game has a calender that spans 9 months; your time in the game. A mission takes place every full moon, an event that occurs once a month. So battling in Tartarus is the only way to build up your characters for these missions. Outside Tartarus you'll be able to explore the island city during the day, and increase your three basic stats in the process; Intelligence, Courage and Charm. This can be done by either; going to the school library, eating at certain restaurants, watching a certain film at the cinema, or participating in certain activites such as karaoke. These three stats are necessary if you want to form a "social link" with the female SEES members. The shopping mall is where you'll be able to purchase equipment such as weapons and armor, and an item shop to buy various medicines for use in Tartarus. The other areas on the map serve as social places filled with restaurants and various key people you can form other "social links" with. "Social Links" are another unique feature to the game in which players can forge friendships with certain key people including the SEES members. Persona's are catergorized into different groups called "arcana", and each social link you make uses this "arcana". By improving that social link e.g hanging out with that certain person after school and weekends, increases the level of that "arcana" allowing you to gain bonus experience when fusing Personas. Persona fusion is also another key feature to the game. When you fuse Persona's they'll form a whole new entity with enhanced strength, and depending on its arcana level, can gain additional stat points. So where does the genre of dating sims come in? Well, if you make social links with female characters you'll soon forge a typical romantic bond with them once you reach rank 5 of their social link. You'll also have the chance to give certain items to them when out on dates to boost their social link even higher. However all available girls have different likes and dislikes, so be careful when choosing an item to give to them, you could end up upsetting her. Be warned, if you choose to date numerous girls at a time they'll soon catch you out and your backstabbing ways, and you could risk "reversing" and eventually "breaking" their social linsk. Broken social links do not allow you to use Persona's of their arcana in battle… Persona 3, graphically is very niche looking for a PS2 trying to compete with the current generation of consoles. The game is meant to capture an anime art design and it does it very well with the character portraits looking very detailed which even change to display their current emotions whilst in a conversation. The 3D character models however could have done with a facelift, but it's nothing to put you off. To compare this game to Final Fantasy X in terms of graphics wouldn't exactly be fair. Final Fantasy X was way ahead of its time back when it was released in 2001, with Square Enix throwing in phenomenal FMV sequences to give it the that "wow" factor that still sends ripples of its brilliance today. Looking back at it you could compare it with the current generation; it was simply that good, and with a Hollywood movie like budget of around $32 million that's no surprise. To be fair Atlus did a great job on the graphics, and they do deserve credit for managing to create multiple Persona's, shadows and epic boss battles to feature within the game. Exploring Port Island can also be an enjoyable and lush experience at times, especially during the summer season. The game's multiple use of anime styled cut scenes was also a nice touch, and although few far and between, were very much appreciated and appeared pretty much every time necessary. However the recycling of shadows in Tartarus do become a bore along with the repetitivelooking floors. Watching your character pull the evoker trigger against their head thankfully never loses its intensity, as you watch little fragments of their soul burst through the other end. To close, Persona 3 can be an incredibly enjoyable experience. Packed with a unique, loveable cast and an intriguing story filled with gob smacking moments, there's so much to like here in Persona. Maxing out all the social links can become one of your primary objectives, or maybe your aim is to acquire all of the available Persona's. With a length of around 50+ hours, the journey ahead will become a difficult one so constant level grinding isn't an exception in this case, sorry... In the end, Persona 3 is an absolute fresh and original take on a genre plagued with the same old thing. It may lack in a few minor areas but it would still be a travesty for any RPG fan to take a pass on it. While there is a significant time investment required for Persona, it is well worth it as this game should be part of any PS2 owner's collection.

author: SgtCashmere
review_title: I Don't Think My Watch HAS That Hour...
review_text: Persona 3: FES is an RPG that features a group of teenage students in Japan. Each night, they secretly experience a moment in time that nobody else can experience called the Dark Hour. During the Dark Hour, they fight monsters -- known as Shadows -- by summoning spirit like forces of their own, called Personas. The game falls into the adventure RPG genre. It has many good qualities, but it also suffers from some fairly large problems including the fact that it has simply just not aged well. STORYLINE A good storyline is probably the most important part of an RPG game, because it allows the player to sink their teeth into the title. In Persona 3: FES, the game runs on its own annual calendar. Unfortunately, the game lacks an interesting storyline for the first few "months" of game playing time. Eventually, the storyline picks up and the characters become much more interesting. However, there was no immediate hook for players to enjoy. Basically, it seemed like the writers held out way too much in the beginning of the storyline. The characters were bland and uninteresting. Players thinking about playing this game should know it requires patience before the story really heats up. Even after the storyline revs up a few notches, some of the main characters suffer from being completely one dimensional. In particular, a couple characters are unnecessary to the storyline, and really seem dispensable. For example, Ken Amada illustrates this point. He has a storyline that has little to do with the main plot of the game, and which could have been condensed to two "weeks" of story telling. Not only that, but his storyline was incredibly predictable. He was a waste of space in the main cast. Other characters, such as Akihiko Sanada, Fuuka Yamagishi, etc. warranted a lot more character development. These characters seemed far more interesting. As a result, they seriously overshadowed some other characters. Basically in this title, each character was either a hit or a miss. They were a fantastic addition, or really just wasted your time. The best characterization, however, would be the main protagonist. You can spend time developing Social Links through him, which means interacting with various other characters in order to strengthen your own Persona roster. You can make him as mean or as sensitive as you want. It's an original system that is highly enjoyable to explore. However, it is also kind of a sham. After all, you can only attain maximum Social Links if you choose specific dialogue options the entire way through the game. As for the storyline itself, it deals with the typical "saving the world from evil forces" storyline found in most, if not all, RPGs. However, the storyline is kind of unique since it deals so heavily with the topic of death. Nearly all important characters have to grieve for one or two lost ones along the course of the storyline. Such subject matter is dealt with realistically, and delivers some pretty good messages to players along the way. GAME PLAY Game play is pretty... well, bland. Dungeons were highly monotonous, and suffered from a cagey, repetitive atmosphere. To succeed in the game, especially during "The Answer" portion, grinding is necessary. You will have to fight the exact same enemies, called "Shadows", over... and over... and over. One element that offers some spice to this monotonous game play system is the ability to fuse Personas. They are the spirit like entities that grant you powers to fight Shadows. The game, honestly, reminded me of Pokemon quite a bit. It was quite a classic throwback to when I was young enough to enjoy those games! It was really familiar enough for absolutely anybody to pick up and learn. Therefore, the game play was not especially creative or mature. Its simplicity results to a very forgettable game play experience. The Social Link game play was much more interesting, as described in my STORYLINE section. Here's hoping that many, many more games adopt such a system! GRAPHICS The graphics are really not half bad. The anime sequences are somber, stylish, and a touch cartoonish. They offered a very nice blend of tones. However the field graphics, with their incessantly dark, horror novel tones, have not aged well. The various fields that you explore, such as Gekkoukan High, the Velvet Room, the mall, etc. look kind of gritty and underdeveloped. Plus, the dungeons are incredibly repetitive! I wish the creators had used more imagination when developing the dungeons. They are definitely the weakest part of the game. The shining point of the graphics were definitely the cut scenes. They are very nostalgic of all the anime shows from the 1980's and 1990's. Honestly, they are rather impressive pieces of animation. It is a good thing that the videos were plentiful because they provided saving grace to the otherwise poor graphics of the game. SOUND Signal a big, lengthy yawn. The music was SO bland! Not to mention repetitive and uninspired. The only good song in the entire game was the lengthy, softer version of the main theme song. Unfortunately, that song was not even played until the final credits of "The Journey" were rolling. However, the music people for this game must be given some credit, because in a rare move for the RPG world, they included some rap and hip hop inspired tracks. I really like that, but perhaps next time they could find some better rap artists? Voice acting was pretty good, except for a few exceptions. Yukari Takeba's voice was dreadfully annoying, and Ken Amada's voice actor was seriously miscast. He sounded so creepy, and not at all like a young boy. However, Junpei Iori's voice actor was one of the best I have ever heard in a video game. He had a great range of emotion, and the voice suited the character really well. Another of my favorite voices was that of Akihiko Sanada. His voice actor does the voice of Endrance, an effeminate, homosexual drama queen from .hack//G.U., while Akihiko is a much cooler alpha male with a very short temper. I was impressed to hear the difference in characters, and thought it was really well done. Therefore, while some of the voices seriously grated on my nerves, the voice acting was overall not too bad. THE ANSWER In addition to the main storyline, Persona 3: FES features an extra game called "The Answer". It follows the character of Aigis -- an incredibly interesting character, by the way -- as she copes with a certain loss. "The Answer" departs from the Social Link system of the main storyline, and only involves dungeon crawling. Since dungeon crawling is not the strong part of this game, you can only imagine how much fun "The Answer" offers to a player. However, it is nice to see the storyline get fully resolved, especially considering the ambiguity of the ending in "The Journey," the primary game from Persona 3: FES. I thought "The Answer" was a rare move for an RPG company, since direct sequels are not often found in the big league RPG series. However, like "Final Fantasy X-2," the sequel paid off. I respect and appreciate "The Answer," even if the game play was not fantastic. OVERALL This is not a horrible title, but it did not age well. Mostly, its game play, graphics, and sound are all very repetitive. Once the storyline heats up, it actually an enjoyable game. It takes some risks in music selection and storyline plots, which is refreshing for an RPG game. I give the game a seven out of a possible ten, and applaud its awesome cut scenes. I also applaud Akihiko Sanada. He is tough and acts like a real man, which makes it pretty funny that he is voiced by the same actor who voiced Endrance! Also, if you like Persona 3: FES, I strongly recommend Persona 4. It is MUCH stronger and more enjoyable than Persona 3: FES, plus it retains all the good qualities of its predecessor.

author: AK_the_Twilight
review_title: Restless Inner Demons
review_text: Atlus has gathered quite a cult following with their Shin Megami Tensei series, a unique twist on the standard RPG formula with monsters and demons abound. The Persona series has been a mostly obscure outing in the Shin Megami Tensei world, with the original Persona and Persona 2 games falling back into cult fandom on the Playstation. In 2006, Atlus struck gold with Persona 3, a massive change that blended the RPG gameplay with aspects of a dating simulation. In 2008, the game was re-released as Persona 3: FES with a brand new sequence called “The Answer.” It’s time to let loose your inner demons with Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 3: FES. Persona 3 follows a nameless character and his journey through school. After encountering a group of students in his class, the hero discovers a deep secret inside of him. Like the students he meets, he can summon (by shooting himself in the head) a Persona, inner beings with the strength to defeat enemies. The enemies, the Shadows, appear during a hauntingly empty time called the Dark Hour. The hero joins the students, a girl named Yukari Takeba and a boy named Junpei Iori, in a select group of characters with the abilities to summon Persona. Throughout the game, more and more characters appear to fight the Shadows. It’s up to the main character and his friends to eliminate the Dark Hour. Shin Megami Tensei prides itself on knowledge of the occult, and Persona 3 really takes the idea to a new level. The game shows off a lighter and friendlier vibe during the school days, and contrasts that with a dark and engaging atmosphere during the Dark Hour. The twists throughout the story feel consistent, while also being plenty surprising. Each character also has a distinct backstory and a unique personality, making the different character interactions a real treat. The entire story setup of Persona 3 shows a mastery of the occult, along with a near-perfect collection of characters, with the end result being an amazing storyline that you’ll want to explore over and over again. Compared to other RPG’s, Persona 3 really doesn’t rely on the battles. In fact, you can actually skip a tremendous amount of the battles initially. The battles take place in the Tower of Tartarus, a massive, malformed world where you can battle Shadows during the Dark Hour. Instead of trudging through battle after battle to level up your Persona, you can win different Personas as spoils and travel to the Velvet Room to fuse them together to form a new Persona. In addition to creating more powerful Personas, you can then use different Social Links to increase their strength considerably. Fusing more powerful Personas will allow for special move combinations and increased ability count. This addictive element of fusing (one mindfully reminiscent of the breeding concept in the Pokemon games) doesn’t just allow for increased Persona powers, but it also allows the player to go through the game using the Persona that they wish. It’s remarkably versatile and makes the battles engaging and exciting. Along the way you’ll find traditional RPG elements like equipment, stats, and battles which, thankfully, are not random. Once you encounter a Shadow in the Tower of Tartarus, the battle begins. The mechanics are simple: select from a menu of options like Attack, Item, and Run, along with the ability to summon Persona for special abilities. Different Personas provide different strengths and weaknesses; balancing your party of Personas is crucial to taking out enemies. Different equipment also varies depending on range, strength, and accuracy, even when attacking for a pre-emptive strike. The dungeon-crawling portion of Persona 3 is random, as the floors will change significantly over time, but the exploration is far from tedious. Persona 3 is a prime example of making the RPG system more user friendly, abandoning the mindless grinding of other RPG’s for a more experimental approach to leveling up. Fortunately, those who enjoy the battles can be accounted for, as you must level up your own character to produce the better Personas. This may seem like the developers are trying to appeal to two different RPG demographics, but the whole thing feels streamlined and nails that excellent balance between battles and downtime. A small problem is that the pacing skyrockets near the end of the game, which is definitely off-putting. However, playing through the game again is opportunistic to see the different nuances. Persona 3 masters the battle system, keeping the different ideas fresh, though accessible, throughout the entire game. On the topic of Social Links, Persona 3 delivers a unique combination of RPG stat tracking and interactivity similar to a dating simulation. By talking with specific characters at school or around town, you can develop different relationships with the supporting cast. Keeping different relationships in balance isn’t just for entertainment; increasing Social Links allows for stronger Persona creation in the Velvet Room, along with new skills with each Persona. This is fun, diverse, and the introduction of unique character interactions (even with some of the main characters) broadens the overall story considerably. What makes it so remarkable is how attached the storyline is to the actual gameplay. During the day, it’s essentially up to the player as to how they will go about their routine. You can talk to a classmate for Social Links, visit the arcade to increase stats, buy items, among many other activities. Practically every activity has purpose, even something as simple as sleeping the day away to increase morale. This is a small bit overwhelming at times, as some cases will require significant planning and organization for the best result, but it’s an addictive element that adds plenty of depth to the whole Persona system. Persona 3, regardless of whether you decide to tackle the side-quests and Social Links, is a lengthy game, clocking in at over 70 hours. The Tower of Tartarus is without a doubt an endurance challenge, but the strong gameplay is addicting and will keep you coming back. In the FES release of Persona 3, there is a special bonus in the form of “The Answer,” where the player follows the character Aigis instead of the main protagonist. It doesn’t have the Social Links or the school-day rituals, but it’s a great inclusion that broadens the storyline even more. At another 30+ hours, “The Answer” just sweetens the already excellent deal of Persona 3. With plenty of side-quests and additional dialogue to uncover, Persona 3: FES is a huge game that will keep you hooked even after its climactic conclusion. Despite being a late-generation PS2 title, the presentation in Persona 3 is actually quite good. The beautifully-designed anime cutscenes are visual treats, despite there being a bit too few of them. In-game, the graphics are respectable, but the artistic design of the Tower of Tartarus is haunting and twisted, a huge contrast from the humble school days of the morning hours. The sound design is really where the presentation shines. The voice acting in Persona 3 has its moments of cheesy writing, but a majority of the lines are delivered with their respective characters in mind. Big name anime voice actors like Michelle Ruff (Rukia from Bleach) as Yukari and Vic Mignogna (Edward from Fullmetal Alchemist) as Junpei are very well done. In fact, the entire cast really gives it their all in Persona 3, making the different dialogue segments, despite being weighted with scrolling text, incredibly entertaining. The music is an upbeat mix of rock, hip-hop, and j-pop, and while it can get a small bit repetitive, it adds a laid-back atmosphere to the game. Overall, the presentation feels stylized, and that more than makes up for its minor problems. Pros + Amazingly dark presentation makes for a captivating world to explore + Accessible, though versatile combat + Plenty of depth in the Social Link system + Over 70 hours of gameplay content, not including new “The Answer” sequence + Great collection of voice acting Cons - Social Link system has its moments of overwhelming you - Pretty text heavy - Balance between storyline and gameplay lacks pacing Persona 3: FES is easily one of the best RPG’s to come out for the Playstation 2. The unique use of Social Links and its strong emphasis on dark and twisted atmosphere gives it a style unlike any other game on the market today. The Persona system is flexible and addictive, and finding your own specific Persona team is entirely up to the player. The superbly presented storyline is deep and rich with stellar characters and a great narrative. With over 90 hours of gameplay and storyline to explore, you don’t have to worry about running out of things to do in Persona 3. “The Answer” is a solid extension of the storyline, making the FES version of Persona 3 one of the most content-packed RPG’s you’ll find on the Playstation 2. This is the definitive edition of an excellent RPG, one that, from start to finish, will deliver unparalleled storytelling, an addictive Persona creation system, and some of the most creative integrations of gameplay and storyline you’ll find in any RPG. Persona 3: FES is an absolute must-have. Clear your schedule for the next few weeks, because the Dark Hour waits for no one.

author: Alfare
review_title: Looking At Death Straight In the FES
review_text: A Gist of the Game Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 3 is basically an unusual RPG hybrid between a dungeon-crawler and a dating-sim. The FES version is a ‘remix’ of sorts from the original game. Its additional content covers several changes in the Persona system, such as changes in the fusion system which include new Personas and different set of abilities; an extra epilogue mode which gives about 30 more hours of additional content with yes, a new story; the cool option to fuse Personas into swords, creating weapons that are so more powerful; new character costumes; new soundtracks; new subquests; and several other in-game changes which have made everything significantly less complicated. To be short, Persona 3 was already a ‘cool’ game back at the time when it was first released. But it’s been made even cooler with FES . Even if you’ve played the original Persona 3 , playing FES is quite worth the effort. The tweaks given in it make out an almost entirely new experience. You can even load your old data save from the original Persona 3 (but not for the epilogue mode) so yeah, FES really is a lot more fun. For newcomers who’ve never played the Persona games, it should be noted that Persona 3 is the start of a new hype. What I mean here is that although there are some references here and there, Persona 3 has (almost) no connections to its previous games at all. So don’t be discouraged to try it out since seriously, there has never been a game like this before. The Presentation Aspect The graphics are bright and colorful. It goes well with the realistic, contemporary Japanese urban setting. The visual designs are awesome as you can feel each of the characters distinctive personalities just by looking at them. The in-game environment is nothing but perfectly normal. Like in previous Persona games, there are places like toiletries, game arcades, fast food restaurants, etc. but Persona 3 brought all this up to a whole new level. Since like I said, they put in dating-sim elements in Persona 3 , giving those seemingly ordinary everyday stuff significance in your character building. On another note, there are also animated cutscenes which in my opinion are each directed very, very well. Visually, Persona 3 is stunning. The design of the world is plain awesome with all of its eerie yet natural atmosphere. You can tell that you like it simply by looking at the package artwork. Audio-wise, however, this game has implemented some really strange music. Adding to the traditional mix of haunting piano melodies and upbeat (techno?) tunes, are combinations of hip-hop raps and J-pop singing. It’s a bit hard to describe for you veteran RPG players. The normal battle soundtrack goes “Ooh yeah! Du du-dudu-du du-dudu-du! Baby, baby!” and no, seriously, I am not kidding. But unusual it may be, although there’s a chance that you may not like it, it actually does go well with the entirety of the game’s atmosphere. I actually enjoy listening to the game’s soundtrack from time to time. It also softens the bore that is occasionally bought by day-by-day nature of the game. I’ll explain more about that later. The presentation, to put it simply in my opinion, is flawless. A Gist of the Story Right. Before the gameplay, it’s better if I give a gist about the story. You’re a male high school student who had just transferred schools. After being placed in your new dorm, you find out that you’ve been recruited as a member of SEES, a secret school club which specializes in dealing with Shadows, ugly masses of monsters that appear during the hidden hour between one day and the next. Yes, you read right. A hidden hour, known as the Dark Hour. And these monsters are believed to be the commonly unknown cause of the bizarre epidemic that’s been plaguing the town: the Apathy Syndrome. Like any other Persona game, the story stems from cases of weirdness (the spooky, cringing kind) which eventually leads to cases of even more weirdness. It’s told mostly through rumors and sporadic character interaction. As you live your daily life as a high school student, dealing with everyday problems that include the relationships with people around you, you must also progress higher and higher inside Tartarus, the mysterious tower which appears only during the Dark Hour, which is the place that is believed to hide the true nature of the Shadows’s appearances and the Apathy Syndrome. Although the premise starts out oh-so-interesting--as it surprisingly deals with the question about discovering the meaning of life by exploring the meaning of death--the main plot is actually quite simple. As you near the end, you’ll actually notice how horribly cheap and awfully flat the real plot actually is. It especially came as a shock for me who expected something jaw-breaking like Satomi Tadashi’s powerful writing in Persona 2 . But the thing is that the game still actually managed to tell it so well, with its cool animation and powerful voice acting, so you won’t really mind about it at all. You’ll only need to endure the several last hours of the game as nearly all character developments come to a halt, and you no longer can expect anything good to come from the plot. The ending itself can actually be considered quite meaningful for some people, although its impact is not exactly 'great' for me. Anyway, recently I’ve been thinking the simplicity of the story which is so not-like-Atlus was actually intentional. So let’s not talk more about that for now. The bonus game mode given in FES (dubbed as "the Answer") on the other hand, taking place during several months after the final battle where the main characters find out more about the events which has transpired, gives a somewhat more proper closure to this game's story. So as unsatisfying it may be, I must say that it's far from bad. When people were saying how it was worth to buy FES for this mode alone, they were actually right. More About the Gameplay and Your Daily Life As I have mentioned above, the game plays out in a day-by-day cycle (imagine something that has a calendar, like Harvest Moon ). You wake up in the morning, go to school, hangout with people in the afternoon, study at night, and when the Dark Hour comes, go to Tartarus with your dorm mates to kick some Shadow butt. Something like that. This is what I call the dating-sim aspect of Persona 3 and yes, I do imply that by building our personal statistics and nurturing our relationship(s), we’ll eventually be rewarded with an in-game girlfriend. Tartarus itself is a massive, random-floor-generating tower infested with monsters that appear during nighttime. You explore Tartarus from floor to floor, going higher and higher up each time. At certain points, you’ll be challenged by bizarre bosses who appear to obstruct your way. You’ll find items and weapons along your way. You’ll also be hunted down by an extremely powerful Shadow called the Reaper if you stay too long on a certain floor. There will be limits on how high you can climb each time, depending on the progress of the game’s main story events which take place from time to time. This is what I call the dungeon-crawler aspect of Persona 3 , which is similar to what you’ll find in Rogue -like games such as Baroque or Mysterious Dungeon . To conquer Tartarus, you need the mysterious power to summon out your magical inner-selves: Personas (by shooting a gun-like thing into your own head) which is the basic requirement for one to be recruited into SEES. Unlike previous Persona games, you as the main character are the only one capable to wield multiple Personas at once. In other words, you’re the only person who can enter the mysterious Velvet Room to consult Igor, its caretaker, and Elizabeth, his new assistant, to create new Personas by fusing old ones Like the demon fusing in classic Shin Megami Tensei tradition, fusing Personas require you to consider fusion accidents, the inheritance of Spells, and the Persona’s level compared to your own, and so on. The catch that Persona 3 has is that there will be bonus Experience Points that power up your new Persona, which its amount is decided by how high your Social Link level is for that Persona’s arcana. A Social Link level basically implies to how good your relationship is with a certain character. How good you are with a certain character is decided by how often you spend your time to hang out with them and also by the way you respond to them during the occurrence of special events. Like I said, since Shadows only occur during the Dark Hour that happens precisely after midnight, you spend your life like any other student during the daytime. You interact and make friends with people, study, go to restaurants, fool around, it’s all up to you. Depending on how well you manage yourself and your relationships, your Social Link levels may go up as well. The Personas are divided into different categories which are based on the tarot card arcanum, and each Social Link represents a one of these many different arcana. So in short, the better you are in making friends, the literally stronger you’ll become in the game. Battles are basically character turn-based. The system is almost identical to the one used in Shin Megami Tensei Nocturne and Digital Devil Saga . You input commands for the main character only. The rest of the party is controlled by AI. If the main character falls, you’re dead. Game over. Considering how this is a Shin Megami Tensei game, that unsurprisingly happens quite often. If you strike an enemy at its weakness (whether by one of the types of attacks of Slash, Pierce, Strike, Fire, Ice, Wind, Electricity, Holy, or Dark) or landing a critical hit, you’ll ‘down’ them. If you ‘down’ an enemy, you’ll gain an additional turn. A so-called ‘1 More’ as the game says it. If you manage to ‘down’ all of them, you’ll get the chance for an All-Out Attack, which is basically an insanely powerful group attack where your party ‘brawls’ all the enemies at once. The same rules apply for the enemies that go after you. The battles themselves don’t come out random. This is a part dungeon-crawler game, so you can see the enemies come and go. The enemies will normally chase you when they see you. You can also see items littered here and there, some are rarer than the rest. Some Shadows are also stronger than the others even on the same levels (I’m not talking about bosses here). And since you’ll find access points that can immediately take you out to the exit, the dungeon-crawler aspect of the game is never unforgivable. It’s fun. It’s risky. It becomes suspenseful especially when it nears the full moon. Or when your characters get tired since yeah, you can’t be level grinding in Tartarus forever. Since your characters could always interact, and ‘dungeon crawling’ is interspersed with the ‘dating-sim mode’ after daybreak arrives, it never really gets boring. So if you ask me about the gameplay, I think this game definitely rocks. The gameplay in the bonus mode is essentially similar, only without the dating-sim elements. There's a good reason for that. But I think that if you're already interested, its best you see it for yourself. The Good and the Bad The good thing I really like about Persona 3 is how it kind of ‘stimulates’ you to become a better person. To meet people, you need to build up your statistics. So you’ll also need to study to earn respect, you’ll need to practice to build up courage, and so on. You’ll also be needed be considerate as you make choices in what to say to other people. All these dating-sim elements can sometimes be bothersome and a bit overwhelming. But it’s really fun as it also works that way in real life. Especially since FES actually made this whole Social Link issue slightly easier compared to the original version, it no longer feels like much of a chore. On the other hand, while the voice-acting is pretty good for most of the part (it’s even amazing at certain points, and goes really well with the music), one bad thing this game has is how it sounded ‘disharmonic’ for me during several critical scenes. It’s as if the recording for the voice actors were done independently instead of together, so it makes the mood of the voices sound jumbled up when the event plays. It’s like a recurring killjoy, since the events in Persona 3 are supposedly pretty exciting (counting out the events that occur when you near the end), and this voice acting discrepancy is what annoyed me most throughout the game. Some of the voices took quite a while for me to get used to too. But overall, it’s still pretty high above my normal standards. Another bad thing is the absence of the many meaningful lines and riddles that are found in Persona 2 . Though overall good, Persona 3 ’s underlying theme just doesn’t live up to the impact that the previous Persona games gave me. Yes, I find the story to be even less impressive than the slightly-messy first Persona , although Persona 3 ’s idea had such great potential. This game doesn’t show how human the characters can be, showing the past demons they posses, nor how desperate they try to discover themselves and change. This mushy feeling that I’ve been hoping for is almost entirely absent in Persona 3 , somewhat replaced by the uneasiness of pondering how we should react instead of teaching us how to be true to ourselves. This game just manages to make flat characters actually look cool. The excitement actually crumbles as we near the end of the game instead of going up, and is suspended in a strange way as we play the bonus mode. Still, I’m a grown up Persona fan who bought a second-hand PS2 just to play this game and I can’t say that I was disappointed. Persona 3 is a unique thrill. If you’re sick and tired with any other game in the genre, play Persona 3 FES . Buy it. Nothing compares to it. At least until Persona 4 came out.

author: TLHunter312
review_title: A wonderful beginning for the new era of Persona - Persona 3 FES
review_text: Overall Rating: 9/10 Introduction: So I'll start by saying this isn't my first persona game, my first one was Persona 5, then I played Royal, Strikers, and now Persona 3, and shortly after writing this I'm going to start my first playthrough of 4. During my playthroughs of the Persona 5 games, I fell head over heels in love with the series, to the point where I actually bought Royal only a few hours after finishing my first playthrough of 5. I did 2 playthroughs of Royal, one of which was on NG+ where I maxed every social link, got the Persona compendium to 100%, among other things (you get the idea). Just a warning, I will be comparing the two since I consider Persona 5 to be a better game, but don't take that as me trying to say Persona 3 is a bad game. Story 10/10 : I won't go in-depth with the story but I will say this. It starts slow, but that's common for the series, however, it will hook you fast. The story begins relatively normal I guess for a teenage Japanese boy transferring to a new dorm and school, however, it quickly takes a turn for the worse (or better if you don't enjoy a normal life). As you progress you learn more and more about your situation and things take a really crazy turn at some points that I was not expecting, this definitely has a lot of shocking moments and it ended in a way I won't tell you about but it's something I wasn't ready for. If you play this game for any reason at all, let it be for the story, this is a once every so often kind of story. From what I've read online it seems to be universally agreed that this game has the best story in the series and I understand why, of course, I haven't played 4 yet but from what I already know I don't think I'll like it as much but I know I'll still love it. S.E.E.S. 9.5/10: Right away the team is by far the most mature in the series, sure you have your comic relief, a young boy, and a literal dog as part of your team but I promise you all of these characters are more complex than they come off. They each have dealt with their own fair share of problems and as you learn more about them you really learn to care about every one of them, and their character arcs are so special and interesting and something I think this game does excellently is STORY BASED PERSONA EVOLUTIONS. Atlus needs to bring this back, every one of these is so important, special, and impactful, and it isn't "oh hey MC, thanks for helping me out I'm stronger now, new persona now!" I don't want to spoil any of the character arcs, but my favorite is a tie with Junpei and the Aeon arcana, their arcs solidified them as some of my favorite characters in the series. (honorable mentions for favorite S.E.E.S. members: everybody, Junpei and Aeon just stand out the most for me) Music 9/10 : Now a big chunk of this comes down to personal preference but I would say Persona 3 and 5 are equal in terms of music, at least for me. Persona 5 changed my taste in music, I was quite the metal head before playing it but it really opened my ears to other kinds of music, and I love it for that. However when it comes to final boss themes (something important for the series) Persona 3 kills it when a song that's a name I can't put here because just the name is a spoiler. I do wish it was Burn My Dread, however, the theme from the opening. Regardless, the music in Persona 3 bops, slaps, whatever you want to say it's got it. This game is super consistent with the music and without a doubt, it has my favorite main battle theme, Mass Destruction (though Royal has my favorite battle theme overall with Take Over). The music also hits hard with the emotional moments, in fact, some of the best music only plays during the last month of the game, arguably the hardest hitting part of the game for reasons I refuse to spoil. Villains 6.5/10 : I would say the villains of P3FES are arguably better villains than Palace rulers 3, 5, and 6. That doesn't exactly mean they're good though, they do their job as antagonists and that's enough, however, they do some things that really got under my skin and made me hate them way more than said palace rulers ever could, had it not been for those things, they would probably be like a 3 or 4/10 for me. Social Links 6/10 : Some of the social links in Persona 3 didn't quite have as much impact as some of the Persona 5 social links did for me, but I will say the biggest standouts for me were: The Fool, Judgement, The Star, The Sun, The Lovers, and Aeon. The characters connected to these really impacted me a lot with The Lovers being who I ended up really romancing (but due to Persona 3's mind-boggling out-of-date romance system any time you max a social link with a female character you are immediately locked into a romance with them. I ended up maxing out a few female social links which is why I specifically mention The Lovers, thankfully this is changed in 4). I didn't get every social link maxed during my first playthrough, but there are a few honorable mentions: The Hanged Man, The Priestess, and The Tower. If you are only going to do 1 social link aside from the two that are automatic, it has to be The Sun. The Sun social link can be accessed on Sundays after getting The Hanged Man to rank 3 and it's one of the most touching and heartbreaking stories I've ever experienced while playing a video game, it did also make me look at things differently and be more thankful for what I have, not every game can do that for me. Gameplay and Tartarus 4/10 : Hoo boy. Tartarus and gameplay. Yeah so Mementos in Persona 5 is Tartarus done right I have a lot of negative feelings about Tartarus, but I decided to combine these two since they go hand in hand. The gameplay is fine, it's not good, it's not bad, it's serviceable. Tartarus, on the other hand, is really not enjoyable to get through, it's just a roadblock that you're forced to play through if you want to beat the game and win important battles, this also happens to be a majority of the fighting. Tartarus is frustrating, a massive chore, and the first couple chunks are dreadful because of how little exp they give, combined with the fact that your team is "tired" (a status that is a death sentence and basically forces you out of Tartarus with limited ways to get rid of it aside from resting and not going to Tartarus for a day or 2 which is something you need to do at the start, thankfully this status never came back.) Some bosses in Tartarus are also terrible because it seems like you're forced into using a specific persona or method to take them down, which isn't fun, it doesn't allow freedom and it locks you in. Sure this changes in NG+ because of how powerful you are but it sucks, I can't put it any other way. If you cut out Tartarus from the game, you'd lose like 60+ hours on your playtime. Yeah, a massive chunk of your time will be playing through this awful thing but it is worth it to experience the story I promise, the worst part is if you die in it not only are you sent back to your last save (unless you're playing on easy), which could be anywhere from 5 minutes ago to 30+ minutes ago depending on where you are in Tartarus, but you also lose the items you got on the way and because of the nature of Tartarus with each floor being somewhat randomized you could get some really game-changing items for that point in the game, die, and lose them permanently, I say this because I dealt with it, A LOT. Also unless you're playing Persona 3 Portable, you can't control your AI teammates, which will get you killed more times than you want (again, I'm speaking from experience.), sometimes you'll desperately need your teammate to take down the boss or enemy because it's on one health and you could die the next turn and even though you have them set to "Full Assault", but instead of doing that they'll use Marin Karin and you'll die, or they'll use dia/rama/rahan instead of media/rama/rahan. I couldn't be more thankful to be able to control my teammates in 4 and 5. The Answer 6/10 : So, had the final 5 bosses in The Answer not been what they were, and the story bits non-existent The Answer would be a 2/10. But because they were there this gets a much higher rating. I have a lot of problems with The Answer since it's mostly dungeon crawling, introduces a new character that I didn't like even in the end, and the only reason I was able to get through it with my sanity was because I was watching some shows while playing making things much less mind-numbing, I also used a guide after the first couple areas because I just hated it. Ironically enough it's not really about the answer, it's more about the journey. I really can't say much on The Answer since it's a 30+ hour epilogue for the base game, but what I can say is this: don't play it, watch the cutscenes on Youtube and the last 5 boss fights and skip it. Please, don't make the same mistake I did. Final Thoughts : Persona 3/FES as I mentioned before is a once every so often kind of game, it's really special and is one of my favorite games of all time. I truly love this game and it has a story that I think everybody should experience, more so than Persona 5. It has an amazing story, characters, and really great music to back it up. Of course, because it's a 14-year-old game now, it's aged, and not the greatest I'll admit. Hell, I went through some hoops to play it, in fact, I bought an HDMI adapter with a headphone jack for my PS2 and a 10 foot long 3.5mm audio cable just to play it and it was so worth it. I love this game so much and it might be another game I playthrough every year like I do with Titanfall 2, Metal Gear Rising, and a handful of others. Please give this a shot, but if you do, use a certain thing (wink wink) and take advantage of save states to save yourself from the pain of Tartarus.

author: Tricked_Out_Horo
review_title: They've done it again
review_text: Last year, I blindly picked up the original Persona 3, not really knowing anything about it. I'd played Persona 2 before, but I hadn't heard anything about Persona 3 until I saw it on the shelf. Plot: 10/10 Aside from the original games plotline, now called The Journey, there's a brand new story called The Answer, featuring Aigis, a party member from the original story. The story of The Journey remains the same, with a lot more sidequests and a new Social Link added in. Every night there is a hidden hour called "The Dark Hour" between 12:00 and 12:01 AM. At this time, many people without special abilities become coffins, and the world mutates and changes into a very dark and sinister place. Those who do not become coffins usually have the ability to summon a spirit know as a Persona, which can be used in combat to use magic and amplify other such skills. The game revolves around a group of high school students and their Persona as they try to find out the mystery of The Dark Hour and Tartarus, a 263 floor tower which serves as the main dungeon of the game. The Answer takes place around a month after the original story. The party finds their world stuck in a loop, with the same day repeating over and over. After a giant hole appears in the floor of the lobby of their dorm, they decide to enter it and look for a reason as to why the same day keeps occuring. Gameplay: 10/10 Persona 3 is split into 2 main gameplay segments. It's half dungeon crawler, half dating-sim. During the day, you build relationships with other students by going to the mall with them, going to the movies, playing MMORPGs with them, and so on. By building these relationships you unlock Social Links which improve the stats of your fused Persona later in the game. Also during the day, you can raise some of your characters stats such as Courage, Academics, and Charisma, which have minor effects on your overall game such as which Social Links you have access to. The other half of the game occurs on either the days there are a full moon or the days you decide to go to Tartarus. The game randomly generates a floor with monsters and items and all of your other RPG goodies and basically sends you on your way. There is only one dungeon in the game, but it is so huge and varied and such a blast to go through you really don't even notice. Of course, the game doesn't let you go through the whole dungeon right from the start of the game, it breaks it up into segments and eventually by the end you are expected to be able to clear all 263 floors. Don't fear however, you have about 8 in-game months to do so. The battle system is fantastic as well, and very easy to get the hang of. Experimenting with different Persona fusions is also quite deep and should keep you entertained for the entire game. There are lots of new additions, such as previous buildings from the original that weren't accessible now are. There's a new weapon fusing ability, where you can fuse personas with weapons for devastating results. Theres 20 + new Persona added to the mix as well. The new Social Link, Aeon, also adds a bit more to the playtime. The Answer adds a new character, Metis, to the party, and occurs in a completely different dungeon. Graphics: 9/10 There's quite a bit more variety than last time around, and the world seems somewhat more colorful and prettier. The new dungeon is pretty well designed, but it's nothing incredibly new to the RPG genre. The only thing holding the score back is that the cartoonish style may not be for everyone. This game is no Call of Duty 4 in terms of looks. Sound: 9/10 The soundtrack in Persona 3 is fantastic. The battle music is awesome, which is a good thing, since you will be in battle quite a lot. The music that plays as you explore town and the school is catchy and will likely get stuck in your head whether you like it or not. Theirs quite a few new tracks added, some good, some meh, but none that are just "Oh my god, shut this off!" bad. The new story has the same voice actors returning to reprise their roles from the original release. Control: 10/10 You shouldn't have a problem controlling the game at all. The tutorials explain everything to you very easily and nothing feels too complex to handle. X selects things, the analog moves your character. That's pretty much all you need to know to get started, you'll pick up things along the first hour or so and be a master in no time. Very simplistic controls that will cause you no problems whatsoever. Other Things to Note: This game is long. Very long. There's a new game plus, with three difficulties to pick from(easy, normal, hard). No matter which one you choose, you'll probably have a hard time if this is your first Shin Megami Tensei game. Imagine going through 10 floors of Tartarus and encountering an enemy which has an instant death spell. He gets the first turn because he back-attacked you and casts it on the hero. It connects, and the hero dies. Game over, hope you saved. The game won't baby you unless you play on Easy, in which you get 10 continues.

author: Menji
review_title: The hopeless dream of being - not seeming, but being
review_text: After a long day at school, you return home excited to wind down and play a game. Little did you know you would be going right back to school! Persona 3 FES takes a fresh approach to the standard RPG game. You are an orphaned boy who has just transferred to Gekkoukan High. A couple of crazy things happen on your first day there and you discover your persona has awakened. Naturally, you’re just as scared as your were when puberty first hit and you don’t know what to do now. Fortunately, you happen to live in a dorm where this has happened to everyone else. You see, every night at the stroke of midnight the world is covered a green fog. They call this the Dark Hour. Everyone in the world disappears except for your group of course. Your group is a Specialized Extracurricular Execution Squad (SEES). Their purpose is to hunt down monsters called shadows. They’ve been appearing during the full moon and it is your duty to hunt out and destroy these shadows before they can harm anybody. But that isn’t the only thing different during the Dark Hour. Your school has been transformed into an enormous tower filled with hundreds of floors known as Tartarus. No one knows what is at the top but you have a natural curiosity to find out and destroy all the shadows on the way up. Unlike most RPGs, the game of Persona is structured for you. You follow the days of the year and once you get to the last day (don’t worry I won’t tell when that is) it’s over. Don’t let that scare you away from the game though. It is well over 70 hours and then at least 20 more for The Answer which is one of the new features in the FES edition. Each day has its own advantages. You will go to school Monday through Saturday and attend class. There is free time after school, the evenings and Sunday for you to explore the city and improve your social links. Social links are one of the major things in the game. There around twenty of them for you to seek out. Each one applies to different arcanas like Death, Lovers, Sun, and Moon. Improving these social links gives you bonuses for creating new Personas. Going about improving them is somewhat challenging but fairly straightforward. During your free time after school or during the evening you can visit classmates, join a club, or befriend an old man to establish connections and improve the relationship. Hanging out with each link will improve the level, while neglecting them or dating more than one girl at time will have negative affects on the link. It may sound complicated and annoying if you’ve ever played The Sims but it is easy to figure out keep in order. However, here lies my first problem with the game. Certain characters are only available during certain days, namely Sunday. That also happens to be the only day people will call you up in order hang out. So while you may decline their request which could result in a reverse social link you are going to miss out. Halfway through the game, your evenings become so free that they are extremely wasteful. This open time would be perfect for your overcrowded Sundays. The characters are all unique, maybe a little too much. They are all on complete ends of the personality spectrum. But this makes it easier to relate to one of them and differentiate between them all. The game world is disappointingly small. You are confined to one city with six locations. You spend just about all of your time in only three of them. And for whatever reason only two of them are open at night. There is a mall for improving your attributes and purchasing items. Naturally, the school is a place where you spend a lot of time and lastly your dorm. The other three locations are almost completely pointless. They are fun to explore once but after that they only serve as a location to meet up with friends. Even your dorm is wasted. There are floors for the guys and gals but each character’s room serves no purpose. There isn’t even anything exciting in your room except for a TV and computer. The graphics and music are unique. Everything is straight out of a Japanese anime which allows for colorful scenery. There are also animated FMVs throughout the game. The music is a mix of Japanese pop-rap and it is incredibly catchy. Persona 3 is very exciting at first. It does get repetitive halfway through the game. You will fall into some pattern where you will go to school, establish social links, and fight in Tartarus for the whole month and then a bit of the storyline will occur and get you excited again. If you can get past that, you’ll love it. And even if you struggle, you will witness certain things that will get you hooked again. I would recommend this game to any RPG fan that is looking for something different. This is the version to get because it gives you an extra segment and apparently extended storylines on social links. There is plenty of replay value with the option for a New Game+ so be sure to check it out!

author: Yamate
review_title: Time to grab your 'Evoker' once again!
review_text: August of 2007 was a very good month for the PS2. Why you ask? Another 'Shin Megami Tensei' game just landed on US shores. Now, a lot of people were very iffy about that release, but games of the same franchise like 'Nocturne' and the 'Digital Devil Saga' titles brought fresh RPG experiences and hope that the next game will deliver a new flavor. Then, Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 3 hit the store shelves and gamers are taken aback by this new entry. What made the game so enjoyable to fans of the series are the many features that the game had to offer. A dark and engrossing storyline, a assorted cast of wonderful characters, a deep Social Link system, the traditional RPG turn-based battles, and the 'Persona' system. The game took many players by storm and garnered many awards by the media. Yes, that's how good the game was (with some flaws that don’t really hurt the experience much). Players who have completed it achieved a sensed of accomplishment in ways that keep them coming back for more (some players even underwent multiple repeats). What the hardcore fans also knew from this game’s release was that an expansion game for Persona 3 was already out in Japan back in April 19 of 2007. Now, a lot of people are upset at the fact that Japan got more of the experience than the people in the Americas. But, given the mass reception by the media, as well as the number of fan requests by the people, developer and publisher, Atlus , definitely took this to heart and decided to port the game. The news, however, was kind of a hush-hush situation with a couple of hints, but finally spread word of its release on April 22, 2007. Although, fans should've already seen this coming, anyway! It was on this day that the expansion arrives on US shelves in the form of Persona 3 FES. For those that do not know, ‘FES’ refers to the word ‘festival’ celebrating the fame and success of the original Persona 3. FES offers the original Persona 3 with a number of new gameplay features that really makes this more than a mere expansion. Just how good is this game and will it please the fans of the series? Well, isn’t that why I wrote this review in the first place? Definitely! Well, without further ado, here’s my take on this title. (PRESENTATION) As most of you already know, Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 3 FES is a dungeon-crawling turn-based RPG by Atlus. The game is the supposed ‘expansion’ to the original Persona 3 released in 2007. Although, this is considered an expansion, a lot of content in this game makes this more than just an expansion in my view. How much more is packed into this game? Well, the original Persona 3 gave players a deep story, a deep customizable gameplay element, lots of Personas and Arcana, fun little dating sim quirks, and a likable cast of characters that seam well into the Shin Megami Tensei universe. FES gives more for the players with additional content. The original game now gets more Persona and Arcana, additional characters to interact with, and the option of changing your party’s appearances in battle. But what’s really snazzy is the additional storyline added to the game that follows up after the events of the main story, which reportedly adds another whopping thirty hours of playtime. And in that storyline, a new character joins the party for battle, and several new plots twists and turns takes players on a new ride within the Persona 3 universe. I’d say that’s a big bang for just a $30.00 price tag (which is also a big deal for those new to the game). (STORY) As stated previously, the story of Persona 3 FES is split into two storylines. This time, players have the option of selecting either “The Journey”, which is the original Persona 3 that’s enhanced with FES, and “The Answer” which is the follow of the original story. In “The Journey” you take the role of a cool-looking main character that you name yourself. This storyline takes place in Japan, of course, in which you move to Gekkoukan High School when you realize that strange things have been happening since your arrival into your new dormitory. You then join up with your fellow dormmates who also attend your school, and fend off against the shadows that lurk about in the city during the ‘Dark Hour’, an hour which rest between midnight and 1 am. Together with your allies, you’ll discover the mystery of the Dark Hour as well as the destiny that is set before you. In “The Answer”, the story takes place after the events of “The Journey”. You take control of the female humanoid android named Aigis as you band with your former allies once again. Here, time has been looping, always remaining on March 31 and Aigis and her allies attempt to discover why that is. That’s where she meets up with the enigmatic Metis, another female android like her, and also venture into the Abyss of Time to put an end to the endless loop that’s present before them. It is in the Abyss that Aigis and her friends discover other things inside it's depths (first timers should play "The Journey" before tackling this story). (GAMEPLAY) “The Journey” has players do two things: during the day, the hero interacts with every day life such as school and friends. But when midnight rolls around the corner, the Dark Hour appears and players will venture into the Tartarus, a massive tower with many floors. It’s here where the dungeon-crawling and combat take place. The game progresses in days and split into different times of day: morning, afternoon, evening, and night. During those days, the hero will study at school to raise social status as well as making friends to boost the power of your Persona, buy items and equipment during the day, and visit many locales. Once the Dark Hour comes around, you and your comrades enter Tartarus, from where you will climb from floor to floor to do battle with the Shadows. After you’ve done some exploring, you get some rest, tomorrow arrives, and you start your day again. Repeat. You will also encounter the Velvet Room in certain areas. There, you will manage and fuse Personas together to form more powerful Persona (if you made a lot of social interaction, even better) as well as fuse weapons to create stronger ones (the weapon fusion is new to FES). The story progresses in specific events on the calendar, but you’ll have plenty of time to do some interaction and level grinding. As this is a turn-based RPG, the battle controls are simple, but you only have control over the main character. Don’t fret over that, as you will give ‘Tactics’ commands to your comrades. And as in any RPG game, there will be types and elements with strengths and weakness to tackle. However, striking criticals and weak points of enemies can topple them, allowing you or your allies to attack again in succession. Be careful, because the enemy can do the same. If all enemies are down, you and your friends can initiate an All-Out-Attack to assault all enemies and inflict heavy damage. Your Persona is what give you stat boosts and skills to dish out in battle, but you can only edit you own Persona. Your comrades’ Persona become stronger as they level up and go through personal changes during the story, giving them a better edge to use alongside your own. You’ll have a lot of customization for your Persona and your equipment to suit you strengths. “The Answer” is slightly different in that the Persona customization is limited somewhat, no more day-to-day activities (you are repeating the same day), and going into the Abyss of Time is like that of the Tartarus. Monsters there are also harder to tackle. (GRAPHICS) The world of Persona 3 gives off a mix of colorful Japanese locales and darkness of the aura that is the Dark Hour. The battle animations are impressive as always from the original Persona 3. Graphically,overall, it isn’t as good, but it never really isn’t a big issue as the story and gameplay drags the players into the game. The artwork presented is always wonderful to admire, with the characters changing their facial expressions, and the environments blend in to the typical flavor that is Shin Megami Tensei. Add to that the amazing anime sequences, and you’ve got a solid visual experience that everyone can be comfortable with. (SOUND) This is a ‘love or hate’ category when it comes to this game. The music in the game presents a mix of techno, mood setters, and hip-hop tracks that flow with the theme of Persona 3. A lot of people were in disagreement over some themes, like the game’s main battle theme. But the songs presented in this game never hurt the ears (some players have even grown into them). The sound effects blend into the many spells and effects during the battle, which is superb. The voice acting that brought life to the characters is also top-notch. Although, there are some voices I believe that don’t really fit into the character, but that can be overlooked. All in all, the sounds are what should be expected from any Shin Megami Tensei title. In this sense, it’s very favorable to the fans and to newcomers alike. (CONS) There are some issues (as with any game) that are sometime displeasing. The most obvious is the tedious task of going from floor to floor, which gets really repetitive to those with little patience. Also, powerful Persona cannot be acquired without initiating some higher-level social interaction, and voices in battle can sometimes grain on you. For those who cannot stand any of these gameplay problems should stay away from this one. However, renting this game to try it out won’t hurt, either. Who knows, you might enjoy it despite the issues. (OVERALL) It’s what all Shin Megami Tensei and Persona 3 fans have been waiting for and I mean that when I write this. You got a mix of everything players have enjoyed about the original Persona 3 and add a new level to it. Fans of Persona 3 should’ve already picked this one up. Newcomers will come to expect a very good story plot and great day-to-day elements. If there is any game that can keep the PS2 running in its final years, this would be one of them, I guarantee it! (REVIEWER SCORE: 9/10)

author: Luniara
review_title: The Ps2 isn't dead yet!
review_text: Persona 3 is possibly the easiest to get into of the Series from what I've played so far. (Digital Devil Saga 1 and 2, and Nocturne.) With it being played out in a normal environment and having a pretty easy to follow but well done storyline this is definitely a good first experience for those looking to get into the series! Graphics: 7 They're really nothing all that special. The art work is simply gorgeous, done by the same who did the art work for Stella Deus of course. Each character design is well detailed, and the environments are wonderfully drawn. However when put into 3D the graphics feel like someone spent a few hours toying with Maya and slapped them onto a disc. The concepts are wonderful, but they could have been executed much better. Gameplay: 8 There's still no such thing as a perfect game to me, so 8 is a pretty high ranking. The gameplay involves wandering around a dungeon known as tartarus. This is more so a graphical thing but the dungeon looks very boring after awhile, and while the floors are random everytime you go they carry the same design structure until you get higher, and than that one remains the same for another 30-50 floors and repeat. The fun part is what you can do in the dungeons. You can actually see your party members following you around, and you can talk to them to check how they're doing, and give them equipment. They give you a little thank you message or sometimes wont like what you give them. Im not sure if this effects gameplay at all, but its a nice touch. You can also issue commands to them to split up or regroup, or specifically order them to split up and kill the enemy or hunt for items. Fun stuff.
