Enemies are encountered via poking them on the map rather then random. You determine how the battle starts. Sneak up on them and give em a little poke with your trusty sword and you start out with an advantage sometimes distressing foes, making it easier. If they sneak up on you however, or catch you running it's their advantage! In battle you can attack, issue tactics (as you cant control anyone but the main character,) use items and exploit enemy Weaknesses. The weakness system can make the game VERY easy as knocking an enemy over gives you another turn. If you spam and knock all enemies over you can perform an all out attack, which pretty much kills all monsters. you can summon your persona, which is basicaly a manifestation of some Mythological being. There are alot of them to collect, and each has an interesting background story. If you bother to learn them you can almost see how they fit with the character they belong to, and the social link. The social link is like a dating sim, or a friendship sim. You meet people, you hang out with them and build your relationship. You don't need to do them all, but the stronger bond the stronger the persona you can build. Careful as you CAN make them mad at you, say hanging out with another girl when you're intimate with one of them. Bare in mind you must maximize your bond to be able to unlock the best personas in the game. They are WORTH the time. Music/Sound: 6 The music really drags the game down. While some of the tunes are memorable towards the end of the game the usual dorm room music gets repetitive fast. You will usually hear the same four themes throughout the entire game, and they're just annoying loops. Also, tartarus our usual dungeon has the same boring theme throughout the entire travel. The voice acting is wonderful though, characters brought to life by their voice actors, there are a few exceptions to this wonderful cast, but for the most part the voice actors fir the bill. Story: 10. The story couldnt be any better to me. It's the heart of the game. Each character has a very deep rooted background story which makes you connect with them, and the religious references, (even a hippie Jesus,) add to the amusement. The game seems to revolve around death and the fact that Mankind is wishing for it's own end. There's also the fact that there's a mysterious hour inbetween midnight and 1am called the dark hour. Few know of it, and those that due either are persona users are targets of the shadows, our basic villain of the story. they're pretty much monsters that wander ouf ot the tower which by the way is your school during the dark hour. More than anything it's the characters that drive the story forward, and the little added bits of optional conversation that make the world of Persona 3 seem all the more believable. Ending: 10 I couldn't have asked for a better ending. Why do I put this in a review? Ever ask how a movie is just to hear it was great but the ending pretty much ruins the entire movie for you? Just a tip. There's also an alternate ending. Fes is of course different from the original and here's a short list of what it adds. Weapon custimization using Persona added social links plus more time to complete social links. A higher difficulty setting. Little subtle extras that aren't needed but add a nice touch to the atmosphere. Extra sidequests Alternate costumes for the characters, (Note party members might react funny to being asked to wear them! :D) An additional 20-30 hours of gameplay, somewhat of an Epilogue, (Oh Lunar 2 I miss thee!) Total: 8/10 The game has its flaws in terms of graphics and sound but the gameplay and the story which are the core of an RPG more than make up for it. Its definitely worth a go at! Dont rent, buy as it might disappear. Even Owners of the original version should find something new here.

author: ivory_soul
review_title: Enough upgrades to be worth a purchase
review_text: I heard all the hoopla about Persona 3 , but the next-gen craze sidetracked me from it. I finally rented the game, and I have to say I am very impressed. I’m tired of the same old random battle JRPG with cliché stories, characters, and battle systems. P3 tries to do something different with practically every element. When you start the game, you’ll notice the game has beautifully drawn anime cutscenes. The story doesn’t become very clear until after you start playing, but this is OK. The first thing I have to say is that the game takes forever to get going. Maybe 5–6 hours into the game, you’ll really start getting interesting, and most of the play mechanics will be taught. When you’re not fighting, you’ll be living your regular school life by studying hard and preparing for exams. The game has a calendar event set up, and you go to school, talk to some people, and you can choose to stay awake in class and listen to the lecture to increase your academic skills. Sometimes you’ll have to answer questions (it’s mostly guessing), and maybe your charm will increase. After school, you can meet up with your friends to strengthen your social link (more on that later). Depending on the responses you choose, they will affect your relationships. You can also go shopping at the mall for items, weapons, armor, etc. Another thing I have to mention is that there isn’t enough to buy before the next moon phase (more on that later). So there is one new thing for each member, and that’s it. This can make traveling to the upper levels of Tarturus even harder (more on that later). The game’s story is about shadows that try to wreak havoc during the Dark Hour, which is midnight. During this hour, the dorm you stay at turns into a mysterious tower known as Tartarus, and you must climb the tower, fighting stronger and stronger enemies. Every 30 days, you fight a boss, and some events happen that evolve the story. During those 30 days, you have to increase your social links, level up, and acquire all that you can before the big boss. When you fight in battle, you use your personas, which are like Aeons (think Final Fantasy ), and they are your strongest attacks. You’ll rarely attack yourself, so you always concentrate on your personas. Some personas have different magic abilities, etc. The battles are won by determining the enemy’s weaknesses and exploiting them. When you hit their weakness, you get one more turn, and the enemies fall down. If you get all the enemies to fall down, you can do an all-out attack where all the players will maul the enemies for extra damage. This is key to mastering because you can die very easily early in the game because leveling up takes longer than it should. Luckily, you can switch personas in mid-battle, so you can exploit accordingly. One irritating thing about this game is that they changed the elements’ names. Instead of Fire, Ice, Wind, and Fire, it’s Zio, Bufu, and Garu (light), and it’s really stupid. Why did they do this? Probably just to be cute, but it confuses you, and you have to know what these names mean. Once you win a battle, you may get Shuffle Time, which lets you see the faces of a card and shuffles them around. Some may give you bonus experience, some may be a new persona, and some may be weapons. While you run around through Tarturus, you can see the shadows, so this game isn’t random. If you hit them first, you get an advantage, but if you let them hit you, it’s not so good. The game mainly revolves around personas, so, of course, you can make your own. Take your cards to the Velvet Room, and you can combine them to make better personas. Now there are attributes and rules, but these are confusing and pointless, so you just add a few up and see what it makes. It’s really simple and easy to use, but you can’t do this for a while because you can only create a persona that is at your level. Also in the VR, you can take requests from Elizabeth by bringing her certain items at certain dates for rewards. I found this very hard because you never really know what she’s talking about half the time. I think it’s mainly there for completionists. Social links affect your persona because if you have a friend who is a Magician SL, all your Magician personas will level up faster. Of course, there are events every day that always change. Sometimes you can’t go to Tartarus at night because your members are too tired, some may get sick, some may be busy studying for exams, etc. This changes things up all the time, so not one day is the same. When it all boils down, the game is generally the same. Go to school; go to Tarturus over and over. There are no worlds or levels to actually explore, so this may disappoint some people. When in doubt, pick up Persona 3 because you are going to have a blast, and there are dozens of hours of RPG goodness here. With decent voice acting, memorable characters, and a great battle system, you will truly love this game.

author: rikuthedarkness
review_title: Butterflys floating in the air bring joy and sadness to your eyes
review_text: The joy of life is not getting the most out of life on your own but instead, having friends to guide you on the way as you achieve perfection and become one with the world. Perfection, a word that describes this game pretty much in its entirety. This game has brought tears to a lot of peoples eyes due to its compelling and passionate story line and for its lack of problems Aside from a few flaws this game will blow your mind *excuse the pun* Persona 3 Fes was released in the U.K in 2008 as a Directors Cut of Persona 3 which was released in 2007. The game adds several elements to the previous game such as: A few favoured persona, easier social links, a weapon fusion system and a bit more. Developed by Atlus the game itself is a real beauty the graphics, soundtrack, gameplay, character development are amazingly detailed and enticing. Lets take a look at some of the categories Story:9/10 The setting of Persona 3 takes place in Iwatodai in the year 900CE or as people like to refer as 2010 Iwatodai was built by the Kirijo Corperation and this is where the game is set. You take the role as the silent protagonist of the game referred to in the manga as Seji. who is moved into a dorm when he transfers to the school of Gekkoukan. However strange things start happening around the city and pretty early in the game you awaken your Persona or other self. The rrest of the game takes place over a number of months with the characters trying to figure out why the Dark Hour (the hour between midnight and the next day) occours. You are joined by members of SEEs or the Specialized Extracurricular Execution Squad. who can also use persona. Throughout the game you will recruit more members and make special bonds known as social links. Gameplay: 10/10 This game will take hours to complete, through personal experience it took me at least 100 hours on normal mode and an extra 40 for the answer. Most of your time will be spent levelling up personas or building social links to either : get a girlfriend or to gain extra experience when fusing persona. The raw ability of the gamethat takes up your time is amazing. you can undertake quests or go to the mall and do many things such as :Go to karaoke, Drink coffee, Play arcade games to raise your stats. However the main focus of the game is to make your way up Tartarus which serves as the dungeon for the game. You will visit Tartarus many times to level up and gain new persona. which is awfully hard on hard mode. Soundtrack: 8/10 The Soundtrack for Persona 3 FES is vast but repetitive as most of the time you will be exploring the mall or town or school and you will just get bored of hearing the same song. even if it is upbeat and entertaining, after playing this game you will want to put your volume on mute. However when exploring tartarus each time you move to a different block you will get new BGM to listen to and you can also request other music if you get bored of the rest. The main theme song is Burn My Dread which is played when the game loads and an extended version once you complete the game Graphics:9/10 Many people complain that Persona 3 FES's graphics let it down, I find this to be balony as the anime cutscenes are excellent the summoning of persona and the persona themselves are very detailed, and the detail of background images and places that are explored is just outstanding, some people say it isn't as detailed as final fantasy 12 or 13 so what. in its own right persona 3 FES has its own ability to just take your breath away with the graphics. The drawing of the characters when they speak also shows how carefully they have been thought out, even Junpei who has a beard (kind of) is very detailed. Even Tartarus has very detailed blocks and floors, each coloured in their own specific funky way. Final Score 9/10 From blowing your mind with an evoker to summoning Satan, From flirting with your classmates to getting your teacher to tell you she loves you. This game has nearly everything a Great Rpg needs, Music, Emotional Characters, School, Friends and Monsters fighting for you. without a doubt this game is in my collection of Greatest Rpgs of all time. If you don't buy this and you're an avid roleplayer then I can't see why you play Rpgs. Time stands still for no one it delivers all to the same fate- Quote by Igor Review by RikutheDarkness

author: edestep
review_title: Perhaps a different set of opinions on this game
review_text: A good many of the people in the message boards talk about this game as though it is the greatest thing since sliced bread. The cover says it was RPG of the Year in 2007 and the few other reviews that exist of this game hype it pretty hard. I will fully admit that there are elements of the game that are sweet. Some elements of the game are quite simply confusing. Some are down right disturbed. And finally, a few of the elements are quite simply lifted from other video games (not necessarily a negative, it is what it is). So on to the review: Gameplay: 9/10 The battle system is pretty sweet, though at times it can get a little complicated. Perhaps my video game mind just isn't what it used to be, but I prefer not feeling like I've solved a Rubik's cube after every time I shut my game off. It's certainly not the kind of game that you can casually dedicate 30-45 minutes to here or there... it really requires full effort. There are times when that suits me just fine, but there are times when I really can't dedicate a full afternoon to killing evil monsters that look like somebody spilled pudding on the floor (one single example from extremely early in the game). My main gameplay gripes come from being required to intimately know elements of Japanese history and culture to succeed in some of the... well, they aren't really mini-games... um. We'll call them course related questions. After getting a few of these wrong, I threw my controller in disgust. I'm not an idiot, but Japanese is really just not my strong suit. I don't like being punished for not being up on THAT particular culture. This game would've been better served making that element Americanized. Music/Sound: 2/10 A melange of the most atrocious J-Pop garbage that my ears have ever been assaulted with and a grab bag of terrible and decent voice over work. Sometimes the voices make the situation really feel legitimate. Other times, it sounds like a 3rd grader is reading his hooked on phonics guide. And that J-Pop music I mentioned? Don't get me started. It is so terribly OUT OF PLACE in this game, that it is quite simply agonizing. If I hear the extremely repetitive "chorus" of "I never felt like... doo doo doo doo doo" I think I'm going to never feel like waking up again, because I will assuredly shoot myself in the face... not unlike the characters in the game do. Innovation/Originality: 6/10 Speaking of shooting oneself in the face, this is really a mixed bag in this game. Sometimes, the game seems like nothing else you've ever played before. Other times, the game feels like you are playing one gigantic cliche. Tartarus, the tower that the high schoolers explore, feels almost identical to the Ancient Cave in Lufia II... right down to the look of some of the enemies that you face. Three Card Monty was used in Super Mario RPG to determine certain benefits after combat. Certain activities bestow benefits onto your main character, similarly to River City Ransom, even. While I appreciate borrowing ideas from other games, sometimes it seems almost lazy. I never expect a game to be completely original, as with everything that has already been done, it's pretty impossible to be completely original. The originality in this game mainly comes in the story line... Storyline: 10/10 This storyline is wonderful. The plot, the concept... at certain points it almost feels like Bully RPG as you're wandering the halls of the high school. Other times it feels almost like The Sims as you carefully consider how to spend your freetime to maximize your character. The idea of an alternate time dimension is really cool, and very well executed. The characters and their interactions are very well done. The entire concept of the game is really well done, and absolutely makes it. Overall: 6/10 The music and sound are really that horrible, the gameplay can be frustrating at times, but is immaculate at other times. I look at this game as though it is a niche RPG... it will (and does) have a legion of dedicated fans who proclaim it to be absolutely amazing. But, it's certainly not for people who look to use video games as an escape. The plot and storyline are so deep, that to really get the full benefit of the game, a lot of energy and time absolutely must be dedicated to it, or you'll just end up more and more confused.

author: Cymery
review_title: A game full of Shadows
review_text: When Persona 3 was released in 2007 I bought it not knowing what I was getting into. It was $60 and came with an artbook and soundtrack. In spite of this I couldn't like the game and after spending that much money I tried hard to like it but couldn't. I traded that game in got $35 trade in credit and went along to spend the credit on what I considered to be better games. A year later I came across the title Persona 3 FES. It caught my interest so to see what it was I watched the trailers, heard about the extra content, and loved the new price tag. So I bought it and I'm glad I did. I can now appreciate it as it deserves to be. Gameplay: 9/10 The gameplay is for the most part great. The character you control moves at a good pace not to fast and not to slow. The only true problem with the gameplay is in battles. The problem is that you can only control your character, usually not a big deal but the AI in this game isn't that bright. For example in one battle I fought no matter how many times the other characters said that attack would heal the monsters the AI controlled characters kept using that attack. Another thing in fights that some consider to be a problem is that when your character dies in a fight its game over. Myself I never found this to be a problem. In fact I found it to be a nice idea as you are the main character and without you the story couldn't go on. Sound: 7/10 I'll admit that there is some nice tunes in the game. Other sounds are just plain wierd and leave me scratching my head thinking what was that? The music in Tartarus is great and you have 4 or 5, I can't recall how many options there are to choose from. During the day however in school in one part of the game there's this bouncy music playing with french words repeating itself again and again. Some parts of the music are great and others are.....well I'll stick with the word unique to sum it up. Graphics: 10/10 I've never come across graphics like this and I actually like it. So far as I've been able to tell there is no difference between the original Persona 3 graphics and FES. Not a bad thing really as it would have delayed its release if they had decided to amp it up. The environments are well done and have dark scenery where it should be and bright colorful areas in the right places. The anime cinematics were done in a modern design rather then following traditional anime. Not a bad thing as its pretty eyecatching. Story: 10/10 The story begins when the main character moves back to the town he lived in as a child. As a orphan he goes to live in a school dorm and meets an assortment of colorful if cliched characters. After staying in the dorm for a few days the dorm is attacked by a giant monster called a Shadow. He awakens to his power and defeats the monster and so his story begins. The story is definitely Japanese based and is very good. Not overly long and not too short either. There are quite a few shocking twists and turns in the plot and the end of the game is bound to leave the player feeling sad that its over. Overall: 9/10 Persona 3 FES is a great game. I enjoyed it a lot more then the original Persona 3. It was well worth the $30 price tag. The main storyline doesn't change from the original Persona 3 but that's alright as the story was great to begin with. Definitely a must buy game.

author: ExtantGamer
review_title: Persona 3 FES - Why have I not played this before?
review_text: As a big fan of JRPG games, I was surprised that I'd never played this before. I just never knew anybody who had ever played anything from the Shin Megami Tensei series. Regardless, this game was my introduction into the universe of adult Pokemon and I am very happy with it. The game itself is not perfect but it is very close. Graphics - 8/10 For a PS2 game, the graphics are good. You know exactly what you're looking at, the spell casting is beautiful, and certain floors of tartarus are eye bogglingly fun. The enemies are quite easy to differentiate Even without the talking view of the characters, they still are able to get across a certain sense of emotion through their actions. Not the best I've seen out there, but quite good nonetheless. Controls - 10/10 The controls are quite crisp. Granted it is an RPG and controller lag isn't a big thing, It still isn't difficult to get the MC behind an enemy to initiate a battle. Gameplay - 9/10 The social link system is surprisingly deep as is the vat of Personas the MC can hold. The fusion system takes quite a bit of getting used to to understand how it works. Once that happens, the fusion system is immensely powerful, giving you most of what you need to keep on par with the big baddies that show up throughout the story. The boss fights are deliciously difficult unless you power level way above their heads. The full moon system forces the player to keep up with both their party level and their social links which can be a bit overwhelming for a new person, but again, once you're used to it, it's quite enjoyable. Story - 9/10 Every party character has their own reasons for fighting and the Social Links are pretty interesting for the most part. Even the one I disliked, Nozomu was still interesting to see come full circle. The main story is unfortunately a bit slow though, which may be a turn off for some gamers. Although once you start understanding what is going on and the big reveal happens, you'll be motivated to play through the rest of the game to see how it wraps up, and it does wrap up quite nicely. Special Category: Difficulty - 10/10 As a foolish move, when I started the game, I neglected to look at the publisher's name and though "I'm good at JRPGs, I'll throw it on hard." This game is made by Atlus and is punishing in the difficulty while still managing to not infuriate the player into never playing again. I managed to complete my first run on Hard, but I was a bit haggard at the end of it. You WILL get a sense of accomplishment when finishing this game.

author: carlde21
review_title: This remake has a chance to be a star, but a few minor setbacks along the way hold it back.
review_text: I don't do things the normal way and that extends to the Persona series. I played the most recent mainline games, Royal (5), Golden (4), and Reload (3) in backward order. Because of this, I had lowered expectations going into Reload but they were pleasantly exceeded in many ways. Granted there were a few flaws and some weak points, but this was a captivating experience for the most part. There are many aspects to love about this game but for me, unraveling and figuring out the complex web of interpersonal connections was at the forefront. It is a game that shows people at their most vulnerable and the delicate balance between relationship building and life's priorities. Oh, plus the imposing Tartarus tower which easily dwarves the Burj Khalifa. I didn't fully understand the story but I'll attempt a brief synopsis while tiptoeing around spoilers. From what I understood, everyone has a shadow which is the part of the human consciousness we try to hide because they are the darker parts of ourselves and they manifest in some tangible form. With that in mind, the father of one of the main characters does experiments using shadows to try and manipulate time. I am unsure how the shadows got this power and why harnessing the energy of these shadows would help with time manipulation, but oh well. One scientist goes against everyone else he is working with and divides a powerful shadow into 12 parts before it can do serious damage. The result is these shadows go crazy and chaos ensues. This leads to three consequences: 1. The escape of all the shadows the scientists had collected. 2. The creation of the dark hour, the hidden 25th hour that starts at 00:00 (or midnight), and 3. The creation of Tartarus, a huge tower that houses many shadows, and to everyone's assumption, the answer to the dark hour is at the top. Non-persona users turn into coffins and once the hour is over, go about their lives with no recollection of this hidden hour. That is, unless shadows freely roaming around for this hour lure someone out of their coffin. If they can succeed in this, they feed on the person's psyche, like a vampire would feed on someone's blood giving that person "Apathy Syndrome" which effectively turns them into something like a zombie. The physical world is also altered beyond recognition with enigmatic hues and rivers flowing with blood-red liquid and the moon turning into a mysterious green. Makoto, the main character holds the key to unlocking and solving the mystery of the dark hour. So, that's the story's basic premise, the big picture. But for me, the key point of playing Persona 3, 4, or 5 is the social links the main character comes into contact with day-to-day. The short-term smaller picture that, over 9 months, adds up to huge developments and game-changing impacts. These bonds are formed during free time. By hanging out with a specific link and giving good responses when prompted, you gain points that help to increase your rank with them. Increased ranks allow for stronger personas of that arcana to be fused. Every character and social link has tough backstories filled with loss, betrayal, and confusion but also commendable development. I'll leave it to newcomers to discover these intricate stories, as there are 22 links. Careful time management is key to maxing all links to rank 10. I was only able to max 18 on a blind first playthrough. Some of these links are automatic while others have prerequisites before they can be started like having a separate link at a specific rank or having 1 or more, of the 3 social skills at a required rank. I had all of them, courage, academics, and charm, at maximum (level 6) by mid-November so there are plenty of opportunities to add points to all three. Academics take much longer to reach maximum than charm or courage, which I maxed out at least a month earlier. Outside of the Moon link, they excel at holding interest for the 10+ meetings they require, though they aren't as in-depth as Persona 4 and 5. Still, they are compelling, especially the sun link, one of the most moving links in all three games in my view. The party members are well written and thankfully don't include the typical mascot some games have, Persona like Teddy from Golden or Morgana from Royal. The closest thing to that is the adorable Koromaru, seemingly a tribute to Hachiko, a beautiful story I would recommend anyone look up. Junpei is close to being a carbon copy of Ryuji (5) and Yosuke (4) because all three serve as a sidekick to the main character and are academically low, immature, and impulsive but somehow lovable despite their shortcomings. However, they have vastly different backstories and slightly different growth. But for sure Atlus has that archetype down and I wouldn't be shocked to see another character in that vein for Persona 6. Several other characters can be switched in and out of the party. Ken has a heartbreaking history and must come to terms with his deeply harbored anger midway through the game but even with that said, it was tough to see him as more than the pesky little kid who has to tag along with the older, cooler kids. Fuuka is too timid, almost annoyingly so, and that's coming from me who was painfully shy until around 16. Considering how much she helps the team, she is far too humble, to a fault. Akihiko is the jack of all trades but is mostly associated with his prowess in the boxing ring. Aigis brings to the forefront many questions humanity has had, and will soon have regarding transhumanism in the coming decades as the line between man and machine will continue to blur. Yukari is the most grounded and was the backbone of my team for the entire game, I never took her out unless the game forced it. Finally, there is Mitsuru. I liked her but let's be real, there is no way Mitsuru is a teenager even with her background in mind. Her voice inflection and mannerisms paint her as someone in their mid-30s, certainly not high school-aged. I've had mom-like friends in University who took care of the friend group but she was another level to the point where I didn't find it believable. If Charlotte from Trials of Mana and Lymle from Star Ocean were unbelievable in how immature they were, Mitsuru was the exact opposite. Yes, I get her childhood was difficult, but even with all that said, it didn't strike me as realistic. I started to imagine her as the adopted 30-year-old mom to the group and it worked much better that way. Makoto can spend time with all of the party members at night which may unlock new skills in battle or net useful items. He can also decide to spend time on the computer and use plenty of useful programs including one that helps social links level up quicker. The battle system is reminiscent of Golden and Royal, with some similarities to Shin Megami Tensei 5. They can be tough if you are slogging through them without thought but exploiting weaknesses can speed fights significantly. Attacks are slash, strike, pierce, fire, ice, electric, wind, light, dark, and the wildcard all mighty which works if all else fails. Plus the standard healing, ailments, buffs, and debuffs. Using shift, the majority of battles end within a minute, sometimes without the enemy getting a move. Hitting an enemy weakness knocks that enemy down and gives the player another turn. But this also allows the character to shift to one of the other 3 characters by pressing L2. Shift almost feels like a cheat mode for the majority of random battles and some of the boss battles when there are multiple enemies with different weaknesses because one player can strike one enemy's weakness and shift to another character who can hit the other enemy's weakness and so on until everyone is down. Once all enemies are down, a prompt for an all-out attack occurs. This is a special attack where all four characters join together to pummel all enemies, usually into oblivion. Of course, later in the game, some bosses have no weaknesses and can't be knocked down so all-out attacks are impossible. Instead, they are either immune or even reflect or absorb most types of attacks. The only way to hit them is with all-mighty or Theurgy, which functions as a limit break that once filled, is unblockable regardless of enemy resistance. This isn't a particularly difficult game, I don't recall having any issues, at least on normal so for veterans I'd recommend starting on hard. Stylistically, the in-battle menus are similar to Persona 5 so if you've played that, it is easy to instantly feel at home with this battle system. Ending a battle with an all-out attack or critical often (always?) leads to a shuffle time. Similar to Persona 4, cards appear that can grant tons of benefits such as increased experience (EXP), a new persona, money, skill cards, and so on. There are two issues with this. The shuffle time serves as the primary source of money since monsters don't drop it. Being hard up for cash for the majority of the first half of the game, this seems like the most logical card to take. After all, chests with money are few and far between. However, this is also the primary source of getting new personas other than fusion. This also means there is no demon negation like any many other Persona/SMT/Atlus games, which was missed. Some other subtle but very helpful benefits to this mechanic can be changed depending on social links every time Tartarus is entered. As far as I could tell, entering Taratus with a maxed social link added new, excellent cards to the deck, like permanent stat increases. Speaking of Tartarus, I won't spoil that, just know it is massive. For sure, at least for me, more than I could have imagined. The game does a pretty good job of breaking exploration of this beast of a dungeon into manageable chunks. There are plenty of warp points out and new dungeon mechanics are introduced at the perfect pace without ever feeling overloaded. Plus whenever a new warp appears, it is likely you've gained at least a few levels and can go inside the blue door to the left of the entry to try your hand at fusing any newly obtained personas. This is a pretty straightforward process and I had zero issues randomly fusing any two personas into anything that had a higher level. Makoto can equip plenty of personas, more as he gains in levels, and having a variety of personas is the best way to go. It is possible to have every type of attack covered. Having different types of personas helps social links to level up quicker. Want to get that Chihiro link up quicker? Have a persona that corresponds to that link, in her case Justice, on hand. So, how does one go about navigating the gigantic Tartarus? Are we left to our own devices and the mercy of luck? Not so much, but glad you asked. That is where the overly humble Fuuka comes into play. Her ability to analyze enemy weaknesses is quintessential, though it can't be used until the second turn of a fight. Out of battle, she can also shroud your party in some kind of cloud so they can go undetected while exploring and even provide timely HP or MP healing, or stat buffs during tough battles. I rarely tried escaping from battle as I found her less than useful for that as the few times I tried, it took more than one turn. On the other hand, enemies are viewable in dungeons and I became somewhat of an expert at evading most of them. They simply don't offer enough EXP and by around floor 90, most of my EXP came from mandatory fights, red doors, and the occasional gold hand, which I seemed to have a lot of luck finding, striking, and beating. Despite the steady inclusion of new mechanics, Tartarus did start to feel repetitive after a while and not enough changes occurred as you climbed, not even a window to the outside world. Perhaps that was the point though, to be fully enclosed in the tower as there was a feeling of claustrophobia. By the way, once you get to around floor 70, don't take your time too much otherwise a nasty enemy called the reaper appears and chases your party. This is an optional super boss that requires a powerful party to beat. I mentioned Persona 3 reload is, stylistically a lot like Persona 4 and especially 5 within battles and this extends to the rest of the game as well. Persona 5 was a work of art so I had no issue with getting those vibes within minutes of starting 3 for the first time. This also happens to be a gorgeous game, not as refined as 5, but still a pleasure to look at over nearly 60 hours. I would say the graphics don't match the darker story, as the locations tend to be vibrant and upbeat. I would venture a guess this was done purposely as I have found Persona tends to be a series of contrasts both pronounced and inconspicuous. Another area that doesn't fit in with the story is the soundtrack, sometimes to the detriment of the overall game and vibe. While I enjoyed the laid-back vibes of "Joy", and "Color your Night" as well as the dorm music a great deal I found two of the songs, "Deep Breath, Deep Breath" and "Change of Seasons" to be incredibly grating. I can't express how ear-splittingly annoying I found those last two, especially the first 45 seconds of Change of Seasons. I prefer a classroom of rambunctious 5th graders (Yes, I taught Year 5 in the past) to whatever the opening to that song is supposed to be. The remote was glued to my thigh for the entire second semester and I probably came close to wearing out my mute button. I listen to all sorts of music, noise rock, and experimental jazz included, but could not find any enjoyment from those two tracks. Generally speaking, the wordless vocals didn't work in many of the songs in the game and it is a case of less being more. The genre shifts within each song were interesting, but at the same time, some of the tracks were too busy. Some say this is a darker game than 4 and 5, but musically I'd beg to differ. 3 is also missing some of the moodier, gloomier music from the first Persona: Revelations back on the original PlayStation. For clarification, I adored the theme song to the last dungeon (9) in Persona 5, The Laboratory of Sorrow with the somber, gorgeous piano that worked perfectly towards the vibes of the game. If words need to be included, Persona: Revelations did it best with its industrial-tinged Deva Yuga. So, with all that said, your head may or may not be ready to explode at this point. If it is ready to explode from all that information and the thought of managing 22 social links and 3 social skills is giving you a headache I would understand this creeping urge to check a FAQ but I would still strongly recommend against using a walkthrough, at least on a first playthrough. I found it much more rewarding to get links and skills to max playing blind and you quickly learn how to manage your time when you realize every link has its schedule with the same location (and, ugh, students aren't available a week before exams). Plus this isn't the type of game you'd want to be glued to a guide because it'd likely be 50/50 attention to the game and guide and this game truly deserves 100% attention. With that said I will admit to cheating on a few of the tougher exam and classroom questions. I pride myself in being kind of a Jack of all trades (but master of none) regarding knowledge but wow were a few of the questions the teachers asked obscure! Look at the question above and to the left, is that common knowledge? On the flip side, living in a former Yugoslav country, I got a chuckle out of the question above and to the right although I couldn't help but feel that Atlus was throwing a little shade. Responding correctly added a point to academics...No, not academics, charm, for whatever reason. Sleeping during class adds to courage while staying awake adds to academics, 1 point each. Persona 3 is a rich tapestry of intricate storytelling, addicting social dynamics, and well-thought-out gameplay with an emphasis on strategic actions. I can already tell that tackling Tartarus will be one of my all-time favorite gaming memories. While there are a few flaws, some of which other gamers might even find endearing, this is a must-play for the many philosophical and ethical questions it brings up and an engaging battle system. I'd just recommend playing this first before Golden and Royal.

author: Blk_Mage_Ctype
review_title: The Arcana is the means by which all things are revealed.
review_text: Introduction: I first discovered Persona 3 when it was originally released back in 2007. I was working in an Electronics Department of a retail store at the time and although I had no prior knowledge of either the Shin Megami Tensei or Persona Series, the big box that the game was packaged in caught my attention. Special edition versions of games that came packaged with a hardbound artbook and a soundtrack CD weren't at all common, so I knew that the game must be a big deal. Typically I wouldn't purchase the third entry in a completely unfamiliar series, but since we only had three copies in stock, I decided to buy it during my break before the end of my shift. When I got home I looked up the series online and it sounded really interesting to me, so I started playing it during my free time. The game captivated me almost immediately with its interesting plot, attractive artstyle, catchy soundtrack, and unique blend of gameplay elements, not to mention the unfamiliar aspect of being in a distinctly modern Japanese setting because at the time most Japanese games were in a medieval fantasy setting or otherwise heavily localized for North American audiences. Although I really enjoyed the gameplay, I wasn't especially pleased with the ending, so I didn't play another Persona game until Persona 5 released. Nevertheless, Persona 3 left an impression on me, so when I heard that it was getting a Remake that was to be included with an Xbox Game Pass Subscription, I knew that I had to check it out. Visual Presentation: Needless to say, Persona 3 looks better than ever in Persona 3 Reload, but it's much more than just a simple visual upgrade of an old PlayStation 2 game. ATLUS could have simply released an HD Remaster of Persona 3 FES with a bit of the additional content/QoL tweaks from Persona 3 Portable, and the vast majority of the fanbase would have been pleased, — heck, the game may have actually been better received if they had done so, but we'll get into that in a later section — yet they chose to completely remake the game from the ground up on an entirely new engine and it looks excellent as a result. The original artstyle is enhanced by new high resolution character portraits, remodeled environments/character models with enhanced detail, more fluid animation, and flashy visual effects. Audio Presentation: Not to be outdone by the visuals, Persona 3 Reload includes a completely remixed and re-recorded soundtrack, and most of it sounds excellent. I'm particularly fond of the new track; Color Your Night, but alas, it isn't all a welcome addition. For example, I don't care for some of the remixed tracks such as; "When the Moon Reaches For the Stars — Reload" which is a shame because I actually quite liked the original, nor do I like "The Dorm — Reload" as much as the original. In addition, the majority of plot significant in-game dialog is fully voice acted, including interections with other characters during Social Links. Gameplay Mechanics and Features: Fans of the original will be pleased to hear that the familiar blend of Visual Novel-esq gameplay, Dungeon Crawling, and traditional Turn Based JRPG Combat are completely intact in Persona 3 Reload. No unnecessary changes were made to the core gameplay, only welcome Quality of Life tweaks have been implemented to enhance the gameplay. One new addition however is Theurgy, a special combat ability — reminiscent of Limit Breaks from Final Fantasy VII — which allows each party member to execute a special move with various effects such as unleashing a devastating attack once their Theurgy Gauge has been fully charged in battle. Theurgy moves are real game-changers which can completely turn the tide of battle when used, but fortunately they're completely optional, so players who simply wish to play the game using the original mechanics only can simply ignore them. Story: Save for a few supplementary scenes added in the form of "Linked Episodes" in order to make the bonds between the protagonist and his male companions feel more fleshed out, the story content of Persona 3 Reload is completely unchanged from the original release, so for the sake of keeping the review spoiler free, I'm not going to go into detail on the subject. Unfortunately, such has become a point of controversy surrounding Persona 3 Reload. Because the game doesn't include any of the additional story content featured in subsequent re-releases such as The Answer/Episode Aigis from Persona 3 FES nor the alternate route of a Female Protagonist featured in Persona 3 Portable, a fair portion of the fanbase has is understandably upset seeing as The Answer/Episode Aigis is a canon follow-up to the ending of Persona 3 and the option to play as a Female counterpart of the protagonist with an alternate storyline adds a substantial amount of replay value to the game. If that wasn't already enough to upset fans, it has since been announced that Episode Aigis is being released separately later in the year as Paid Downloadable Content in addition to the full-price game. Personally, I'm not particularly upset by this because in my opinion "The Answer" was a misnomer which didn't add anything particularly meaningful to the story of the base game, nor did it reach a satisfactory conclusion. Nevertheless, I can understand why fans are upset that the game was released in an essentially incomplete state and that in order to get the full experience players must pay extra for DLC. Final Verdict: In a sense, Persona 3 Reload delivers exactly what it was promised to from the beginning, so in all fairness perhaps it deserves a higher score. After all, right from the beginning it was never stated that the game would include anything but the content of the base game. However, selling Episode Aigis separately as DLC just doesn't sit right with me. It would be one thing if they had said so from the very start, but they didn't, they made it out as though Persona 3 Reload would be a stand alone release and that the additional story content featured in Persona 3 FES and Persona 3 Portable wasn't planned, so for them to spring it on players that Episode Aigis was in development and would be sold separately as DLC a few weeks after launch feels dishonest and underhanded. Clearly they knew that if they had announced upfront that Episode Aigis would be sold separately at a later date that a fair portion of the fanbase would opt not to purchase the game at launch and either wait for a sale or a discounted bundle somewhere down the line, so instead they lied to the fanbase that no additional story content was planned so that fans would purchase the game feeling like they were getting a complete package. That's really anti-consumer and therefore isn't something that I can in good conscience support, so frankly I would encourage any fans who aren't pleased with this to hold off on purchasing the game and wait for a sale or discounted bundle in order to discourage ATLUS from employing such deceptive marketing in the future. Otherwise, have at it, as Persona 3 Reload does include the base game story content in its entirety with a few supplementary scenes added.

author: Galactus21
review_title: Fun times during summer break
review_text: When it comes to the Persona series, I was a late bloomer. I didn’t start playing until Persona 5. All of my Persona series exposure has been from the 5th edition, from the original to Strikers. This made things interesting when I played Persona 3 Reload, which is the remake of a nearly 20 year old game. I can definitely see where a lot of the inspiration for the 5th one came from. With that said, Persona 3 plays like a smaller scale Persona experience I’m used to. Persona 3 Reload follows the story of a high school protagonist. Along the way he meets others like Junpei, Yukari, Ken and so forth. They are part of a group called S.E.E.S whose mission is to investigate and stop the dark hour. The dark hour is a secret hour at midnight where unbeknownst to the world, shadows run wild. Being Persona users, our protagonists have the powers to make a difference and fight shadows. Persona 3 was a bit smaller in scope, where the game really only has several locations. There’s the school that our protagonist attends. There’s also a couple of mall like places, with shops and restaurants. Additionally there’s the dorms that you’re staying at and a shrine, but in terms of locations that’s roughly it. These are the areas you’ll spend your time in when not going to Tartarus. The main battle areas will largely take place in Tartarus, a 250 floor plus high location filled with shadows. When not in battle, the player will essentially go through life as a high schooler. You live in a dorm along with the other protagonists. During the day, you will attend school or hang out with friends. At night you can do limited set of activities like eat out or work. The limited scope does make things feel like it drags on a bit towards the latter stages of the game. By then, once you’ve made tons of money or maxed out social stats there’s not much point working or building stats like courage by eating out. Your day to day non combat activities will be a combination of class and activities. In class, you will hear lectures, take exams or answer ad hoc questions. Then after school you can spend time with your friends. You will have a series of social links that you can build with different characters. Spending time with them and choosing certain narrative choices will build your bond with them. One thing that I will say is I felt the links with some of the main characters happened way too late in the game and it felt a bit rushed. In addition to school and social links, you can also build your social stats. These include charm, courage and intelligence. You can build these by a number of activities. This could include working, answering questions at school or eating at certain restaurants. The scope of these activities are finite, so after a while it does drag on a bit. With that said, Persona 3 does excel in both story and combat. The turn base combat is quite fun. Persona 3 does feature plenty of playable characters you can add to your playable party. Narrowing it down to 4 can be tough. During combat, you can use a combination of regular attacks and Persona powers. These powers will generally cost either SP or HP to perform. Additionally, if you are able to attack all enemies weaknesses you can go for an all out attack. While the game uses the traditional turn base combat, the game adds a lot of style to the combat. These range from the team based all our attack to superbly cool theuragy attacks. These type of attacks build up over time. For example, if you use Yukari to heal it will build up her meter much more quickly. In general, trying to find enemies weaknesses will lead to successful fights. One of the great things about Persona 3 is the story and the connection of its characters. While the premise is simple to follow, Persona 3 is able to weave a story together that is quite enjoyable. This is mixed in with a lot of characters in your group that you grow attach to. The various social links help build these up. Persona 3 features a great musical score that helps set things up. The game’s voice acting is also quite good. From the bro like Junpei to the stern elder class men in Mitsuru. Voice overs were quite enjoyable. The game’s graphics were obviously revamped and look good. Character models are crisp and the game runs well. Cut scene and animation also look fantastic. It’s as if you’re watching a quality anime. In the 65 or so hours spent on Persona 3, it was a good experience through out. While there are definitely flaws in the game, it is quite remarkable how well it’s held up in the near 20 years since its release. Had I played this game when it first came out, this would probably be one of my favorite RPGs. Even today, with all of the modern RPG mechanics, Persona 3 still holds up well. If you haven’t played the original or haven’t played in a while, I definitely think this is worth checking out.

author: blitz_0623
review_title: Persona 4 Golden - Gold for the Vita and JRPG genre
review_text: Four years ago, Atlus released Persona 4 for the Playstation 2 console. It wound being one of the console's best JRPGs and best titles overall. Four years later, Persona 4 is back and better than ever with an enhanced port, or remake if you will. Persona 4 Golden (P4G) is a PS Vita exclusive game that takes in its console version, and basically makes everything about it better. What was bad is now good, and what was good is now even better. If you're someone looking for a good JRPG or even just RPG, this is the game you've been looking for. Let's be honest, JRPGs have taken a dip this generation. The most popular franchise, Final Fantasy, hasn't exactly lived up to its expectations when you compare FFXIII and XIII-2 to previous FF games. Unlike the PS2 era, there are barely any good JRPGs out there. Most either stay in Japan, or are just not good enough for people. P4G hopes to change all this. It may be based off an old PS2 game, but there are enough additions and improvements that warrant a game purchase or even a Playstation Vita purchase. Story - 9 Let me begin with the story - an element severely lacking in JRPGs. Not only does P4G have one of the most unique stories out of any JRPG, it also has one of the best. Without giving too much, the storyline involves a murder case that starts as soon as the Main Character (MC) arrives in a small rural town called Inaba. Your task is to solve this case with your highschool classmates without anyone's help, including the police. In fact, like some games, the police will even get in your way. Other than Crime, Mystery and Thriller being the main theme, P4G also contains almost every other story element you can think of - Comedy, Romance, Drama, Action, etc. This is what makes the game very diverse and deep. As you progress in the game, you will encounter all of these elements that, when put together, create a tremendously polished story. Do not be surprised if you get hooked on to it within a matter of hours. And it only keeps getting more interesting. What also sets it apart from most JRPGs is how realistic it is - another element not very common in JRPGs. Every character has his/her own personality. It is very possible that you will get attached to some of them because of how amazing their personalities are. These aren't your usual JRPG Lolita's and characters with a "strong sense of justice and wants to help everyone he sees". No, each character is likened to your usual highschool classmate, your dad, sibling, etc. And the best part about all this, is you get to build a relationship with each and every one of them (will be talked about in gameplay). Graphics - 8 It doesn't look as good as Final Fantasy games, but the graphics complement the game very well. It has a nice anime touch, and the character portraits are nicely done. P4G actually looks better than P4 for the PS2. I'm not exactly sure of the resolutions, but P4G contains some HD quality graphics on character portraits and Personae. It's not really a big deal, but it adds to the flavor of the game. The dungeons also look fantastic. They haven't changed a whole lot from the original game, but they're an accurate description of what the game is trying to convey to the player. Sound - 10 Another weak JRPG attribute P4G does extremely well - voice acting. Voice actors (VAs) did a tremendously good job. I cannot stress this enough since most JRPGs out there have horrible forced voice acting. Not this game. The voice acting is what makes the game the realistic game I was describing earlier. It is as if you're actually listening to real people, or watching a movie. There is, however, one problem, and this is completely subjective. P4G doesn't use the same voice actors from P4. Teddie and Chie both have new voice actors and while I don't have a problem with Teddie's, Chie's has taken some time to get used. Actually, I don't think I'll ever get used to Chie's new voice. It's not bad, but the original voice was just better. Enough of voice acting. Let's talk about the fantastic soundtrack. P4G has a very memorable OST, memorable enough that it will definitely stick to your head if you've played the game for hours. The music is not purely instrumental. In fact, most of what you will hear are songs, most of which if you listen carefully to the lyrics (or read them somewhere on the internet) are about the game itself. And just like how the graphics and voice acting complement the game, the music adds excitement and fun to every battle. You may find yourself itching to battle just to hear the battle music. P4G contains 2 kinds of regular battle music. The first is triggered normally, while the second is triggered with a Player-Advantage (hitting a Shadow from behind - will be talked about soon). The original P4 only had the second. The Boss music is just as good, and so is each dungeon's theme. Gameplay - 10 Let me just get this out of the way. P4G will take a lot of your time. By a lot I mean 60+ hours of your time, at minimum. The game is progresses like a calendar. It starts sometime in April, and ends sometime in Mach. For every month (save for January and February), you will be doing all kinds of things any regular person would every day (okay, not really any regular person). Yes you heard that right - you will play through April 21, 22, 23, all the way up to March. Some days will be 2 minutes long, some days can take hours depending on how you play. This basically explains the length of the game. The game is split into 2 parts - dungeon crawling and character building. For each day (ie April 21, April 22, etc), you will have the option of doing 2 things - one After School and the other during Evening. You can only go dungeon crawling After School, and it will take up your Evening time as well. Let's talk about dungeon crawling first. Dungeons are where you power up your characters. Each dungeon has several floors in it, with the last floor containing the boss of that dungeon. Shadows live in dungeons, and are what you encounter on a regular basis. Each floor also has treasure chests to loot. Battling Shadows is part of what makes the game so much fun. There are 2 ways to hit a Shadow - using your character's weapon, or his/her Persona. The Main Character is able to hold multiple Personae (kind of like having a lot of Pokemon!). Strategy comes in when you take into account weaknesses. Most Shadows and Personae have an element that it is weak to. Learning to use this to your advantage greatly aids you in battles. Be careful, as Shadows are also capable of hitting you with your weakness. So how do you get stronger? When you level up, only your HP and SP increases. Your attack, agility, etc are all based on what Persona you are currently holding. Not to worry, Personae also have a level associated with them. And as I mentioned, your party members only have one persona (meaning if they level up, so do their persona and so do their attack, agility, etc.). The MC, being able to hold multiple Personae (and switch between them during battle) is capable of 'fusing' Personae. Let me explain. Whenever you beat a Shadow, there is a chance called Shuffle Time (ST) that could trigger. In the old P4, Shuffle Time only contains Persona cards that you get. Not in P4G. P4G adds various gameplay elements, however, you are still able to get a Persona from the new ST (think of it like capturing a new Pokemon). As your level increases, your mind (as the game calls it) can hold more Personae, eventually capping at 12. From the Personae on your mind, you can go to a special room and fuse 2, 3 or more of them together and create a more powerful Personae. You can only create a Persona as high as your level. Every time you fuse a new Persona, you can pass a limited number of skills from the Personae you are using to make it. There are hundreds of skills in the game, and before you know it, you will hard-pressed on deciding what skills to transfer over! This is another part of what makes the game fun - testing out your new Personae. Adding to the Fusion game play are what we call Social Links. The MC has a social link to characters in the game. The deeper the relationship with a character, the higher the level of the Social Link, maxing out at Level 10. How do you level up? This is the other part of the game. The first was dungeon crawling, and the second is character building. Every After School or Evening, if you are not dungeon crawling, you can 'spend time' with a character and build your relationship with him/her. Some of the women can even be your girlfriends. What's the point of leveling this up besides having girlfriends? Social Links are important whenever you fuse a new Persona. Every Persona is associated with an Arcana (or class if you will). These Arcana are the same with your Social Links. Let's say you have a Social Link with someone of the Magician Arcana. Whenever you fuse a new Persona that belongs in the Magician Arcana, it will be granted bonus experience based on the level of that Social Link! Sound too complicated? Yes, but once you get to try it out, you will find it unbelievably addicting. Experimenting will definitely help and before you know it, you will be hooked onto creating the perfect Persona. P4G even makes the Fusion interface more efficient and detailed. For those curious, visit a FAQ guide to see the improvements in the Fusion interface. New to P4G is the inclusion of the SOS system. When connected to the internet, you are able to ask help or help other people in the same part of the game as you are (more specifically the same dungeon). It can be really helpful for people that are finding it difficult to trek the dungeon. Replayability - 9 There are a lot of incentives to replay the game in New Game Plus (NG+). Let me tell you right now, if you don't follow a well thought-out guide, you will NOT be able to max out every Social Link in the game. Maxing out a Social Link has a lot of benefits and you will want to experience maxing out most of them, especially your teammates' social links. Trust me on this one. NG+ carries over the expected things which will allow you to have more free time during the game and thus have more time to max out your relationships with characters. There are also content in the game that can only be accessed via NG+. An incredibly well-told story, great graphics, catchy music, and unique gameplay all make for one of the most rewarding experiences you could ever find in a game. Persona 4 Golden is easily the Playstation Vita's best title as of November 20, 2012. If you need a reason to get a Vita, this is it. If you already own a Vita, then there is absolutely no reason not to own this gem. + Fun and engaging Battle System + Very rewarding relationship building and Persona fusions + Well-written story and dialogue + Beautiful presentation - Game can be too long for some people - Slightly high learning curve, can take a while to get used to

author: mistermikeymike
review_title: It's the 5 soda blend you make at burgerking. It's different, but not necessarily better.
review_text: Persona 4 was originally released for PS2 over half a decade ago to relative success and gaining a cult following. Persona 4 Golden is Atlus's port of Persona 4 to the PSVita. But with a cherry on top; Atlus decided to add a boatload of new content to this game. A quick overview of what Persona is. It's a dungeon crawler/dating simulator mix. What you do in the "real world" affects how you fare in the "TV world" aka the dungeons. As you level up in your relationships (dating sim) your ability to fuse powerful personas become stronger. The game revolves around personas, (which not so surprisingly is what the game is titled after) which is what the battle system revolves around. If you've ever played Pokemon, then that's the best analogy I can give you. In battle, you switch between Personas to best take advantage of the situation much like you would in Pokemon. Each persona has unique strengths and weaknesses that make them better suited for your current battle. You can fuse personas (sort of like breeding a Pokemon who is actually usable immediately after fusing but as the name implies you lose the personas used in fusion) to create new ones and it is essential that you master that in order to succeed in Persona. You can even "catch" wild personas by winning a battle! The difference however is that there is no sentimental value to your Persona. You are encouraged to cycle through them, and discard them at will. You fuse them often without a second though so you can get stronger. It's sort of like if Ash threw away his Pikachu for a shiny new Mewtwo. So how does the dating sim relate to the dungeon crawling? In order to level up your social links (basically your skill in fusing personas), you play a dating sim. You play as a second year transfer student in the small quiet town of Inaba,Japan. Throughout the game you spend a majority of your days boosting your social links. You boost them by choosing to spend the day with a friend and you watch a cutscene and share an often endearing moment with them. Social links are the basis of the game. STORY 8/10 The story starts off with you moving to a small town in Japan named Inaba. You live the life of a second year transfer student from the big city. You begin your life in Inaba right as two mysterious murders take place. Throughout the game you chase the killer and it is your duty to stop him from killing again. As a typical video game story Persona 4 tries to draw you in from the start. And it does (multiple murders seem to do that). And then the story falls off a cliff. It suffers from poor pacing and poor storytelling. For about 80% of the game you are shoved into dungeon after dungeon while the plot simply decides not to progress. You would think that the dungeons would each offer something vital to the plot right? Maybe a clue as to who the murderer is or some significant event. But in reality, it's about as creative as Pokemon's story. SEE GYM, BEAT GYM, GET BADGE, REPEAT x8. The dungeons are not relevant to the plot and do not feel relevant to the plot. Throughout most of the game you are just playing in filler dungeons designed to get more hours out of a game with poor RPG mechanics. The killer? You know the moment of truth? You know how you spend an entire game anticipating who the killer is? Yeah well, you should prepare to be disappointed. It feels as if Atlus just decided, "hey, who is the most inconspicuous person we can think of so we can outsmart the player?" There are no hints. There are no clues. There is no foreshadowing. You're left saying "what the hell." The main story was awful and an extremely cheesy anime storyline marred by fillers and poor writing. So you're probably wondering why I gave the story an 8/10 right? The reason I gave the story an 8/10 is simple. Being a dating sim you spend a lot of time with your friends and dates. The time you spend with each person allows them to tell you an often heartfelt and touching story (though sometimes annoying) that strengthens the bond between the two of you. These short stories are what make up for the awful main story. You start to grow and like the cast. The stories are short; 10 custscenes for each character. But during that time you really start to understand what makes each person tick. My personal favourite is Dojimas. It's a prime example of how even a side character can make you sympathize with them. Through the game you talk to a variety of people from grieving widows to typical high school girls. It is these side stories, and little interactions with the people around you that make the story so great. Much of the emotion that is devoid of the main story comes from here as well. It's in these little stories, that really makes Persona a game that you form an emotional connection with. There are no cliches are awful writing in them. I'm almost certain that you will be able to identify with a few characters if not at least half of them GRAPHICS 7/10 The game is drawn in anime style and it's hard to argue that the graphics are poor or outdated because anime/cartoons aren't about being graphically impressive. That said, even for anime-style graphics Persona is rather plain and lacks detail. Of course I'm not a particularly big fan of anime (actually I hate anime) and my familiarity with it extends only to the most popular ones that I watched as a kid. Though I will say that characters in this game described as beautiful, did not look beautiful. And the average girl was a step down from that. Of course the anime is only a small part and the models and the world itself is beautifully done and among the best you can get from a PSVita game. SOUND 9/10 Boasting 50% more voice acting from Persona 4, Persona 4 Golden is pretty amazing in the voice acting department. Voices were synchronized well and most genuinely fit the character with the exception of a couple. Chie and Teddie, two characters from the original Persona 4, have new voice actors. Teddies voice actor is generally embraced by the community while Chie's is controversial at best. Seeing as this is my review I'm going to flat out say that I disliked it and thought it sounded bratty and did not fit the character. The music was amazing as a whole. Music isn't something you can just describe because everyone's tastes are different. Persona 4 however, will appeal to a majority of players due to its rather safe song selection. There are however, a few vocal tracks sung in J-pop style. One of them being the battle theme. If you don't like J-pop you might want to mute the game because though few in number, they are frequent in appearance. GAMEPLAY 3/10 Persona 4 honestly feels like a series of short videos rather than a JRPG. Everyday you are given a choice on how to spend your afternoon and night. You can either choose to spend the day exploring a dungeon and fighting monsters OR you can spend the day boosting your social link. Let's start with the combat. It sucks. The balance is poor. And by poor I mean it's terrible. Your party members, if you let the AI control them, are the kind of people who drool while sitting on the couch. That's fine because you can control them manually. The game almost forces you to grind due to how it penalizes you for being under-leveled. That alone robs it of some of the strategy that it should be encouraging. Further degrading the experience of combat is how combat is about trial and error as opposed to strategy. Your job is just to keep smashing the enemy with attacks until you find one that sticks. Resistant to Ice? Let's see if Fire works. Fire not working? Let's try Holy. The balance though is atrocious. A spell that heals your entire party to max hp? Only 30SP (1/10th of your SP bar maybe). Another issue is how utterly RNG reliant this game is. Half of your game overs will be because the RNG gods frowned upon you. There's a lot of frequent instant-KO spells that bosses will chuck at you. 50% chance to instant kill your MC and game-over you is frustrating. Even random monsters will occasionally toss out an instant-gameover at your and you're left angry as hell because you have to restart due to RNG. Personas "gimmick" however is called knock downs. Basically hitting an enemies weak point or getting a critical strike results in a free turn or just a gang beatdown for loads of damage. But all this rewards is trial-and-error (for finding weaknesses) OR RNG (for crits). Now maybe the world is a lot better right? Not really. Dungeons are randomly generated. That means every floor looks the same. And feels the same. Randomly generated means no hidden loot, no exploring and hoping to find something of interest, no secret passages, no nothing. There is no joy in exploration due to how nothing you do grants you a feeling of progression or even a change of scenery. The loot is awful and quite honestly the dungeon design is worse. Now the dating sim part of the game isn't really a game. But hey, it's definitely my favourite. This part ties into the story. Basically what happens is, if you choose to spend your day with a person you watch an optional cutscene. Each person has their own short story and the more time you spend with each person the higher your social links are. They cap out at level 10 which will give each persona a hefty level boost (often more than enough to learn all their skills). But other than a few dialogue choices, it's not very interactive. It's like picking a level-up option from a menu. Now as bad as the gameplay is the game is kind of addicting. Which is primarily because of the story. REPLAY VALUE 4/10 What does a game full of randomly generated loot and cutscenes offer you once you've experienced it once? Not a whole lot. New Game+ is alright but hardly worth the effort. Your money and persona library carry over (as well as a few other things). Now you can summon personas from your persona library which pretty much breaks the game. There is bonus content for NG+ but it's hardly worth the effort. I mean who's going to spend 60+ hours just so they can fight an optional "super boss" who isn't even that great? Overall 6/10 Definitely worth the experience in my honest opinion. There are obvious gameplay flaws but you won't notice them until you're too far into the game to care. The short stories will also suck you in. If you're into anime this is definitely down your alley. And even if you're not it was a touching game.

author: Kayos90
review_title: Golden shines brilliantly as a paragon for the genre
review_text: Persona 4 Golden stands as a testament to both JRPG lovers and Vita owners that the two ecosystems aren’t quite ready to disappear. Although the core experience of Golden isn’t different from its original PlayStation 2 release a number of changes and new additions make the trek back into the rural town of Inaba worthwhile for both old and newcomers of the title and franchise. So, should you go headlong into experience this new Persona? The answer is easily, and obviously, a yes. You, the young and silent high school student, will live in the city of Inaba for a year due to your parents being away for work. From the moment you enter the town you’re greeted by a friendly face, your uncle accompanied by his daughter, who doesn’t really give a friendly face. After arriving at home and a strange visit from a mysterious big-nosed man in the Velvet Room, your new life begins. However, not all is as it seems in Inaba as a series of murders begins to occur soon after your arrival and rumors of weird showings on the Midnight Channel on rainy days. It’s up to you and your fellow classmates to solve these occurings in Inaba when you discover you have the ability to enter a world through the television and summon powerful beings called Personas. The narrative premise of Persona 4 is extremely simple and the progress you make towards solving the mystery of the murders and the world beyond the television doesn’t get much complex. People mysteriously disappear and it’s up to your merry band of friends to rescue them from the other world. Once you rescue them you wait until they join your crew and wait until it happens all over again. This repetitive narrative cycle becomes almost insulting due to its nonchalant way of trying to add people to your party. At the same time, you realize that you haven’t made much progress in trying to find the culprit behind these preemptive murders. When it finally comes down to the end you realize that there wasn’t much foreshadowing involved for who the culprit was and the payoff for catching the criminal isn’t anything worthing noting. Still, while the simplicity and the unimportance of the main narrative may be a shortcoming of the series it gives strength to the other aspects of story. The game is primarily concerned with character development and character interactions between the extremely large cast. As the silent protagonist your direct responses to your friends will be minimal but you will see your friends sides of their selves that they hid away and see how they learn to accept their identity and reality as their own. It’s this self-recognition and acceptance of their true selves that truly differentiate Persona 4 from other JRPGs or even its predecessor. For instance, Yukiko struggles with being a successor to the local inn and being tied to the town, however, over the course of the game you’ll find that she slowly comes to terms with how she defines herself and what she should do. Relationships is a huge theme in Persona 4 and it’s no surprise that with each person you meet, you’ll find something to learn from him or her. The characters that you interact with aren’t realistic but the constant interaction and the large amount of time you spend with each individual makes them unforgettable imitating the relationship forging that occurs in real life. For all intents and purposes, Persona 4 is a social simulation as you make a large amount of friends and knowing who to hang out with and when will help to forge greater and tighter bonds. In this aspect, Persona 4 exceeds in telling the stories of individuals but more importantly your story as you craft your own unique adventure living in Inaba. All of these character interactions and relationships you have are housed under a system called Social Links. There are numerous Social Links in all and they have ten stages in total. Once you grow closer to someone you’ll level up in the respective Social Links. In order to level up you must spend time with them and make proper responses or actions when around them to maximize your affection. Of course rather than exploiting the relationship to maximize affection in order to level up you’re free to role play and choose responses as you see fit. The system doesn’t penalize you for doing so and as a result Social Links give great freedom in trying to undertake a different persona or manifest your own in the game. Social Links at first may seem like an artificial system included to give meaning to an already meaningful gameplay component but it doesn’t feel tacked on. Rather, Social Links serves to further expand and make Golden an even more impressive game. Social Links serves as an invaluable asset in battle whether it be forging new powers or receiving aid from allies in the midst of a fight. While the real world serves as a meeting ground for friends the other world serves as a place to fight enemies known as Shadows. In order to combat Shadows, you and your friends must invoke your Personas to combat them, but unlike your friends you have more than one Persona at your disposal. Each Persona is delegated into a certain type of Social Link that is named after a tarot card. For instance, your relationship with your bud Yosuke is titled The Magician. Depending on what your Social Link level is with Yosuke, when you create Personas of The Magician, it will receive bonus experience making it with a high starting level from the get go. Creating new Personas in the Velvet Room becomes more of a puzzle as you will need to decide if it’s worthwhile to create Personas that won’t benefit from Social Links or not. At the same time, if you wish to create Personas of a certain tarot then it’s best to focus on that respective Social Link.
