The relationship that Persona creation shares with Social Links is one of the quintessential, and enjoyable, aspect of the game. Golden uses a turn-based system where you control a party of up to four people. While the turn-based system may seem dated in an age where real-time rules the genre, Golden manages to keep it interesting with unique features and systems. Every party member has access to a Persona with its own strengths and weaknesses, however, you being special can utilize your pool of Personas that you discover and create. Being able to switch between Personas in the middle of battle is essential as some Personas will have movesets that will exploit enemy weaknesses or help to defend against enemies that might exploit your own. It’s an extremely versatile and flexible system that punishes you for playing complacently but rewarding you for using the various Personas at your disposal. The other three members of the party can be controlled manually or you can let the AI handle it. Whichever way you choose, the rules of the battle will remain the same. Each Persona can learn up to eight moves and you must take out the opposing party. Luckily systems such as One More and All-Out Attacks keep you engaged. When you attack an enemy using its weakness or land a critical hit you get a chance to attack once more. Doing so may knock down the enemy making it vulnerable to any subsequent attacks that may cause dizziness. It’s an easy way to chain multiple weaknesses and knockdown all foes on the field. You may even have an ally pitch in and dish out additional damage or hit other enemies out on the playing field. All-Out Attacks come into play when all foes are knocked down and your entire party will join and bash the enemies for a good amount of damage frequently resulting in their deaths. Utilizing One More and All-Out Attacks help to move battles along and it’s an excellent supplement to the tried and true turn-based combat system. Under certain conditions your victory might result in Shuffle Time. It’s a cool little system where you have the option to choose one card out of several. These cards may increase your experience gained from the battle, your money, your health, or even grant you new Personas. There are other cards that decrease the amount of experience or money you get but doing so may benefit you as picking up all the cards during Shuffle Time will result in a Sweep. If you Sweep then Shuffle Time will automatically occur after the next fight and you will be able to choose from three cards rather than one. Chaining up Sweeps may level up your party extremely fast but at the same time might cause you to gain money at a slower rate. Regardless, this feature is a welcome one as it just adds more depth and customization in choosing how you want to pick your rewards, or punishments. Going back to reality after visiting the other world is something completely different. The stark contrast in the types of gameplay you engage in is startling and may feel incohesive but it works to the game’s advantage. If you feel like hunting Shadows or finishing up some quests in the other world then you should do so. However, if you want to spend more time in the real world making friends, building yourself up to be a paragon of sorts, and undertake part-time jobs to earn money then entering the other world so often may not be best for you. The game is all about choice and choosing how you want to spend your time. However, be mindful that if you don’t have a healthy lifestyle of training in both the real and other world, you might not be so ready when fate needs you to be. Golden adds a good chunk of new content that are extremely enjoyable and also serves to flesh out the Persona 4 narrative and its mythos. Two new Social Links are available and maxing them out along with the existing ones will be tough but it gives veterans something satisfying to look forward to. There is also a new dungeon, and while it isn’t challenging or anything substantial, it offers more plot for those wanting more story. All of Golden is complemented by its excellent pop soundtrack. The vocal tunes are extremely catchy and fun to listen to. At the same time, the game’s somber and ambient tunes exemplify some of the more darker toned events. If anything can be said bad about the exemplary soundtrack is its repetitiveness. The game can easily be a 60+ hour journey and the same songs might pop up again too often for your patience. The voice acting is just as stellar as each actor does a superb job displaying emotion. Most of the voice acting is heavily attributed due to Golden’s amazing writing. Each line feels like it was crafted with the utmost care. The witty humor found when your friends are interacting with each other are some of the best parts of the story as their banter never fails to cause some sort of laughter. The writing also vividly describes many of the game’s colorful and vibrant events considering the protagonist remains silent. In short, Golden presents that a JRPG doesn’t have to be bogged down by stereotypical and cheesy lines but can break out and do something unique. While the game doesn’t push the Vita’s hardware to the max in terms of graphics it does capture the vibrant and colorful Golden creates. Even watching the intro video you get a sense of joy just because of all the colors flying everywhere. The animations are solid and the Japanese high school life is depicted well visually. The various atmospheres and tones the game exhumes is reinforced by how the game looks and in this department Golden does well. Persona 4 Golden is a monumental achievement in both game design and gameplay. How all the mechanics and systems come together and work in tandem to create such a meaningful experience is a feat in and of itself. To make this experience last for dozens of hours without trying your patience is another. The endless achievements and accolades that could be given to Golden shows the genre’s potential to achieve excellence but most importantly: it’s a damn good game and you should get it.

author: MegaXFan
review_title: A Brilliant JRPG and a system seller!
review_text: Persona 4 Golden Review by britton1207 Persona 4 Golden (P4G) is a PSVita remake of the PS2 JRPG Classic Persona 4. As I haven’t played the original version, this review will not reference any differences between the original and the new version. To be blunt, this game is a work of art. If you own a PlayStation Vita, and have even a passing interest in the RPG genre, you deserve to play this game. It is a sublime experience, blending a huge range of gameplay styles into one brilliant package. You begin the game by transferring from your old school to Yasogami High School in the small, boring town of Inaba. For the next year you will be staying with your Uncle Dojima, who is a police detective, and his daughter Nanako. Inaba is about to undergo some major changes, and of course these changes will revolve around you and your destiny. Recently a rumor has been circulating among the city about a TV program called The Midnight Channel. It seems that if you look at your TV at midnight on a rainy evening, your soul mate will appear on the TV. Shortly after hearing this rumor, you decide to try to view the Midnight Channel yourself. Not only do you learn that the Midnight Channel is real, but you also discover that you can place your hand inside the TV! Over the course of the next few days a series of murders rocks Inaba. You and your new friends soon begin to suspect that the murders are related to The Midnight Channel. One accidental fall into a big screen TV later, and you and your friends are off to solve the murders and discover the true nature of The Midnight Channel and the world inside of the TV. The story from that point forward is a deep and rich as you want it to be. You see, your character can develop Social Links with various characters throughout the city. You simply spend time with these characters and the social link “levels up” as you learn more about the character. You can develop your relationship with your Uncle Dojima and his detective partner Adachi. You can learn about and care for your cousin Nanako. You can befriend the Fox who lives at the local shrine and help him answer the prayers of the townsfolk. Each of your fellow party members also has a story arc you can explore by cultivating their respective Social Links. You could, if you feel like it, choose to completely ignore these social links and simply progress through the main story of the game as quickly as possible. If you do, you’ll be treated to a wonderfully crafted murder mystery full of twists and turns. As more people appear on The Midnight Channel, and you subsequently rescue them, the mystery deepens. What is this TV world? Who is throwing people into the TV world? Why do those who enter the TV world appear on the Midnight Channel? With 3 different endings, 20 social links to discover and grow, an entire school year to complete, and a lengthy main story, you will not be disappointed by the amount of story involved. As amazing as the story is, no game will entertain you long without compelling gameplay. P4G has this by the bucketful. The gameplay is broken up into two separate areas, the real world and the TV world. The real world is where you go about your day to day activities and expand your social links. The TV world is where you go to fight, level up, rescue people, etc. The real world is your day-to-day life. In most RPG’s the concept of the day/night cycle are driven by specific story elements that the game developers want to occur at night, or your characters merely rest at the local inn to recover their strength. This is not the case in P4G. This day/night cycle is expanded into the very core of the gameplay. Nearly everything you do is driven by time management. Since you are in high school you begin most days of the week by going to class in the morning. Other than being asked a few questions throughout the school year, going to school isn’t a bother or a time sink. You wake up, you go to school, time elapses, and then school is over. The remainder of the day is where the meat of the action is, where things are broken up into the After-School time and the Evening Time. How you manage these two phases of the day shapes the way your game plays out. Moreover, there is a real in –game calendar. You don’t get an infinite amount of days to do what you need to do. Each day that passes brings you one day closer to the end of the school year…and the end of the game. The first of the two phases is your After-School time. You can explore the town of Inaba looking for quest givers, spend time with one of your friends in order to improve your Social Links, go down to the river for a bit of fishing, or maybe just choose to do nothing at all by returning home. Depending on the day of the week you can also choose to go to work at the day care, attend drama practice, and even participate in soccer or basketball. Finally, you can choose to enter the TV to explore for the day. The second phase is the Evening Phase. During this phase you can spend some more quality time with your team, which will help you rank up your social links even faster. There are part time jobs that you can take in order to obtain extra cash or rank up your social skills. You can read books which grant bonuses to fishing skills, bug catching, or social skills. There are even a few Social Links that level up almost exclusively at night. When you aren’t busy spending time with your friends and working part time jobs, you’ve got to be a hero and save the world. Throughout the story various people enter the parallel universe known only as the TV World. This world is inhabited by shadow creatures and is filled with a mysterious fog. The problem is that after a period of rain in the real world, the fog empties from the TV world and the shadow creatures go berserk. Anyone stuck in the TV world when the shadows go berserk ends up quite dead, with their body deposited in the real world. Your party will enter the TV world and travel to a dungeon inspired by the person you are required to save. You’ll explore a steamy bathhouse, a sexy strip club, and even an old school inspired dungeon. Each dungeon floor is randomly generated, but the enemies aren’t. You’ll see the enemies as blobs of shadow stalking the dungeon halls. If you can manage to attack them from behind, you’ll get a preemptive strike. Likewise, if you try to run around the enemy and they manage to attack you from behind, they’ll get the advantage. Once you’ve engaged the enemy in battle, you’ll discover a ridiculously deep battle system. By pairing up with creatures called Persona, your party gains new attack and magic spells. It is this Persona, rather than your character itself, that allows your party to grow stronger and learn new skills. Each enemy has specific weaknesses, be it physical attacks, elemental attacks, or light/dark attacks. If you strike the enemies weakness, you will score an automatic critical hit, which knocks the enemy down, and gives you a second turn. In this state, you can hammer them for additional damage or cause them to become dizzy and skip their next turn or two. The flip side of this system is that it also works against you, even giving the enemy a second turn if they manage to strike one of your party members’ weaknesses. A wise leader seeks to exploit weaknesses to knock down all of the enemies in a single round. If you can manage that, you’ll be granted an opportunity to perform an all-out attack and deal huge damage to every foe. Dealing critical hits also gives you a chance to be dealt a set of cards after each battle, of which you can only take one. These cards have effects such as health recovery, double experience, or double money. There are also cards which gives you the opportunity to draw even more cards, though these generally have negative effects such as taking away all of the experience you earned in the battle. If you can manage to turn over all of the cards, you’ll earn a sweep bonus. This automatically earns you cards in your next battle, regardless of your battle tactics, and increases your initial number of card draws to three. These card sweeps also earn your main character new Persona, which you can then level up or fuse together into even more new Persona to equip. From the bright and colorful opening sequence, to the day to day interactions with your friends and classmates, this game is always finding something new to draw you into the world. The fact that I found myself looking forward to taking a digital character to school every day should speak as a testament to the high quality writing. I can’t think of a single social link that wasn’t interesting or dungeon I didn’t have a blast exploring. Even if you’ve never heard of this game series, you can be assured that it easily stacks up to the Final Fantasies of the world. This is an amazing game that any RPG fan, casual or hardcore, needs to add to their collection. Graphics – 7 / 10 It’s a remake of a PS2 game. It’s pretty, but nothing mind blowing. Sound - 9 / 10 The sound track to this game is wonderful. The voice acting is superb. Gameplay – 10 / 10 Battles are fun and exciting. There’s always something to do in the real world. Story – 10 / 10 The characters are lovable and the mystery is a blast to solve. Overall – 9 / 10 What few cons I could list are easily overshadowed by just how much fun this game is! A rare gem!

author: Morpheme
review_title: Staying away from this game for too long is unBEARable!
review_text: Introduction Persona 4 was released in 2008 for the PS2 as a follow-up to the crazy successful (by obscure JRPG standards) Persona 3 and Persona 3: FES, a game that subverted nearly all of the traditional mechanics of JRPGs to deliver a vastly more satisfying experience. As a spin-off of the long-running Shin Megami Tensei series, the Persona series has generally sought to deliver a SMT-lite experience, on that focuses more on story compared to the stark, bleak stories of its cousins Nocturne, Digital Devil Saga, and Strange Journey. Though, it does retain it’s parent series’ penchant for the supernatural, macabre, and insane—but it remains wrapped in the adorable veneer of a Slice of Life anime series. This version, Persona 4 Golden, is a remake/port of the original for the Vita, and with the update for a modern console comes a host of amazing new features that bring this amazing game up to Killer App status. HEY KIDS, DO YOU WANT TO TALK ABOUT MURDERS?! The real reason that JRPGs are still even relevant is the story, and it’s here in ample and ridiculous supply. So, then, do you want to talk about murders? The story begins as our Hero (Yu/You, see what they did there?) arrives in a sleepy burg in the middle of nowhere, consigned to a dreary year in the middle of nowhere at a new school with nothing to do. At least, that is, until a local celebrity and a sexy upperclassman are found dead at the hands of a serial killer. This, combined with the series’ disturbing fascination with the occult and macabre, eventually land the player in a Jungian nightmare of Shadows and repression. But once the player and his various companions master their own insecurities and embrace their true emotions, they can unleash the power of their Personas, the true self ( or the Super Ego, for all you Psychology buffs out there). With this power, You and your Investigation Team must go forth, prevent the murders, find the killer, and solve the supernatural mysteries that plague the small town of Inaba. Now, this mystery is the vehicle that drives the plot, but the story is truly brought to life within the side stories of the various NPCs. The ‘Social Links’ tie into the game play as well, but we’ll discuss that in the next section. The theme of this game is finding one’s true self, and all 20-odd social links contribute to this goal. We see these people (many of whom are your party members in the game’s many battles) go through many ordeals, be it coping with the loss of a deceased family member, the manliness of creating plush animals, tutoring a wild student, or even just hanging out with an animal, these social links run the gamut and remain consistently fresh and interesting. It’s actually so engrossing that at times it can overshadow the main game, the addictive dopamine drip of simulated amicability can cause a player to want to rush through the occasionally long-winded story sections and dungeons to get right back to leveling one of the various Social Links.There’s also feels. Lots of them. Many of the game’s characters will feel like old friends by the time you’re done, and Marie’s social link path will make you cry like a little girl. So, yeah, put THAT on the back of the box. IT’S TIME FOR AN ALL-OUT ATTACK! But players don’t care about all that nonsense, do they? All people look for is bang for their buck, a decent value. Well, good news: this is probably more game than the average player can handle. That isn’t an exaggeration. There’s nearly 70 hours of content in this game, and that’s just for a standard non-completionist playthrough. It’s BEAR-ly beatable by most people’s standards, but it’s a thoroughly satisfying experience all the way through. From the strategic All-Out Attack mechanic to the intricate Social Link system, this game is a unified and beautiful whole. Also, IT HAS COSTUMES. What would satisfy a player more than Battle Panties?! First of all, the combat is a great twist on the classic turn-based formula. Unlike MMOs and WRPGs and rival JRPGs that mostly reward a time investment and grinding, Persona 4 and Shin Megami Tensei games in general reward the player for strategy above all else. In earlier incarnations, SMT games have employed a “Press Turn” system wherein the players and the monsters are both vulnerable to certain types of attack, similar to the SUPER EFFECTIVE type exploitation in Pokemon. Being hit by a weakness will cause you to lose a turn. Conversely, exploit every enemies’ turn and your spunky party goodtimes feel-good crew will perform and ALL-OUT ATTACK with the requisite cartoon cloud effect and huge, devastating, delicious damage. Mercilessly murdering shadows gives the player EXP, of course, but it’s really only useful for the player character, since Personas rarely level up. This leads us directly to the blue-painted doorstep of the games’ deepest mechanic: Fusion. In a system most akin to Pokemon or Dragon Quest: Monsters breeding, players must combine their various Personas into ever-more powerful forms. But remember how Personas rarely ever level up? This is where the Social Links return! It turns out that Social Links are integral to the growth of your personas: the stronger your bond with a character, the more the Arcana that they represent will level up, tying going out and drinking with your bros back directly to your strength in battles. Who’d of thought that dates could make you stronger? IT’S A GOLDEN SHOW The presentation section is perhaps the easiest section to write home about: the game, while it doesn’t have the highest resolution, manages to keep the player visually interested thanks to its lovely primary color pallet, and generally well-done and creative art direction. The artwork for each Persona was lovingly hand-drawn by Katsura Hoshino and reflect a great deal of interpretation on many culture’s myths and legends. Each dungeon as well has a distinct and um... Unique visual style, with the various locations ranging from a castle, and 8-bit wonderland, and my personal favorite: a sauna, replete with all the jokes you can imagine. The music is also wonderful, and it’s astonishing how I’m not sick of hearing the in-game battle themes when they remain mostly unchanged for 70 hours of playtime, though it does help that a decent player will be in and out of a battle relatively quickly. This is all thanks to the marvelous compositions of Shoji Meguro, which range from the smoothest of jazz to the hardest of rock. THE SHADOW WORLD In addition to being a VERY solid port of a PS2 game, P4G contains several additions from the base game, including but not limited to: Two new social links, new areas, the ability to explore said areas on foot, costumes, trophies, new events for major holidays, new Personas, network connectivity features, costumes, new animated cutscenes, motorcycles, and even an interactive version of the Midnight Channel! Atlus really went all out in making sure that old fans of the game have new things to look forward to, and it’s really shiny. It also helps the overall visual appeal that my Vita is currently decked out in the (amazingly high quality) Vita skin that Atlus provided with my pre-order, and they also offer some seriously amazing wallpapers that really make the Vita's gorgeous resolutions pop. Final Recommendation THIS is the Vita’s killer app, right here and right now. Along with being perhaps one of the best games ever made, it’s easily worth both its own cost and the cost of the system. What are you waiting for?! THERE ARE BEAR PUNS APLENTY, COME ON IN!

author: Exodist
review_title: An enhanced version of a classic JRPG worth owning a Vita for.
review_text: Persona 4 is one of my favourite games. Prior to this, I'd always loved the JRPG genre, but never really went outside the bigger series such as Final Fantasy. One I'd never heard of (to my shame) was Shin Megami Tensei. I got Persona 4 on a whim. I'd heard it was good, it was cheap on launch in the UK, and boy did it blow me away. Persona 4 was hugely popular, along with its excellent predecessor Persona 3, which has helped boost the awareness and popularity of this excellent JRPG series, and now, Golden, released exclusively for the Vita, has boosted its popularity even more. It's as good as they say. Persona 4 has a long and complex story, and here, nothing has changed from the original. You play as a protagonist who has travelled to the sleepy country town of Inaba to stay with your relatives for a year whilst your parents work away. Upon arriving, a mysterious murder occurs where the victim is hung upon an antenna. Meanwhile, rumours about a 'Midnight Channel' are circulating around school. Watching the TV at midnight when its raining reveals your true love on screen. Of course, this isn't quite the case, and you soon find out you can actually enter the TV into an alternate world. You obtain a power which enables you to summon 'Persona', monsters that fight by your side. You also gain allies who will help you on your quest to solve the mysterious murders of Inaba, all of which are linked with the TV and your mysterious power. It's a brilliant setup and the story has plenty of twists and turns along the way. The game fortunately has a fairly satisfying conclusion (although the true ending is a bit out there), the story is overall quite memorable and complex without being confusing. There is also particular emphasis on character in Persona 4 and this aspect excels over the story itself. The main cast of characters are all memorable and likeable, each with complex personalities and traits. This is no surprise considering the main premise of the midnight channel: a persons true inner feelings are revealed by a 'shadow'. The game explores the main cast of characters personalities through this by getting straight to their true feelings, the feelings they hide away and ignore, feelings that make them flawed characters. The game has a few deep themes here and there, but its also fairly light and won't present the player with anything overly dark like other Shin Megami Tensei games might. The game also explores other side characters through social links (more on those later), these stories also explore peoples problems and inner feelings, although these typically range from good to bad and aren't as interesting as the main stories. This said, its a game which places emphasis on its characters and it succeeds. In terms of story, what does Golden bring to the table? One of the biggest additions is the new character Marie. She does not fight for you, but serves for you in the Velvet Room. There is a social link for her to be done, and towards the end of the game an optional dungeon can be cleared relating to Marie. The story is somewhat weaved together with Marie and her story, but its also very unimportant and not particularly interesting. Sadly, Marie is perhaps the weakest character in the game. Her personality is a generic tsundere type (prepare for plenty of insults) and her social link mimics that of Elizabeth from the previous game. Her mysterious past storyline, as said, isn't particularly interesting but they at least tried to link her to the main story. Her addition to the game doesn't make it worse, but as a character she is a little disappointing. The gameplay in Persona 4 takes on two main forms: RPG dungeon crawler, and a kind of social/dating sim/life sim kind of thing, and both aspects are great. The dungeon crawling is obviously the main attraction here, the game IS an RPG primarily, after all. It's pretty similar to other Shin Megami Tensei games. You can collect multiple Personas to fight as, each with different spells, stats, weaknesses and strengths. There are about 100 or so in the game and are collecting by finding them after battles, or the most common method (and much more fun): fusing. You can fuse together personas to create new ones. The system encourages curiosity as fusing together personas can only lead to stronger and better personas, and there are plenty of combinations. It's similar to Pokemon in that there is an urge to collect and find as many as you can through fusing. Only the protagonist can change their persona however. You are essentially that persona and you can swap in battle. Your party members however, all have their own persona which cannot be changed (but later upgraded), although you have full control over them and can choose their skills as they level up. The actual dungeon crawling is perhaps the games weakest aspect, although saying that it isn't exactly bad. The dungeons consist of usually around 8 or 9 different floors most of which will be randomly generated as you enter them. You search the floors for enemies to fight, chests to gain items and of course, to find the stairs to the next level. It is entirely functional but also lacks that extra something to make exploring dungeons interesting. Each floor usually consists of long boring corridors, and each dungeon, although having a different aesthetic theme, use the same art for every floor giving them a somewhat bland look. A few floors in some dungeons have a few 'puzzles' here and there but it's never actually beyond finding keys and something like the camera spinning which doesn't really actually do anything. The question is what you're looking for. For those who are more interested in battling and the persona aspect, you probably won't mind the dungeons. They're merely here to provide an arena to find monsters and fight, and this is perfectly fine. Just don't expect dungeons with different puzzles and traps because there are none. The battle system is where the game truly shines, taking the classic turn based system and adding a few interesting spins to make it more challenging and most importantly, very fun to play. The system is designed on the idea that hitting an enemy with a weakness, or a critical attack, will knock them down and grant you one more turn. If you knock all the enemies down, you can do an all out attack, dealing lots of damage for free. Its entirely desirable and will help clear our random encounters. Almost every enemy will be weak to something and half the fun is figuring out what. Some will also absorb or reflect elements, providing the player with trickier enemies, for example ones that will absorb physical attacks, making you resort to magic only. The best part however is that the same rules apply to the enemies. Your own characters also have weaknesses, and if they're hit, they also get knocked down and the enemy is given one more turn. Its an interesting spin that creates a sort of equal playing field between the player and the monsters. That said, social links will also create a number of opportunities for your party members, giving them the ability to slap people out of status effects such as confuse, help people up when they're knocked down, and take a mortal hit for the protagonist (if he dies, you lose the fight). During your stay in Inaba, you live your daily life as a teenager which means doing certain things during the days. You go to school, and afterwards, you have the opportunity to hang out with people and build social links, or do activities which end up boosting your stats or helping you in some form or another. Social links are particularly important for a number of reasons. Each persona in the game belongs to a different arcana, whilst each social link is also linked to a certain arcana. The higher the level of the social link, the more bonus experience that is granted to a persona of that arcana when fused. This is particularly important because personas require much more experience to level up. The boost on fuse means, if its high enough, you're likely to get an ability or two simply by fusing them, and having the right abilities is pretty important. More useful however are the social links for your party members, as you will see benefits in battle. I already mentioned these previously, but maxing out a social link also evolves their personas, making them stronger, giving benefits such as blocking their own elements. The other activities in the game merely provide aids to the player when there isn't much else to do. Different foods at a restaurant will upgrade social stats (courage, knowledge, that sort of thing, which are required to do some things and pursue certain social links) whilst other activities such as fishing, side quests (usually just collecting items from dungeons), shops and the cinema (which levels up your party members) are also available Here I want to mention some of the new content added for Golden. This is less of a remake and more just an 'enhanced' port, but that being said, they did go all out and add a lot of stuff. You can now leave home at night giving more opportunities for social links and things to do, and you can also visit the city and the beach, again, giving you more options. A lot more has been added for you to so you never have to miss out. The previously mentioned cinema lets you level a party member for each month, whilst the coffee shop lets you earn skill cards, also a new feature. Skill cards are items you can collect which let you teach different abilities to personas. It has great use as it means you're not limited to what a persona can learn, although I have to admit I never actually used any. I've already talked about how Marie's addition to the game was particularly disappointing. Sadly, her new dungeon is also very disappointing. The 'Hollow Forest' appears right near the end of the game which can optionally be beaten by players by maxing Marie's social link before this date. This is where the developers tried to add something interesting for the game and it fell flat on its face. In this dungeon, all your items are taken away, your equipment is gone, and after every fight, you SP is halved. Sounds tricky right? Well not really. The enemies in this dungeon, for this stage in the game, are very weak. They deal barely any damage, most of them appear to be weak to pretty much everything, and worse still, they give out 1000 experience points, nothing compared to the previous dungeons 4-6K average. This means that whilst your SP is taken away, there is absolutely no incentive to fight these battles. The bosses are also particularly easy and provide little challenge. Even worse however is that you will find items to use in the dungeon as you travel. This includes accessories which restore SP upon each turn in battle. This leads to an incredibly tedious process where you have to guard a bunch of times in battle when you need to up your SP totals, and its no fun. Something different was tried with the dungeon and fair enough, but when there is no challenge on display (I played normal difficulty, of course, it could be harder the higher up you go), it just ends up being incredibly annoying. The difficulty of the game is a particularly hard point to talk about since things seem to have changed. When I played the original Persona 4 on normal, it was challenging but fair, with minimal grinding (more necessary in the earlier stages) required later on and more about your skill. This isn't to say this still isn't true, however, Golden on normal difficulty just seemed too easy. Easier than before, and I can't quite figure out why. For me, the worst offender is the new shuffle time. In P3 and 4 there was an element of 'skill' involved whereby you had to guess the card or press at the right time. This is gone, the cards are simply lined up and you pick what you want. This is actually kind of irrelevant, but it gets worse. There are basically no negative cards. You can get half EXP and half gold, but this gives you extra cards, so its entirely up to you. You can also quite easily get skill cards, money, experience, level ups to your personas, upgraded abilities and also permanent stat increases for your personas. There are also plenty of other things, for example getting Rise's social link up allows her to just jump into battle and buff your party. Spells such as one which restores 5% SP after every battle have been made obtainable much earlier in the game (once you get this you can basically keep going forever), and party members are given really great spells for levelling their social links, along with the other benefits. Now this is a kind of doubled edged sword. These additions make the game more convenient certainly, and I'm not necessarily against these additions. The problem is it just made the game on normal seem too easy, and this is a problem as you at least expect a challenging game still from a Shin Megami Tensei game, even on normal. On the flip side, the game has plenty more difficulty levels available which can appeal to a variety of players, with easier difficulties allowing you to revive in fights, gradually decreasing the benefits as you go harder. A good move was to add the option for normal difficulty to respawn at the start of the floor if you get game over, something that I'm actually glad in the game as losing hours of gameplay because you made a mistake in one battle isn't fun or 'hard'. This said, if you are returning to the game, I definitely recommend choosing a higher difficulty as you may find the game a bit more boring to play on normal. The difficulty is varied, just be careful what you pick. Persona 4 is a game which has a ton of personality and charm and this is what makes playing the game so appeal. Everything is particularly stylish in design from the menus to the brilliant soundtrack, whilst the setting of the game also provides pleasure. If you're interested in Japanese culture, this is a Japanese game through and through, providing a somewhat authentic look on rural Japanese life from the types of places they have to just giving a nice idea of what this place in Japan might actually look like. The town stays the same but the game gives off a good sense of atmosphere, for example during the summer the music changes and everything is bright, whilst winter takes everything lower and calmer with an appropriate theme. The graphics may look somewhat basic, there's no improvement over the PS2 version, however this really doesn't matter. The areas still look great and the anime artwork is as always still strong. The soundtrack ranges from great instrumental pieces along with plenty of vocal pieces. The new battle theme is pretty great, whilst the old remains for surprise attacks. The soundtrack may not appeal to everyone’s tastes, giving off a strong J-pop type vibe, but its something I don't listen to at all and I still love the soundtrack. Whilst some of the new content, Marie and her dungeon in particular, may be a little disappointing, this doesn't hurt an already excellent game. This is the best JRPG in the last few years providing an excellent experience in all areas. The dungeon crawling can be considered a bit lacking in some ways, but for many players this will probably not matter. I definitely recommend people who have played the original game to pick this version up and have another playthrough, however if you've played the original to death, the new features may not be enough to warrant another playthrough. Its a long game with plenty to see and do, and its an absolute joy to behold.

author: Bkstunt_31
review_title: Truth is elusive...
review_text: Very few games really grab me and demand my attention. Very few. But Persona 4 Golden recently did just that. In fact, I enjoyed it so much that I've played through the game multiple times now and even got the platinum trophy for it. Since you are reading this review, you are likely wondering what to expect out of this game, so let me share what I know about it with you as well as why it grabbed me so completely. Would you even know the truth if you saw it? "Truth" is a ringing key-word in Persona 4 and for good reason: the entire game centers around your character's search for the "truth" throughout the game. So in that vein, let me share this game's ultimate truth with you early in this review (don't worry, no spoilers!): This is a very TEXT-HEAVY game. Literally, it is filled with text and has story bursting to the seams. Being an RPG though, most people will find this a good thing. If you are turned off by a story-heavy game though it would be wise to run away from whatever device you are reading this on, preferably screaming out to Cthulhu to save you! Still here? Good! So, the game focuses on story, but is it any GOOD? There's the real question! Persona 4 features a high-school student (like all Persona games...) coming to the town of Inaba as a transfer. Soon after his arrival in town, mysterious murders start occurring... murders that are somehow forecast by a mysterious midnight TV show called "The Midnight Channel". The protagonist is naturally drawn into these murders and they serve as the game's mystery framework. Nothing like a good "Who-dun-it?" storyline, right? What truly makes the game's story good though is not just the mystery angle (which is indeed excellent), but the quality writing and immersion. The writing itself is both clever and quirky and never failed to put a smirk or scowl on my face at will. However the immersion into the protagonist's life is what will really grab you and never let you go. You control the protagonist day by day, more often than not deciding exactly what to do, who to talk to and how you spend your time. This kind of control gets you really invested in the characters since you spend so much time with them. The game's main story carries ever onward of course, breaking up your peaceful days at school with the grim reality that there is still a murder to solve. To cap all of this off, Persona 4 Golden features multiple endings (some of which are unique to the "Golden" Vita version of the game). By the end of your Persona 4 playthrough, you will likely find yourself sad to leave behind your friends and family at Inaba... just the way a good story should make you feel. One more time! I could probably lump this first paragraph in with the story section above, but let's talk about Social Links! Why not!? Another reason the Persona series got so popular was the fact that it incorporates a relationship simulator into the core game play mechanic in the form of Social Links. As you spend your time with friends around school and town you'll slowly form relationships with them and level up those relationships. Each friend is tied to a tarot card which is in turn tied to a group of personas (the mythical beasts that your main character uses to battle with), so by increasing your relationships around town you will in fact power up your ability to summon personas. The actual bonuses you receive are actually fairly minor but relationship building is not only addicting game play wise but also provides great bits of story and background. There I am talking about the story again! Bah, this is the game play segment! As you play through the game, you will encounter dungeons that you will be able to explore with your team of fellow truth-seekers. The vast majority of these dungeons are randomly-generated and are filled with treasure and monsters. You and your allies will fight these monsters with your Persona, which grants you various powers and abilities. Most of the characters in the game have a single persona, but naturally your main character is special and can store multiple personas at the same time, switching between them at will and vastly expanding your range of abilities. With hundreds of personas to find and acquire throughout the game, Persona 4 Golden starts to feel like it has a pokemon problem. Not only can you acquire these persona entities, but you can also store them in a compendium and even fuse them together to create new, stronger personas. All of this collecting and fusing can very well be addicting ( Gotta catch 'em all! ), but limits how much power you can gain by not allowing your persona's level to be greater than your current level (a great idea). The game also includes a skill-card system that lets you give your personas specific skills, allowing for a touch of customization. Addicting, indeed! All of this fighting wouldn't be complete with some tried-and-true RPG tropes of course. You'll be equipping weapons, armor and items to take into battle. There is also an element system in place that allows you to target enemy weak-points. Persona 4 places an emphasis on critical and weak-point hits though by allowing the attacker an extra turn whenever they achieve such a hit. But beware: this system can work against you just as easily as for you! So fighting and building relationships... yep, that is Persona 4 in a nutshell! But of course there's more to it than that. Your character can choose to read, build models, shop around town, fish, catch bugs, cook, go for coffee, get a part-time job or any number of other things to fill your time. Try not to forget that you have a murder to solve! What're YOU looking at!? Despite originally being a PS2 game, Persona 4 Golden holds up extremely well. This is likely due to the (relatively) simplistic 3D models used throughout the game. While the characters don't really show a lot of emotion through the 3D art, the game does its best to cover for this fact with 2D facial artwork accompanying the clever writing combined with anime-inspired emoticons (totally a word... seriously!). Areas throughout the game are well designed but often either suffer somewhat from repeated visits (the town of Inaba itself only has so many locations) or repeated backgrounds. The latter issue there is noticeably bad in the game's many dungeons where the floors are all randomly generated and look just like the floor before it. Again: they try to cover this up with the occasional color change (in SOME dungeons) but adding a different shade of color doesn't do much. It should also be noted that Persona 4 does indeed fall into the trap of enemy palette-swapping. Ah, that trap is so easy to fall into it seems! So while the game's locations and character/persona designs are done extremely well, variety unfortunately suffers a bit. This is of course compounded by the fact that Persona 4 is a LONG game and will have you spending a LOT of time in the same areas over and over. To be perfectly honest, the graphics may very well be the game's weakest link. However, the graphics are still quite enjoyable. Of special note are the abundance of animated scenes scattered throughout the game that are always a treat to see. Growing on you daily... Ever since I first heard Persona 3 I've been a fan of the unique music Persona 3 brought to the table. Thankfully Persona 4 not only upholds its predecessor's musical chops but surpassed them. Music in Persona 4 plays in a very logical way. Certain events will trigger theme songs while each dungeon and battles often have longer songs to accompany them. As you play through the game you'll encounter several songs that you will often only hear snippets of due to the short times you'll be in dialog with them, but even those short exposure times will cause these tunes to grow on you. "Signs of love", "Your Affection" and "Like a Dream come true" are all excellent shorter songs (Arg, there's so many! Check out "Smile" and "Heartbeat, Heartbreak" as well!). Many of the game's tracks are up-beat, pop-music inspired pieces that make great use of brass instruments; not something you see everyday in your RPG soundtrack. These are often combined with English lyrics, but are often sung by non-English speakers, which has a tendency to make you strain to understand some of the songs. Persona 4 is far from a one-trick pony though, as the game also has a handful of melancholic pieces that are hauntingly beautiful. My favorite track in the entire game has to be "Heaven", although "Reach out to the Truth" and "A Corner of Memory" are right up there. The game features quite a bit of voice acting throughout as well, which is always enjoyable. The voice actors themselves do a superb job and really give it their all even when the scenes themselves may amount to little more than typical anime scenarios. Still, the audio in the game is fantastic. Time to switch the channel! Atlus is developing a pattern with their Persona series... you can almost guarantee that at some point down the line Atlus is going to release a better version of a Persona title. After all, they are batting 100%. As I mentioned earlier, Persona 4 was originally a PS2 title. Amazing, no? Well, this version of Persona 4 is "Golden" for a reason. Not only does it include the extra endings I mentioned earlier in the review but also has new social links, animations and dungeons. Don't forget that it also now includes trophies since it is a Vita title (man I really wished Persona 3 had trophies...). Besides all of the new content, you can also choose to play a New Game +, which makes a second play-through drastically different when you are able to customize the game's difficulty and don't have to worry about leveling up certain statistics. Persona 4 Golden also has a slew of special features including concept art, music boxes and live-concert recordings from Persona concerts. I defy you to find a game that offers this much extra content and built-in goodies for a port or remake (it really is impressive!). Overall: 9/10 Persona 4 Golden is, to date, the series shining masterpiece. I say "to date" because Persona 5 was announced recently and I'm very hopeful, but if you are looking for one of the TOP RPG's for the PlayStation Vita, you are looking in the right place... as long as you can stomach a lot of reading that is! Have fun and keep playing!

author: DarknessSphere
review_title: Persona 4 Golden lives up to the hype, and more!
review_text: Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 4 Golden The 2008 Japanese RPG Persona 4 has been given an updated release for the Playstation Vita. While core elements of the game are the same, new content, visuals and audio have been added to this 2012 release. The game has been extremely well-received by both gamers and reviews, and there is good reason for that. Every portion of the game has been given great detail, from the characters and story to the music and game mechanics. The overall high quality and polish of the game has certainly made its positive reputation well deserved. Story/Narrative: 10/10 In Persona 4 Golden, you assume the role of a teenager who has been sent to live with your Uncle and cousin in the remote town of Inaba. Upon your arrival, you become involved in a series of murders that are connected to ‘The Midnight Channel’, a show that shows the victims on television before they are kidnapped and murdered. You realize that you have the power to intervene and save those that are kidnapped by jumping into the ‘television world’. Slowly, you uncover more clues about why these kidnappings occur, and the true culprits behind these incidents. The game takes place over one school year, where you attend school while also solving this murder mystery. The story itself is very engrossing, holding the player in suspense all throughout the game. Multiple clues are given throughout the game, but almost manage to keep the player on their toes. More importantly, the characters that accompany you throughout the game are well-written and detailed. This makes the time you spend with your classmates during the social aspects of the game highly enjoyable. When dealing with the concept of immersion, the game makes you feel heavily invested in the game. You feel like you are directly involved with the lives of your classmates, and the game is influenced by the decisions you make. During the quests to save those that are kidnapped, they undergo deep, personal revelations about who they are as individuals. In order for them to use their persona, they have to recognize and accept facets of themselves that were buried away. This showcases a really devotion to quality and writing that help make you personally connected to the characters that fight beside you. Gameplay: 9/10 The game takes place over one school year, where you choose how to spend most of your time. During any set day, barring any special events, you would attend school, and have options on how you would spend your afternoon and evening time. This may involve training through dungeon-crawling, spending time with friends, or increasing your personal character traits through various activities. Persona 4 Golden retains most of the game mechanics from its predecessor. This game is characterized as a dungeon crawler, meaning that the action portions of the game have you and your team explore multiple floors of a dungeon while fighting through monsters. During combat, each character takes turn committing one action. These actions may involve doing physical attacks, using offensive or defensive based magic, defend or use items. The game heavily revolves around innate strengths and weaknesses. By exploiting these weaknesses, your enemies can become incapacitated and further damaged. Increasing your level in this game means to strengthen one’s ‘Persona’, a subconscious entity one awakens inside them. Gaining more levels upgrades and unlocks new abilities to be used in combat. The main character has the ability to possess multiple personas, giving options to fuse them in multiple ways to create new, stronger personas. While this feels segregated from the action portions of the game, the game strikes a perfect balance between the two. The friendships you build, called ‘Social Links’ have direct ties to your combat prowess. The higher your social links are, the more you unlock personas you can obtain when fusing personas, as well as bonus levels while fusing. When you improve social links with those that fight beside you, it also increases actions they can do during combat like healing status ailments and executing unique attacks that incapacitate opponents. A strong balance between your social life and dungeon crawling is important to increase your combat prowess. More importantly, they help you get the most out of your Persona 4 Golden experience! The only minor (and potential) complaint with the story is the pacing. Throughout the school year, you are given a set amount of time to complete your mission of saving anyone who has been kidnapped. If you choose, you can rescue these individuals very early on within the window of time given. In cases like this, the adventure becomes stagnant. The story will not advance until that window of time has passed. During that time, you simply have to wait for that window of time to end before anything happens concerning the story. Graphics – 10/10 The graphics for Persona 4 Golden showcase the high definition capabilities of the Playstation Vita. The 3D graphics while exploring the town of Inaba and exploring dungeons is crisper and more vibrant than the original PS2 release. The overall animations of the personas and their combat abilities are dynamic. Powerful attacks really do look as though they possess lots of power. Furthermore, the portions involving the anime drawings of each character are also of high quality. They give the game a unique feel, especially with its portrayal as a Japanese role-playing game. Replayability – 10/10 The game offers a lot of replayability once you complete the game. When you finish the game, it allows you to start a New Game+. This means you start right at the beginning, but a lot of what you accomplished is transferred as well. This involves personal character traits you developed, the money you earned, and all the personas that you collected and fused during your first game. The significance of this is that a large amount of time spent improving or collecting the things mentioned above is now removed. This means you have a lot more leisure time when starting a New Game+. Lacking character traits or money hindered you from completing various activities in the game at certain points in the game. Without these boundaries, more time can now be devoted to other activities like developing social links. Furthermore, transferring personas from the previous game allows you to have powerful personas that you would not normally have at that point in the game. This allows you to spend less time grinding. This also allows more leisure time in the game to do as you choose. The New Game+ feature is well made, allowing you to experience the game more on your terms without having the same amount of time investment. Conclusion – 10/10 The critical acclaim for Persona 4 was well deserved, and this updated release helps a whole new generation of gamers experience this game with updated content. One minor barrier some newcomers might have with this game is that it is a very stereotypical Japanese role-playing game. Without going too in-depth, it means that there are a lot of themes and tropes that you usually find in Japanese games, and not so much in Western games. Regardless of this minor cultural difference, I would encourage any Vita owner to pick this game up.

author: NettoSaito
review_title: Persona 4 Golden - It truly is Golden!
review_text: Back in 2008 an RPG called Persona 4 hit the Western shores. It was the long awaited sequel to the well known PS2 RPG Persona 3, and before we knew it, it became a hit. Fans fell in love with the character's, the gameplay, the school life "life sim" aspects, as well as it's story. Although the game before it was just as popular among fans, Persona 4 took things to a whole new level. Soon there was a manga series to go along with it, a full anime, and even a direct sequel fighting game produced by Arc System Works. To put it simple, Persona 4 was a game that fans liked a lot, and because of that it evolved past just being a game. Well, things didn't stop there. In 2012 a brand new version of Persona 4 hit the shelves for the PlayStation Vita called "Persona 4 Golden." Just what is Persona 4 Golden? Is it worth owning if you already had Persona 4? What about the new comers, is this a good place to start? Well, how about we find out? The Golden Story: Persona 4 Golden opens up with "you" being face to face with a strange man in what seems to be a limo. You are in the velvet room, a room that exists between reality and dreams, and you have been called there for a very special reason. Everything that happens in that room is tied to your fate, and it seems your life is about to change. The strange man sitting at the end of the limo is named Igor and he tells you just that. While your future is unclear, he gives you a warning, and asks for your name. At this point you are asked to name your character whatever you want, but the main character's "canon" name is Narukami Yu (Yu Narukami by English standards). After telling Igor his name, Yu (or whatever you named yourself) then comes to reality. He is traveling on a train to a small town called Inaba, where he will be spending the next year of his life. It turns out his parents had been transferred overseas due to their job, and they have decided to send him to live with his uncle Ryotaro and his cousin Nanako Dojima. Once Yu arrives in Inaba, he is greeted by his uncle and cousin, and taken back to his new home. As he sits down with his family for dinner, his uncle gets a call to go into work, and apparently like always, Nanoko is left home alone. It turns out Dojima is a police detective, and because of that he is rarely home alone. Poor little Nanoko is left to fend for herself most of the time, and today is no different. After finishing dinner, Nanoko helps Yu get settled in to his room, and the very next day they both go off to school. While at school Yu slowly begins to make some new friends. Yosuke, just like Yu, is a big city boy who was forced to move to the small town after his parents became the manager of the local super store Junes, Chie is a tomboy kung fu nut, and Yukiko is the shy girl everyone seems to hit on. At first this small group doesn't seem like much, but not too long after they all met, things began to change. During his first day of school, a dead body was found hanging from a TV antenna close to the school, and the strange rumors of a "Midnight Channel" began to circulate. It turns out, if you look at the TV at midnight on a raining night while it is turned off, your "true love" will appear; however only the latter part turned out to be a rumor. As the police investigated the murder, Yu and his friends decide to check out the midnight channel rumor to see if it was true, and sure enough, it was. A young girl showed up on the screen, but it wasn't Yu's true love. As he reaches out to touch the screen, Yu is shocked to find his arm going into the TV! Although he at first tries to climb all the way in, he gets stuck in the TV's frame, and decides to pull himself out and tell his friends about what happened the next day. The next day at school Yu discusses the Midnight Channel with Yosuke and Chie, only to find out that they had all seen the very same girl. Although everyone is confused as to what the midnight channel is, Yu decides to tell the others about what happened to him; how he went inside the TV. At this point everyone thinks that he was just dreaming, and they decide to pretend he never even brought it up. Although within the next few hours, all of them would come to learn the truth, and their lives would be changed forever. After going to Junes to look at a brand new TV, Yu finds himself falling into a big screen TV, with his friends close behind. They all ends up in a strange world, wonder into a strange blood stained room, and then on their way out they find themselves face to face with a strange bear like thing named Teddie. According to Teddie someone had been throwing people into his world, making the once quite land into a world filled with noise. Since Teddie didn't want to be bothered, he opened a portal back to the "real world," and sends everyone back home. Deciding to put everything that had just happened behind them, Yu and co decide to return home, and pretend it never happened... Although it seems fate has other plans for them. It turns out the girl on the Midnight Channel was a friend of Yosuke's, and the very next day she is found dead hanging just like the first victim. Yosuke takes the news of her death hard, and that is when he decides to drag Yu back into that strange world with him. If the Midnight Channel and that world are connected to her death, Yosuke was determined to get to the bottom of it. After talking to Teddie about what happened, Yu and Yosuke follow him to a strange dream like version of Inaba. There they find a strange door to the liquor store the girl's family ran, and coming out of it are strange creatures Teddie calls "Shadows." Upon seeing these shadows, a voice rings through Yu's head that tells him "I am thou," and a card magically appears in his hand. "Per, so, na!" Upon yelling the words, a warrior appears above Yu's head, and with its sword it slices the shadow's to bits. Yu had gained the power of "Persona," the ability to summon your inner self. Now with the power to use persona, Yu dives into the TVs to save the poor lost souls who show up on the Midnight Channel. As the months go by, more people become kidnapped, Yu and Co dive into the TV world, they use their personas to fight the shadows, and help each victim face their inner self. Upon facing their inner self, that victim also gains the power of persona, and joins Yu in the search for the truth. Just who is behind these murders? Why are they throwing people into the TV? Just what is Teddie? What are shadows? Why does the Midnight Channel show the victim even before they enter the TV? Why is there even a world inside the TV? How come Yu gained his power before facing his shadow? Is he different? The town of Inaba is filled with mysteries, and it is your job to get to the bottom of it. All while still being a high school student! School Life: The gameplay of Persona 4 Golden is split up into two main sections, and because of that I'll be discussing each aspect of the gameplay separately. The first part of Persona 4 is your everyday school life. This section of the game plays a lot like a visual novel mixed with a dating sim or life sim. Since the game takes place over a year, you actually do go through most of the days. Now sure, at times there will be small time skips (such as during midterms and finals), but for the most part you really do spend a full year in Inaba. Normally your schedule will be as followed. Monday through Saturday Yu will wake up and go to school. On the way to school you may see a cutscene with him walking there, and along the way Yu may talk to one of his friends, or overhear something from other students. After that is class time. Although most of the time you won't even see the class, sometimes an important topic will be brought up, or you'll be asked a question in class. If you answer one of these questions correctly, your stats will increase. Once class is over, you then enter the "after school" part of the day, and the entire world is open to you! After school you can basically do anything, and there is a LOT to pick from. Whatever action you do will advance the time to evening, and that is why it is important to plan out what you want to do for that day. You can hang out with one of your friends, go to the movies, study in the library, work at one of the part time jobs, go to one of the school clubs you may have joined, and so on. There are also some activities you can do which will not advance time such as doing side quests, talking to NPCs, buying stuff at the store, buying books, etc. Either way, there are a lot of things you can do after school, and they all help you in different ways; although Social Links are the main parts of it. In Persona 4 you can become friends with your classmates, or other people around town, and this comes in the form of social links. By hanging out with people after school, you will build up your friendship, and that will in return help you in battle. While becoming closer with your party members may unlock special skills and abilities for them, hanging out with people in general will help you with your personas. By having stronger social links you can create stronger personas, and that really helps out in the long run. As I said before, doing well in class will increase your stats, but that isn't the only way to increase them. By eating food, doing jobs, and reading books, you can increase your other "social skills" as well. These social skills will allow you to do different things, based on what level you have them at. For example if you're brave enough, you could tell your teacher off in class, or if you're a very understanding person you can help tutor a student. Getting your skills up gives you more options to say to your friends to help build your friendship faster as well, so its always a good idea to get them as high as possible. After you have did your one "main action" of the day, the game will then advance to the evening section of the day. Now in the evening you'll sometimes start out by watching a cutscene (usually you'll be eating with Nanoko or watching the news to find out about the latest events and the weather), but after the scene is over you can do whatever you want. Although in the original Persona 4 you were limited on what you can do, in Golden you can actually go out into the city at night. At night Inaba is a slightly different place. The store becomes a bar (which you can also work at), you can visit the shrine to make a wish and become closer to people faster, you can sometimes meet up with friends who'll discuss the latest events in the story (also it'll make them closer to you), you can go night fishing, you can catch bugs at night, there are quite a few night jobs you can take (such as working at the hospital), or you could always return home and do some things there. At your house you can make models, make box lunches to eat with friends the next day, you can do other forms of part time work from home, you can read books (which will increase stats or give you new abilities), or you can even study for school. You really have quite a lot of options at night, but even so a lot of the cities areas are limited. While in the day you can travel allover, at night you are stuck mainly at the shopping district. Although for the most part you'll have complete control over what you do, there are special events that happen during the year that you must attend to. You'll go on school trips (which are normally quite funny), go on vacations with friends, go to special events, hang out on holidays, or even be forced to take exams at school. These sections of the game give you little to no control, and are completely story based. Still they help break up the daily grind, they add in comedy, and help pull you into this world even more. As you manage your daily live and investigate the murders, you can also preform one other major action which leads us to the second main part of the game. By going to Junes during the day, you can enter the TV world, and begin the RPG aspect of Persona 4 Golden. The TV World and Personas: While in the TV World, the game turns into a dungeon crawler. You will form a party of 4 characters, pick an area to go into, and begin exploring. Each area is simply just hallways and doors, but they do have their own themes, and enemies to encounter. Enemies will show up on the map as black shadows, and by hitting them with your sword first you can gain the upper hand in battle. While in battle you'll have the choice to either directly control your other party members, or let the computer take care of it, and you will also have a verity of options to help plan out your attacks. Although you can simply hit "attack" to bash an enemy with your weapon (Yu's is a sword), this isn't always the best option. The real main aspect of battles is the personas themselves, and it is up to you to figure out how to use them best. Each persona has their own abilities and stats, and Yu has the ability to switch between personas during battle. This is something you'll want to do quite often, and for very good reason. The entire goal while fighting in this game is to actually knock every single enemy over so you can pull off an "All Out Attack." Every enemy in the game has a weakness, and by exploiting that weakness you will knock them over, and gain an extra turn. For example, say you're fighting against three enemies who are weak to electric type attacks. Well, Yu's default persona is electric type, and he has an electric attack called "Zio." By using Zio you'll be able to knock over an enemy, gain another turn, use Zio to knock over the second enemy, gain another turn, then use it gain for a final time to knock the last one down. Once this happens you can press the X button to pull off the All Out Attack, and flat out destroy everyone. This is the basics of the battle system, and to fully use it you will have to switch around your personas. Still, this is only the half of it. The personas themselves are a very complex system, and it takes some time to learn. Although you can randomly get more personas at the end of each battle, the main way to get them is by going into the velvet room (which you can access from both the real world and tv world), and fusing your personas together. By fusing two or more personas, you can create a completely brand new persona that will receive skills from the two you used to make it, as well as level up based on your social link bonuses. These personas are stronger than what you would normally find, and by fusing you can create personas with the skills and attacks you want them to have. You can also get skill cards to use on them by fighting enemies, but skill cards are rare, and its even rarer to get the one that you actually need/want. Leveling up in Persona 4 Golden is the final main feature of the game's RPG elements, and it is also a system which is a little bit different from most RPGs. As you fight and kill enemies, your character (Yu) will level up, but so will the persona he has equip at the time. While leveling up Yu will increase his HP, and SP (which personas spend when they use their special attacks), it also allows Yu to hold more personas at one time. Other than that no other stats increase on Yu (or the other characters), and the only way to make him stronger is buy buying better armor or weapons. The personas on the other hand, their stats DO increase. Each time a persona levels up, they become stronger, their attacks do more damage, and they learn new skills to use. Leveling your personas becomes a very important part of the game, and will be how you'll get stronger. While actually exploring the areas, running through halls, and opening doors is pretty basic (and can become repetitive), the battles and personas help keep the RPG action fun, and it never really drags on for too long. Each area is actually pretty short, only taking an hour or so to complete. If you're the type of person who hates dungeon crawling, you really don't have to worry in this one. By rushing through it, these areas only take up about 10% of the game, but if you actually like that sort of thing, you can easily spend as much time in them as you want. The Music and Style of P4G: Once in awhile in my reviews I'll bring up something outside of the main features. This "something" is normally a feature or aspect that really just stood out in the game, and helped give it it's charm. For Persona 4 Golden, that would have to be its music, and overall style. Persona 4 Golden uses a style that really makes the game pop. It is filled with bright anime styled graphics, detailed anime mugshots, it is filled with Japanese themes, and the music really stands out. The first time you go into a battle and hear "Reach Out to The Truth," you will be shocked! Every song in the soundtrack just fits the game' so well, and it all really helps set the mood. The game features anime styled comedy to give you a few good laughs, and there's a wide verity of extras added exclusively to Golden. You can watch live persona concerts, watch Japanese trailers for the games, listen to the game's soundtrack, view art galleries, and even play a bonus trivia game. The extras are a really nice addition, and I often found myself going back to them just to rewatch a cutscene, or listen to one of the game's tracks. If you're a fan of modern day anime, Persona 4 Golden will really stand out to you. Like I said before, everything about the game just "pops," and it is filled with memorable moments. The Good and the Bad: Persona 4 Golden isn't a game that everyone will like, but if you own a Vita and like JRPGs or even Visual Novels, it is a MUST have! The game's story is great, you will fall in love with the characters, the combat is fast and fun, fusing personas can become addicting, the music is great, and you will just be flat out hooked from start to finish. Really the game doesn't have any bad points, and is one of them few games I can review and say it is truly perfect for what it is. The only real issue with the game is the fact that its a dungeon crawler with hallway after hallway to explore, but then again a lot of people out there love that. On top of all of that, Persona 4 Golden was designed in a way so that EVERYONE could enjoy it, and that comes with a wide verity of difficulty modes. While the easiest mode lets you retry battles you die (your characters are revived with full health while the enemy retains the damage they received), the hardest mode is there to really push you and give you a challenge. If you have a Vita, and you like this sort of game, this is one you just CANNOT pass up! It has quite a lot of features the original PS2 version didn't have, and it even has a longer story mode featuring new areas and story arcs not originally seen. Even if you played the game before, you really have nothing to lose by getting Golden. Even when you finish the game it makes you want to come back for more, so you might as well come back to Golden. It really is, well, golden! Persona 4 Golden for the PlayStation Vita gets a solid 10/10.

author: carlde21
review_title: You'll never look at a TV the same again!
review_text: I am so happy I played Persona 5 Royal but it also made me nervous to return to Persona 3 and 4. That game was epic, classic, and filled with moments that will tug at my nostalgia for years to come. Persona 4 sat in my backlog for months but I've been looking for Christmas-themed games, or at least games with at least a portion taking place over the holidays. Cthulhu Saves Christmas and Parasite Eve were obvious choices and I learned that there was a small portion of Persona 4 taking place during Christmas too so that's all I needed so away I went! For the most part, this was a memorable experience with a few notable drawbacks. I'm sure everyone has heard of some kind of urban legend and that is the foundation of this game. It is said that if you look at a turned-off TV at midnight on a rainy night a vision of your true love will appear. Only something much more creepy and sinister shows up for the main protagonist, Yu Narukami (you can name him something else) when he tries his luck. The fog soon descends on the small town Inaba and with it, a brutal murder. Imagine moving to a new place like Yu and immediately being thrust into a murder mystery! Yu and his new friends have to unravel this perplexing case quickly before more tragedy strikes the sleepy town. Joining him is the rambunctious kung-fu-loving Chie, the trendy Yoskue, who resents having to leave his city life for Inaba, Yukiko a typical girl next door type who helps to run the family inn, and the rebellious punk Kanji who has a reputation for being a troublemaker. They are later joined by the famous teen detective Naoto, mature beyond her years, Rise a famous teen idol looking to start a calmer life away from the spotlight and the ever-exasperating Teddie. If you could barely stand Morgana in Persona 5 or generally don't like mascot-style characters, Teddie is infinitely more irritating than Morgana or most other similar characters from other games. He had few redeeming qualities and ruined most scenes, including, unfortunately, some of the most serious scenes. There are 24 social links to find and dive into. These are in-depth friendships that can be formed with teammates and other key NPCs around Inaba. By spending time with them and approaching conversations carefully, these links can be leveled up in the form of ranks, each with 10 levels. Some of them are formed automatically while several require some steps to start. What generally starts as run-of-the-mill relationships between Yu and his social links become very deep by the time you increase their ranks a few times and become significant by the time the rank is maxed. My advice regarding social links is to avoid temptation and try to play this game blind, rather than being glued to a guide. I'll only say there is one specific social link to focus on to extend the game to two extra dungeons, one of which is painfully annoying and takes away all the items and equipment earned throughout the game. I despised this dungeon (in February) but otherwise liked the game enough to see it through to the end and thankfully the last dungeon was much more manageable. The dungeons are the weak points in this game. Other than that failed gimmick in February they are standard, randomly generated, and usually ten floors but overall tend to be bland even when trying something new, like with the void. Interesting in theory, but not ten floors of the same thing. Thankfully enemies are viewable and if approached and slashed from behind, you can start battles off with an advantage, acting before they can but enemies can also sneak up on you and act first. Attacking their weakness can knock them down and if all foes are down an especially strong attack can occur. Generally, I avoided most enemies only seeking out those weird hand monsters, you'll know when you see them because they give out a ton of experience and money.
