Jobs are another way to get money but many of those require one, or more of your social qualities to be at a certain rank. There are five social qualities, courage, knowledge, expression, understanding, and diligence. Don't ignore any of these and methodically work towards ranking them up! Reading books helps these qualities to eventually rank up and taking jobs is another way to not only earn money but improve social qualities and, in a few cases spend time with a social link! For example, working at the hospital or as a tutor is one of the best ways to spend your nights if Dojima or Nanako aren't free. These two, Dojima and the detective and his sweet daughter Nanako are who Yu lives with during his one-year stay in Inaba. Bringing back memories from when I worked at daycare at University, Yu can also work with children on certain days. This all might seem overwhelming and that is normal but this game is generous in the time it gives to work on all of this. Even playing blind, for the most part, I was able to max 19 social links, an additional 2 at rank 9 (of 10), all five social qualities to the maximum level, and even the top rank on 3 of the 4 exams! The game asks several interesting, difficult questions. After a few months, you just get into a flow and a routine and know when and where to find everyone and who or what to prioritize at any given moment. Though it can be tiresome when the game takes your time for a vacation, band practice, helping Nanako to study, etc. On one hand, I appreciate the game changing up the routine but it always seemed to happen when I had at least a dozen things on my mind regarding what I wanted to do! As is the case with a high school setting, some love interests pop up and it can be hard to determine who to pick, even if some morons try to get in the way. When it is all said and done, go with your heart! Many of the mechanics explored in this game would be expanded on in Persona 5 so in that sense, I am glad I eventually got around to playing Persona 4. There are some excellent ideas here but, by and large, music was not one of them. Now one of my favorite things about being with my love is we can sit in the same room and do our things and it still feels like quality time and we support each other regarding our hobbies. Sometimes she comments on the games I play, the shopping street under the quickly approaching sunset was gorgeous in her eyes. However, the same J-pop music playing constantly aroused her attention and I remember her tone when she asked "Haven't we heard this song enough already"? Indeed, it is painfully overplayed and sent my hand diving for the mute button. This shouldn't happen in a game, music should be more varied. This is a shame because there are some excellent songs, the instrumental piano track that plays during the fog and other mysterious moments is top-notch, a track I won't soon forget. Other tracks during poignant moments are fantastic. The artistic style is spectacular and, in a world where so many developers seem keen to make everything so life-like it was especially refreshing and admirable. If so many games are moving towards real-life graphics, doesn't that, by definition limit variety, at least to some extent? Persona 4 has its unique style and is very graceful in pulling it off, though I did sense some "Spirit Away" influence regarding the shadows. It is an interesting world despite the limited locations (just 7). I don't think I've played an RPG with such a small world to explore, there isn't much. But what it prides itself in, is the social aspect, it excels and there is a ton to explore with the wide variety of people in the game. In fact, by talking to various people 69 side quests can be uncovered. I finished 58 and found, by and large, there was nothing special about them. Many of them boiled down to revisiting the same bland dungeon to beat a specific enemy and get a drop Usually the first enemy after a specific quest is accepted drops the needed item. Great, I guess Just boring. But the rewards are usually worth it Plus excess items can be sold at the weapon shop which eventually leads to the weaponsmith being able to develop new weapons and armor. As is the case with any other Persona or Shin Megami Tensei game, fusion plays a central role in a player's ability to successfully advance. For the most part I just kind of winged it and at any chance, fused two weaker personas into a stronger one. Personas can only be changed for the main so it's not like you can screw this up too much because the other playable characters have set personas that provide enough variety to beat any boss while, at the same time, having growth that is, by and large, consistent. The only annoyance is that every Persona only has 8 slots to fit in magic and other buffs. That is standard for Atlus games and I understand the logic and agree with it, but it is still irksome and vexing. One aspect that seasoned Atlus fans might miss is demon negotiation, one of the only Atlus games I've played without this mechanic. While negotiation could prove burdensome at times in some Atlus games, such as if demons ran away with tons of money and/or items, it still adds another interesting twist to battles and allows players to escape without actually having to escape. Instead of negotiation, players are randomly presented with shuffle time. When this happens, various cards show up on the screen. Some are positive and heal HP or MP, increase experience or gold, improve persona skills, allow a new demon to join, or many other awesome benefits. However, some negative cards can half experience or money, or even drop them to zero. The catch is you often have 5 cards and only 1 choice, for example. The catch is taking negative cards increases the amount of tries you get. If you can take every card on the screen you get a "sweep bonus" which guarantees a shuffle time in the next battle, as well as increased tries. So in the end, there is a strategy to how you choose the cards and if you are looking to get more shuffle times hoping for more benefits, such as some extra demons, taking a well-planned negative card in the interest of the sweep bonus is the forward-thinking action to take. I had a string of about 15 sweep bonuses in a row at one juncture in the game and in the end, it was a high-risk, high-reward game of chance. I wouldn't mind seeing this in a future Atlus game! This isn't the immense time sink that Persona 5 is but I still clocked over 70 hours and other gamers should expect to, at the very least crack 60 hours. Getting to know each of the 20+ social links during downtime proved to be an addicting part of the game and figuring out how to maximize your limited time was rewarding. In the end, this is time well spent because this is a well-done game, flaws and all.

author: BlueBoy675
review_title: Step into the Shadow World
review_text: Every now and then there comes a game that truly changes you; a game that provides an experience that you'll never forget. I must admit that as I've gotten older there have been fewer games that have had this effect on me. I don't have much time for gaming these days, so games rarely leave an impact as I hardly ever finish them. That being said, I was hesitant to step into the world of Persona 4 Golden. I had heard talk that an average playthrough of the game could take up to 70 hours. It sounded daunting, and it wasn't sure if I would have the time or attention span to see that game all the way through. However, as soon as I booted up the game I knew I was in for a treat and that I would stick around for the whole ride. Right at the start you are greeted with a stylistic animated opening which serves to introduce the main characters and they gleefully dance to the tune of the game's upbeat theme song, "Shadow World." It's hard not to smile or sing along while watching this opening. It's then that you start a new game and step into the world of Persona. In Persona 4 Golden, which I'll now refer to as just "Golden," you play as Yu Narukami, a high school student moving from the big city to the small rural town of Inaba. As his parents are away on business, Yu is to spend the next year living with his uncle, Dojima, and younger cousin, Nanako. Yu will also attend school in Inaba, starting at Yasogami High the next day. It's here where he meets Yosuke Hanamura, Chie Satonaka, and Yukiko Amagi, three fellow students who will go on to become some of his closest friends. While at school, Chie tells Yu a rumor about something known as the "Midnight Channel." As the story goes, if one looks into a turned off television at midnight on a rainy night, an image of their soulmate will appear on screen. One student claims that he saw a TV reporter on the Midnight Channel, meaning she must be his soulmate. However, things take a grave turn as the very same reporter is found dead. Are the two events related? On top of this, Yu and his friends discover that they have the power to enter TVs, transporting them to an alternate world where monsters known as shadows roam free. Here they meet Teddie, a mysterious bear like creature who quickly befriends them. It seems that this world has some connection to the Midnight Channel, and with more and more people showing up on the mysterious program, Yu and his friends resolve to explore this new world and get to the bottom of things. Golden is half life sim, half dungeon crawler. While Yu and his friends do spend time exploring an alternate world, they are still regular high school students by day. You'll spend many of your days simply attending school, interacting with classmates, visiting shops, and hanging out with your friends. This is where the game's "social links" come into play. Social links represent Yu's relationships with the various people he meets throughout the game. Each link is connected to a specific arcana (more on that later). As Yu spends time with people, these social links rank up, eventually maxing out at rank 10. These social links provide little side stories as well as character development. For example, the social link for the Death arcana has Yu spending time with an old woman whose husband recently passed away. Over time she forms a bond with Yu, confiding in him her feelings regarding her husband's passing. While this little story is completely optional and adds nothing to the overall plot, it helps make the town of Inaba feel more alive. These are real people living in this town, not just lifeless NPCs. However, forming and maintaining relationships with people is only half of the game. There will be times when Yu and his friends need to enter the TV world. It's here where all of the action takes place. As people show up on the Midnight Channel, the gang realizes that this is an omen that the person shown will die. That is, however, unless Yu and the gang can find them in the TV world and bring them back to safety. To do this, you'll have to explore dungeons, where shadows will roam around and attack you on sight. These dungeons are made up of randomly generated floors, so it's never quite the same. Shadows can be seen roaming around, and if you make contact with one a battle will ensue. If the shadow strikes you first, the battle will begin with your enemies getting a free turn. If you manage to land the first strike, the same will happen for your party. Battles are turn based, with the order the characters act being based off of their ability. While your party members can attack with standard weapons such as swords, daggers, and guns, you'll be doing the most damage with your personas. A persona is a representation of the mask one wears in public to hide their true selves. Yu and his friends all have the power to summon them, and they are capable of dealing heavy damage to your foes. This is how the gang is able to cast magic spells and whatnot. Spells come in different elements (fire, ice, wind, etc.) and almost every enemy has a weakness. If an enemy is hit with their weakness, they will be knocked down the party member who hit them will gain an extra turn. If all enemies are knocked down, you will be able to initiate an all out attack. With this, all party members attack at once, doing massive damage to every enemy on the field. Be careful, though, as your party members also have weaknesses and will also be knocked down if hit. Battles are accompanied by high energy, uplifting music tracks that get you pumped to kick some shadow butt. Golden's soundtrack truly is a work of art, featuring a strong mix of both j-pop and hard rock. These tunes are catchy and they most definitely will get stuck in your head. A personal favorite of mine had to be the main boss theme. It truly conveys a sense of both tension and excitement. Going to back to personas, each member of the cast has their own personal persona unique to them. That is, everyone except Yu. Yu is special and has the ability to summon multiple personas and shuffle between them. This makes Yu the most versatile party member, giving him access to a wide variety of abilities. New personas can be obtained as rewards from winning battles, or through fusion. Fusion is exactly what it sounds like. By taking two or more personas, you can combine them to create a brand new, stronger one with skills carried over from the personas you used. Each persona is linked to an arcana, which there are over 20 of. Each arcana has a corresponding social link. If you've managed to rank up said social link, you're new fused persona will get a boost in strength. For example, going back to the social link with the old lady. If you have established the social link with the old lady and make a persona of the Death arcana, that persona will receive bonus experience giving, potentially giving it a few free level ups. This is where the incentive to spend time with people during the day comes from. If you max out a social link, you are given access to the ultimate persona of the corresponding arcana, making you more powerful. Persona 4 Golden is truly an experience. With an engaging plot, memorable characters, and addicting battle system you'll find yourself constantly coming back for more. I sure did, and before I knew it I had actually made it to the end of the game after a grand total of 68 hours. I didn't want the game to end. I had grown so fond of these characters and I didn't want to accept that the journey was over. At least there are multiple spinoffs that involve the gang getting back together for new adventures, but those are reviews for another time. Persona 4 Golden is quite simply flawless. Do yourself a favor and play it immediately. You won't regret it.

author: furygods
review_title: One of the best games I ever played but still have some faults.
review_text: Persona 4 Golden was essentially Persona 4, that was released earlier for the PS2, with extra content. But keep in mind, this is not a reason to undermine the game just because of that. This review sees that the game is judged as if it is a entirely new release, to be fair for players playing the game for the first time without any prior experience to the original Persona 4. In this review you will see that I would compare this game to Persona 3, which is the predecessor to this game, often. Graphics/Music [5/5] Although one should never truly judge a game solely on its graphics, the graphics department for Persona 4 Golden is indeed top notch. Replicating the entire town of Yaso-Inaba with some minor redesigning, you would not be disappointed in terms of graphics. The game keeps PS2 quality, which when looked at via the Playstation Vita screen looks more than competent. The music in Persona 4 Golden, unlike that of Persona 3 FES (The most complete version of Persona 3), is quite enjoyabe and less "looped" in some of its lyrics as I found in Persona 3's music. From the calm sounds of Yaso-Inaba to the vocals in battle, this game has a nice presentation in terms of music. Although some of the lines in battle are a bit odd, the lines for the story was done very professionally, even better then the voice acting for Persona 3. The grunts within some of the conversations throughout the game was a added plus. Story [5/5] The main bulk of any RPG should be the story, and Persona 4 Golden has it. The story for the game is engaging and easily serves as a good mystery that intrigues the mind and keeps the player guessing. Extra content exclusive to Golden is even more of a reason for seasoned veterans to pick this up. The game presents you with a number of choices throughout the game that allows you to choose your own path on the story and each and every character, and their respective social links provide a story of their own. Unlike Persona 3, where there would be several periods where the story would seemingly not advance, Persona 4 Golden constantly has the player in the story, whether a side story or the main story, the player is always progressing in the story. Truly, the story is indeed worth noting for a newcomer and I advise you to not spoil yourself if possible regarding the story. Also unlike Persona 3, the story of the game has a constant amount of humor in it, unlike the entirely dark approach in Persona 3. The scenes in this game is outrageous in its humor while maintaining the drama and dark parts maintaining a good blend. Gameplay [5/5] The very nature of a turn based battle system in a RPG could only hold so much depth. The highest pinnacle of a RPG that utilizes such a turn based battle system, in my opinion, is that it be not too complicated, has a good degree of depth, and fast. 1) What I meant by "not to complicated," was that there could only be a limited amount of complexity that could be attributed with a turn based battle system that Persona 4 Golden had. The game presents a easy to understand table of weaknesses that allows a newcomer to easily get familiar with the battle system. 2) What I meant by "has a good degree of depth," was that although the battle system of the game was easy to get used to, it doesn't mean that it was entirely "streamlined" for a casual audience. By "streamlined," I meant that the gameplay was not "dumbed" down to the point where all you had to do was to press one action and the game played itself. No, we are not looking forward for a game that plays itself for you, or otherwise what's the point? Besides a game that played itself would had gotten boring rather quickly. Persona 4 Golden provides the player with a variety of choices in battle from analyzing the enemy to dishing out the pain, and allowing you to control what your allies do. 3) What I meant by "fast," was a that a turn based battle system that moves slow, either by extra long animation or simply the amount of thought needed for every action, would had been quite "boring" quickly. The animation for all of the abilities within this game is short, which would be a fault in which I would explain later, but it keeps things fast which is good for gameplay. Although there was depth, we are not playing a game of high level chess, so a enormous amount of thought was not expected for this game. The game keeps a good amount of depth while keeping it fast. Persona 4 Golden truly had fulfilled the above three conditions to what I believe to be a "perfect" approach to its turn based battle system. The loading time transitioning from exploring to battle is practically non-existent. The ability for you to pick your fights adds to the amount of choice that the game presents you with, rather than forcing you to fight such as that of a random encounter system. The battle system is not the only thing that this game has. The game provides you with a large amount of time between segments for you to explore the town of Yaso-Inaba, build up what the game calls "social links" with various NPCs within the game. Not to mention the game also has a system where you could perfect what I would call the player's "external stats" such as that of his academics, courage, and whatnot. You may spend your time in certain areas to increase your "external stats" so that you may become closer to your friends and improve your battle capabilities. The free time that the game grants you with allows the player to have the choice on whether to do something and presents various amounts of goals for the player rather than just grinding. The "Persona" system that this game employed was much like that of Persona 3's but greatly enhanced. Presenting with a enormous amount of Personas one could create, it provides the player another choice to create more powerful and distinct personas to help him in his journey. Each Persona has a certain weakness and strength and as you built your social links with the characters in this game, you will uncover even greater Personas. The game also gives the player the opportunity to check the "Fusion Forecast," which is new to Persona 4, that allows you to check when would be the best opportunity to create additional Personas, which is essentially another choice for the player. Persona 4 Golden removes the annoying concept of "randoming" in the "Shuffle Time" segment of the game, which I greatly dislike in Persona 3. Instead of that, Persona 4 Golden presents the player yet another choice every time a "Shuffle Time" segment occurs, in which you could choose what you want to obtain and how you want to obtain it. The game also removes another annoying concept where in Persona 3, your allies and yourself could get "tired" and be less effective in battle which more or less forced you to quit early to rest. By removing that, the game presents the player with the choice on whether or not you want to stop exploring a "dungeon." The game constantly gives the player the power of the choice, and it is determined by the player in what he/she wants to do, which is important in RPGs. Art Style [5/5] The art style was either a hit or a miss for players but in my opinion the characters in this game was wonderfully drawn, everything was much more colorful instead of the pale colors of Persona 3. In my opinion, some of the characters in Persona 3 looked like zombies or just really pale like Makoto from School Days. Persona 4 Golden's art style felt more alive and updated. [What makes this almost perfect] So what makes this almost perfect? The fact is that the corridors/hallways within the game's "dungeons" are bland and reeks of "copy and paste." As you adventure onward, you will find that the "dungeons" hallways look exactly the same as in the previous floor and in the next floor. Aside from the few "event" rooms, the interior of every dungeon looks the same in the sense that the 5th floor design looks exactly like the 1st floor design but with a different layout of course. This could be why the game's loading times is so short. However be assured that only the "dungeons" in this game is full of "copy and paste," as Yaso-Inaba and the interiors of buildings are well detailed. Not only that but the game provides only the bare minimum of extra content in terms of optional "dungeon" exploring. Each story dungeon provides 1 optional dungeon that is the same as the story dungeon but with a optional boss in the end. Counting all of the optional dungeons that are variants of their story dungeon counterparts as well as the whopping 1 new optional dungeon exclusive to Golden, is definitely noticeable, as sometimes the player would desire some "extra" challenge to test their newly created Personas. However, one could spend as much as 50 hours of game time with just those dungeons and the extra activities outside of battle that it should not be too much of a issue. But for a game that gives so many opportunities for choices to the player, it is indeed quite lacking in the part of "optional dungeons" for the player. Fast (a.k.a. short) animations for abilities are good for gameplay but bad if you are expecting some cool effects. Almost every ability is quite short and underwhelming, with the exception of some of the top tier abilities which are more impressive in its effects but still short. Most of the enemies you encounter, with the exception of Story Bosses, are just a alternate color of a existing enemy. There are some variation here and there, with a few new enemies later in the game, most noticeable in the very latter parts of the game, but you would be mostly facing enemies in a different color. This could make the grinding process, which is unneeded on normal mode, more boring. [Conclusion] Judging Persona 4 Golden as a game on it's own, one would expect more designs for the enemies you would be facing but this game could easily be one of the best RPGs for the Playstation Vita. Rarely do one see a company putting so much content into one game without cutting out content or doing a lazy job in favor of DLC. But Atlus really outdid themselves with presenting a RPG of this scale, while keeping it fun and the story humorous yet mysterious. I definitely recommend, for a newcomer player to RPGs, to try this gem out. And if you tried Persona 3 and was bored by it (Like I was), rest assured Persona 4 Golden's worlds more fun than that game; and if you did play this game and would like to continue on the story of Persona 4, then you could try Persona 4: Arena, which was the canon (in terms of the story) sequel to Persona 4. However be warned, Persona 4: Arena is a fighting game.

author: LoneCourier2281
review_title: Atlus Rises to the Occasion with Persona 4: Golden
review_text: The Persona Team Strikes Gold With Persona 4: Golden Important Note: I have yet to play the original, Vanilla, Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 4, so this review will not be handling any comparisons between the two on purpose, as I do not necessarily know what has been added to Golden or removed, if anything. Introduction: The Persona series has fast become one of my favorite video game franchises. Every release I have had the opportunity to play has been phenomenal, as is the case with Persona 4: Golden (P4G or Golden). It is a title that has virtually everything I could ask for and more in a role-playing game. P4G is very different from your standard JRPG, it stands out for good reasons, in a genre that has very little change, Atlus was not afraid to take risks in terms of story-telling and gameplay. While a lot of these things might not be new for veteran Persona fans, it does not take away from the merits that P4G has. The ability to take this game with me is an added plus, with that being said, let us begin: Story: The Persona games tend to have exceptional stories and intriguing plot-lines, and P4G is no different. The game takes place during the school year of 2011-2012, in the sleepy little town of Inaba, Japan. The protagonist arrives from the big city to live with his uncle, Ryotaro Dojima and cousin, Nanako Dojima. The protagonist is then introduced to the characters Chie Satonaka, Yukiko Amagi, and Yosuke Hanamura who fast become some of his best friends. A series of mysteries arise and together the friends decide to investigate the incidents in Inaba. Rumors of a TV program that appears at midnight appropriately named the "Midnight Channel" begin to be spread around the town, which involves accidentally entering the TV and discovering another world. While there, they encounter Teddie, a bear mascot who lives within the TV world, together they work together to solve the mystery of the Midnight Channel and to save the people of Inaba. Also accompanying them are the characters: Kanji Tatsumi, a tough-looking delinquent with a secret life; Rise Kujikawa, a famous idol; and Naoto Shiragane, a young detective brought on to help the local police solve the mysterious case. Supporting characters also make up a huge chunk of the story, both in mandatory story events as well as in the form of Social Links. These Social Links are, for the most part, optional, but are an important part of the Persona series. You can choose to become closer to the citizens of Inaba as well as romance many of the female characters, you can remain loyal to one girl or you can decide to be a player of immense proportions, which could let to you getting pricked by the thorns of love. However, you wouldn’t want to play around with a bunch of caring people’s hearts and end up being a heartless monster in the end, now would you? The story has enough turns and twists in it to keep you entertained from beginning to the very end, keeping it from being a generic murder/mystery plot. Also, in many instances, the way the story plays out is left up to your decisions, which is something that many JRPGs still lack in today. Story: 5/5. Gameplay: P4G is a turn-based JRPG, and I realize that might turn some people away, but it is not just your average "press X to attack" game. You can do that, however, you will most likely not make it out of the first dungeon alive. Golden’s combat relies a lot on tactics, as you can change your teammates in before each dungeon but also you need to assemble a set of Personas that will be beneficial to you as well as take advantage of enemies’ weakness. The game relies on buffs and debuffs more than your average JRPG and you need to be aware of that. Each boss adds additional challenges and you cannot rely on the same Persona for every battle, you need to at least have a decent grasp on the Persona fusion function as well. Persona fusion allows you to take multiple Personas and make a new one out them while carrying over some skills to the new Persona. Persona fusion is not a skill you necessarily need to master in order to beat the game, although, in order to complete a specific Social Link, you will need to do so. The game does end once the main character is knocked out, so early on you will need to pay extra careful attention so this does not happen, some enemies do have attacks that can one-hit KO your entire party or one character and that can be annoying at first. Golden alleviates some issues with this by allowing you to start over from the beginning of the current floor you are on and also by allowing you to leave the dungeon to save and then return to certain floors, that way not all your progress is lost. Unlocking character abilities that prevent your MC from dying from critical blows also basically eliminate that issue later on. Which brings us to how the dungeons are set up. I won’t spoil anything, but the TV world is set up by different dungeons which their own number of floors, which usually range around 10 or so randomly-generated floors with some having less and a few having more. Each dungeon has one main boss, with most of them having minor bosses. Once you clear the dungeons you can return later to defeat optional bosses if you so choose to. Outside of battle, the gameplay is very straightforward, you can traverse around Inaba, from Yasogami High School, the shopping district, the Junes department store, as well as two locations located outside the town: Okina City and Shichiri Beach. All these locations can be accessed via a point and click map, however in most the locations you will be able to walk around and talk to the NPCs as well as party members. P4G also has a sort of fast travel system in each location, if you need to go to the northern part of the shopping district and you don’t want to walk all the way to the top, you can just press square and click the northern part to get there. Since the game does not utilize the touchpad on the Vita you can fully play the game on a Vita TV, which is not a bad way to play it if you do not like portable games as much as other people. Gameplay: 5/5. Presentation: Okay, so the original game came out at the very tail-end of the PS2’s lifetime, in 2008, so it still in many ways looks like a 2008 game. That being said, because of the way Atlus designed the game, it still looks fantastic, the character models are not perfect, they aren’t anything that will make you say, "Oh gee wiz, that Persona 4: Golden game sure should win the graphical achievement award of the century." They still fit perfectly though, especially on the PS Vita’s small screen. The enemy designs are also for the most part well designed, however, later on, you will find out a lot of the enemies are virtually color-palette swapped, but I understand graphical limitations probably had a play in that. Although your Personas look awesome and unique, Atlus did not skimp out on them. The town’s design has a certain charm to it and it was not too much and they did not too way too little as well. It is not crowded and there are just enough locations and NPCs to make it seem like an actual small town and not just an empty game space. Inaba is completely believable in being a sparsely-populated location. The best part of the presentation of Golden is by far the character portraits as well as the anime cut-scenes found within the game. Each character is drawn beautifully and help bring their characters to life. Every major character, whether a party member, supporting character or potential Social Link has their own character portrait that changes facial expressions depending on what they are saying, which I absolutely adore. Presentation: 5/5. Music: Oh. My. Izanagi. The music in P4G is impressive, to say the least. Not often do I find myself wanting to download an entire video game soundtrack, but Golden is different. The soundtrack is a mixture of different genres and it is hard to put a specific name on the entire soundtrack, however, trust me, Shoji Meguro did an absolutely awesome job in composing it. There are several tracks performed by Shihoko Hirata, such as "Pursuing My True Self" and "Reach Out to Truth" that in my honest opinion rival many of the commercial songs out there in terms of quality and catchy-ness. Other songs such as "Signs of Love, "Backside of the TV," "Your Affection," "Heartbeat, Heartbreak," "Heaven," "Shadow World," "Time to Make History," "True Story," and "Snowflakes" all are wonderful in their rights. Even the regular tracks are fitting and will keep you entertained as you play the game, as well as possibly humming and singing along as I found myself doing a lot of times. Music: 5/5. Length and Replay-ability: P4G can be an incredibly long game if you want it to be, it took me well over 100 hours just on one single playthrough alone. If you like to speed-run though games, it can be probably be done in 50-60 hours, although I honestly don’t see why you would want to speed through your first playthrough of Golden. The fact that you have a lot of Social Links as well as multiple possible romance options alone makes the replay value of the game shoot way through the roof. Not to mention that there are optional bosses as well as multiple endings that you can choose from as well as early events that take place that you will need to return to in order to go through with certain dialogue and options make P4G even more worth playing again. The game has trophies, just like most Vita games, so if trophy hunting is your thing, P4G is great for you in that aspect. Oh, and if you are trying to do multiple play-throughs, the game has an option to fast forward through story events as well as skip cut-scenes, so don’t worry about that. Length and replay-ability: 5/5. Final Verdict: Should you buy Persona 4: Golden? You betcha! It is one of the finest games on the Vita as well as one of the best Role-Playing Games of the decade. Golden will keep you entertained for many hours and everything about from the story, to the gameplay, the characters, as well as the music is phenomenal. Needless to say, the game is beary good. 5/5 My personal favorite PlayStation Vita game.

author: SNeIa
review_title: Building Upon Greatness
review_text: Introduction: Persona 4 Golden is an enhanced remake of the PS2 classic, Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 4. Offering two new social links, a new dungeon, new skill choices for party members, new scenes chronicling the hijinks of the Investigation Team, hilarious and/or fan service costumes (both showing off the Investigation Team members and providing tribute to Persona 3), more user-friendly gameplay, and much more, P4G makes for a very satisfying experience. The game is not without flaws, but it has so many strengths that they seem irrelevant in comparison. Story: Excellent (9/10) P4G's storyline is mostly the same as its PS2 predecessor's. The protagonist, also known as Yu Narukami in Persona 4 Arena and Persona 4: The Animation, moves to the rural town of Inaba to live with his relatives, the Dojimas, while his parents are away on business overseas. However, he quickly finds himself caught up investigating a bizarre kidnapping/serial murder case that appears to be linked to the mysterious Midnight Channel, a realm of the human unconsciousness accessible through T.V. screens. Within the dungeons of the midnight channel, Yu leads his friends to help rescue those who have been kidnapped before the fog that spells their demise rolls over Inaba. In doing so, they must help the victims confront their repressed thoughts and desires and learn to control their power as Personas, manifestations of the self capable of fighting the monstrous Shadows that lurk in the T.V. World. And all the while, they must struggle to pierce the fog of lies and unmask the true culprit behind the murders and the Midnight Channel. The narrative is wonderful for any fans of Jungian psychology (the ideas of which are further developed in bonus features) and existential philosophy, while remaining at an accessible level. For such a dark premise, the game has no shortage of lighthearted cheer. Besides just working on rescuing the victims and solving the case, the protagonist spends time bonding with the fellow Persona-users on the Investigation Team, studying at high school, and doing odd jobs. In these segments, the story is like a slice of life anime, and reads similarly to a visual novel. For some people, this is a turn-off: there is a lot of text and many lengthy scenes highlighting the Team’s (mis)adventures. But I personally find these scenes and the comedy within them to be part of the game’s charm. The protagonist may also become closer to his friends and the people around the town by developing their Social Links. In these, the game plays like a dating sim, although many of the social links are not romantic in nature and instead feature the development of friendships, such as those between fellow athletes at school, a student you can tutor, an oddly intelligent fox living at the local shrine, or the familial relationships with the protagonist’s Uncle Dojima or his young cousin, Nanako. Still, the protagonist can pursue a romantic relationship with one (or all) of the girls on the Investigation Team or at school, or instead become close platonic friends with them if the player wishes. P4G features two new social links. One of them allows the protagonist to better know Detective Adachi, Dojima’s bumbling partner on the local police force. The other acquaints the player with Marie, a character exclusive to P4G, an amnesiac girl who is also a guest of the Velvet Room, a realm between mind and matter where the protagonist can strengthen his Personas. And indeed, pursuing their links, or those of the other townspeople serves to further strengthen the protagonist’s Persona ability, offering experience bonuses or unlocking new Personas. This ties in in very well to the game’s other core theme, which is the power of friendship. The pacing can occasionally be poor between rescue missions, which may themselves feel repetitive to some, and many have raged against the pitfalls littering the path to the game’s True / Golden Endings, but overall P4G’s story and characters are superb. Gameplay: Excellent (9.5/10) Since I’ve already discussed the social links in the preceding section, I will focus on the battle system / Persona mechanics here. The protagonist starts with a single Persona, Izanagi, and can obtain more either by drawing them or other rewards during “Shuffle Time” which occurs at the end of battles, fusing Personas together in the Velvet Room to create new ones, or re-summoning previously owned Personas from the Compendium in the Velvet Room. Each Persona has its own skills, strengths and weaknesses, and using the protagonist’s ability to switch Personas and create new Personas tailored to fight the Shadows he’s encountering are crucial to success. Other members of the Investigation Team cannot change Personas, but they gain may gain additional skills and improved resistances through their Social Links. Investigation Team members may also learn new skills or recall old ones after spending time biking with the protagonist and then relaxing in the local hot springs, offering a level of customization that the original P4 lacked. Likewise, P4G allows the protagonist to apply “Skill Cards” to his Personas, granting them abilities they could not otherwise learn. This and the new ability to choose which skills a fused Persona inherits are great anti-frustration features. The key mechanic in battle is the “1-More” system. Striking an enemy’s weakness or scoring a critical hit grants the character an additional turn and knocks the enemy down. Striking the same enemy again may make them dizzy, causing them to lose their turn. Alternatively, knocking down all enemies enables the active members of the Investigation Team to perform an All-Out Attack, rushing the enemy party to cause massive damage, but also allowing any survivors to stand once again after the attack’s conclusion. The Investigation Team members are also susceptible to enemies scoring “1-More” against their weaknesses, so the player must take care to guard against their weaknesses, especially on the protagonist. If he dies, it’s game over. Fortunately, most difficulty levels of P4G are fairly forgiving in that one may choose to restart from the current floor of the dungeon. The battles, however, especially on the harder difficulties, are not forgiving, at least until one becomes skilled enough at fusions to create Personas that dominate over the opposition. The bosses deserve special mention for their challenge, although with careful Persona fusion and liberal use of buffing spells on the team and debuffing spells on the bosses, one can prevail. And in addition to the storyline bosses, most dungeons have a bonus boss that can be challenged afterwards to raise the protagonist’s courage (which is needed for some Social Links) and earn powerful pieces of equipment for the team. The dungeons themselves are randomly generated, with the exceptions of a few floors. They tend to be quite lengthy, making it important to manage the team’s Spirit Points, which are used to perform Persona spells (physical skills consume HP instead) carefully. Fortunately, Golden partially alleviates this through the SOS system. If one has a wireless connection, one can send a message requesting assistance from other players. During the next battle, each team member will receive HP and SP proportional to the number of players who responded to the request. The player may also encounter “Gold Hands” in the dungeons, special Shadows that grant vast amounts of EXP and Yen if the player is able to defeat them, reducing the need for grinding compared to the original game. In summary, the game’s balance has some minor issues, initially against the player and eventually in their favor, and it is generally harder than most other RPGs on the market, but triumphing over the difficult early game and ever-refining one’s Persona powers is a blast. Presentation: Excellent (9/10) P4G mantains the graphical quality of its PS2 counterpart. Some of the character models are less detailed than other games from its system of origin, but this does little to detract from the experience. The anime-styled character portraits are very well done, and the game features extensive voice-acting, with nearly 50% more than the PS2 version. Most of the voice acting is also superb, featuring professionals well-known in modern anime dubbing circles. Several scenes also receive animated cutscenes, also in anime style. The score of P4G has several J-Pop tracks, the piano and choir of the Velvet Room’s Aria of the Soul, the intense “I’ll Face Myself” for the main boss theme, and a mellower yet uplifting version of the same song when a character is able to come to terms with their Shadow. The original game’s battle theme, “Reach out to the Truth”, is replaced by “Time to Make History”, but makes a reprise whenever the player manages to secure the advantage at the start of the battle. The new dungeon’s theme is haunting, and the theme of the true final boss encourages the player to make a triumphant comeback against a seemingly implacable foe. Extra Content: Amazing (10/10) This deserves special mention, offering an incredible tribute to fans of the game. Besides just offering a wide range of costumes that characters can wear in battle (ranging from casual clothes, the school uniforms of Persona 3, the clothes of the powerful attendants of the Velvet room, festival garments / kimonos, Power Rangers-esque costumes, secret agent suits, Halloween costumes, swimsuits, maid uniforms, and more), P4G comes with many bonus features. These include a music player with the game’s soundtrack, a cutscene viewer, promotional and concept art, excerpts from Persona Live Music concerts, a series of lectures on Jungian psychology, and a quiz show minigame based on the characters, events, and setting of Persona 4 Golden. There are also many trophies for the devoted player to earn during the course of gameplay. Play Time and Replay Value: Excellent (9/10) It will probably take between 80-100 hours to beat the game and claim its Golden Ending. Upon beating the game, one’s Persona compendium, social stats, yen, and items that unlock special Personas carry over, making it much easier to maximize all Social Links on and complete the Persona Compendium on a second playthrough. New Game Plus also allows one to challenge the game’s ultimate bonus boss. The ability to dynamically adjust one’s difficulty setting beyond the five default difficulties is also unlocked, allowing one to further customize their experience. If you enjoyed playing through the game (or its PS2 counterpart) the first time, it’s very likely that you’ll enjoy playing through it again. Overall: Amazing (10/10) Persona 4 was one of my favorite RPGs, and Golden made it much better. If there is an RPG that makes a PS Vita worth owning, it would be P4G.

author: neptunerune
review_title: Facing your true self
review_text: ***Disclaimer: P4G may be untouchable to some but here's my objective review as a superfan.*** Persona 4 Golden (or P4G as it's fondly called) is my first game on the Vita and also my 1st in a decade. The last game I played before I stopped was "Persona 2: Eternal Punishment", the sequel of the sequel. I started to love the Persona series with it and I thought it'd be a good way to start playing video games again in 2014 if I were to pick up the series' latest non-spinoff release. I was right! I couldn't put it down!! It was only when I got the untrue ending that I looked it up and discovered it's the highest-rated game on the Vita. The game isn't perfect, however. I'm a superfan but I didn't let that fog (lol) my judgment. Objectively speaking, its closest cousins on the Vita are "Digimon Story: Cyber Sleuth" and "World of Final Fantasy". It's an acquired taste like most jRPGs that have similar mechanics and some gamers will probably get turned off by its simple and time-bound nature. Let's take a closer look at the game so we can examine the way its parts flow as a whole. GRAPHICS AND SOUND - This may be considered an HD remaster and remake in one. P4G not only looks and sounds better than the original P4, the story was expanded and the additional content made the game even bigger. The OST is pretty addicting, too! The songs won't stop playing in my head! The only letdown in graphics is the repetitive nature of dungeon floors and heavy palette swapping of enemies. Sound effects also lack variety. The murderous thing I heard throughout the game is the glaring use of 2 voice actors for Margaret to, perhaps, make a particular conversation with her fully voiced. If you've played the game and listened intently to her resolve, then you'll get what I mean. STORY - You'll be following the daily life of Yu Narukami (you'll be asked what your complete name is so you can change it) for a year as he moves from the city to a small town called Inaba. He'll be living with his detective uncle, Dojima and his daughter, Nanako. You'll also be a new student in Yasogami Highschool where you'll be meeting new friends and acquaintances. Strange occurrences begin happening not long after you arrive and it's up to your Persona-weilding gang to unravel the truth while protecting everyone dear to you. The story is not the most groundbreaking but the way it's told, presented and unfolds is superbly done. Along with that, character growth is tremendous, even supporting characters matter. You will really feel a strong emotional connection to the entire cast and, by the end of the game, you'll find yourself missing them. Getting the players emotionally involved with realistic, fully fleshed-out characters facing and conquering their true selves and fighting against a greater evil may be what makes P4G so loved. GAMEPLAY - P4G is another title that has really tight gameplay. I'll lump the game's important elements together as they're almost always encountered one after the other. The prologue up to Yukiko's scenario is an extremely slow and verbose burn and might bore you into oblivion. The game is divided into these very distinct parts: Dojima's house, Yasogami Highschool, the rest of Inaba, the Velvet room where Personas are called, social link bonding scenes, main story scenes, dungeon exploration and battles. You can do anything you want everyday like answering incorrectly during recitation, getting bad grades in exams, going out for a movie after school on a weekday, not attending sports/arts club practice, or rejecting an invitation to go out but you'll still manage to get the true ending if you want to. You can even tend your garden, do some TV shopping, go bug-catching and feed them to the item store owner's fish, go fishing or pray at the shrine. Returning home will cause time to advance and you can't go out at night for a good chunk of the game if Dojima is home. Just don't forget to RESCUE the people who'll get taken before the FOG sets in or it's game over. Studying hard, taking on part-time jobs, being considerate of and doing favors for others (SIDEQUESTS) and saying the right things at the right time, on the other hand, will make people like you. Your SOCIAL QUALITIES will grow, ultimately leading you into building SOCIAL LINKS with them. Strengthening social links is needed for calling Personas or making the other charcters' personas evolve. As busy as it sounds, the P4G world is actually small, making traveling between locations a breeze. Some may find the lack of variety off-putting. The MAP doesn't have many areas so it's not cluttered. You can press the square button while, let's say in school, and you'll be asked where you want to go. Going to the mall's rooftop to gather everyone will enable you to assess the current situation and get the option to enter the TV and explore the dungeons in it. DUNGEONS follow the kidnapped's suppressed emotions and give you hints about their internal struggles. They have a fixed number of floors but each are randomly generated (including treasure chests) and almost always have a mid boss. You can only save at save points (I only know 5 save points in the entire game) and there's only one before you enter. You can do a quick warp back out if you have the item or skill that does that and do a quick jump to the floor you were at if you re-enter. Enemy sprites can be seen on patrol. Some inhabit treasure chests. You can speed through all dungeons by avoiding enemies but you have to find the stairs to the the next floor. Hitting an enemy from behind will make you enter the battle with an advantage. The opposite can also happen if an enemy attacks you from behind. Returning to your world will advance the time and force you to sleep due to exhaustion. Finish everything up before exiting/entering the TV. Time won't pass while you're in a dungeon so abuse this if you feel like grinding or farming items. Be careful with treasure chests that have an ominous vibe with the sound of chains being pulled. A REAPER is inside and you won't be able to beat it until your at a high enough level. It's sort of like an optional superboss that drops one character's strongest weapon/armor/accessory each time it's defeated. BATTLES are turn-based and only 4 people can enter dungeons and participate in battles. Those left behind won't get any experience. You have to cycle people around if you want to strengthen them evenly. In battle, landing a critical hit or abusing an enemy's weakness unbalances them and gives you an additional turn. You know you did it when you see the screen flash blue and say "1 more". Unbalance an entire enemy group and your party will do an all-out attack for tons of damage. Some can even partner up for unique attacks. Be mindful as enemies can also do a " 1 more" on you if they unbalance you. At the end of well-fought battles is SHUFFLE TIME. Pick a card and get rewards like a new persona, increased money, a skill card, etc. Since the number of cards to be picked is limited, managing to get them all will give you a SWEEP BONUS and ensure that shuffle time occurs after your next battle. SKILL CARDS will force a persona to learn an ability. These can be obtained by dozing off at Chagall Café and your equipped persona has a skill card icon beside its skill's name, from monsters or through shuffle time. They can also be registered in The Velvet Room and purchased in bulk. EQUIPMENT also makes a huge difference and new ones can be made by selling a certain number of a certain items that monsters will drop. Make sure to sell them all at the only equipment shop, Daidara's, when you happen to be nearby. Lastly, calling a PERSONA requires you to be at a certain level or if you have the other personas needed to call a stronger one or both. Don't be afraid to experiment to see what you'll get but filling the PERSONA COMPENDIUM is a lot of work that requires time, patience and cash! You can also read on the respective mythology and/or cultural significance of each as additional knowledge. You'll even find familiar faces you may have encountered in world history like Suzaku, Vishnu, Sandman, the archangels, etc. REPLAY VALUE - You'll never get tired of this game if you come to love it. It's my 3rd playthrough yet it all still feels new. If you've never played P4G and this is your first playthrough, then start a new game in very easy for quick battles and truckloads of money and build your inventory/armory. You can also train your favorite Personas to Lv 99 and save their progress in the compendium so that their strength will get carried over to NEW GAME+. You'll start at level 1 with your strongest equipment. You can also call the protagonist's evolved persona at a certain part in the 2nd playthrough. You can also activate TV LISTINGS and watch your favorite animé cutscenes, view the characters' conceptual and final designs, watch concert footage of a live performance of P3 songs, participate in a quiz show and much MORE! OVERALL - It's no surprise that many hail P4G as the best game on the Vita. It's a solid game with excellent storytelling that tackles issues that are too close to the bone and lovable characters we all may have versions of in real life. There's not much when it comes to variety and exploration but there's so much interconnected stuff to do and it will keep you wanting more. It's an unforgettable game for fans and newcomers alike.

author: SilverSmoothie
review_title: One of the worst casts and narratives in modern JRPG history
review_text: Longtime Atlus fan, huge SMT fan and I generally love the stylization, ost's, and attention to details given to these games. Not a fan of the dating aspects or the school life, so prepare for some hardball boys and girls. Let me start by saying this title improved tremendously on the games before it in terms of combat; it took large leaps to get us to where the series is today in terms of mechanics / fluidity and visuals/ pace of the structure. Being able to control all the party members was great, similar to persona 3 portable; this is essentially what I wish Persona 3 was, a combination of FES and p3p. It has the great animated cutscenes, lots of nice filler moments that rival naruto filler; its absolutely pointless but it can be funny in a silly way. I was fond of the dungeons initially mostly because of the osts, but honestly their randomly generated feel and shallow design made it feel extremely repetitive / tedious. To add on to this, each time you went into a dungeon the story went the exact same for all your protagonists; your party members feel like a band of power rangers immune to the world at which those around you seem to fail in. This game to me is the tales of graces f of the persona series. A game the casuals seem to love, however its got some of the worst characters and dialogue in the franchise. There's no way you can save a narrative even if the idea is good with that as a base.The Scooby-Doo comparisons are warranted, and I'm going to dig in and explain why. The dialogue, pacing, and end-game story arc paired with the social links makes this one feel like a game that could've been something great. Instead, we received heavy tropes, lackluster plot twists, and one-dimensional dialogue that may show different sides on some characters, but poses no benefit onto the mainline story(s-links). The format in this game is where a lot of the problem lies. The plot revolves around a string of Murders occurring in Inaba and the MC and his band of school-mates discover the capability to jump into TVs to battle demons and creatures which are effecting the reality of their world. The pace and start to this game is fantastic and it only takes a few hours to really drop you into the meat of events; And the upbeat OST and ease of traversal made it really enjoyable to immerse myself in. However, this is where my enjoyment ended. The school-life simming; from doing homework, studying, answering ridiculous questions to improve dating stats, and social links are all where this RPG began to take a tumbling nose dive. Because of how restricted you are and how many missables and requirements there are to do certain things later, you really need to sit a guide for these games; and if you don't, you can bet you'll have missed some key things, especially if you haven't played Persona 4. The majority of the social links and characters were simply a waste of time or offered no benefit whatsoever to the MC in relation to the mainline story. They felt to dating sim / life sim to me. I'd rather have a true narrative with character detailing included than this social link mediocrity. There was no connection to the plot, They rarely, rarely discussed other characters, and there was no segue into the main plot. When a s-link was completed, that was it. You never saw those character changes for that character in the main story. The majority of S-links are uneventful and pose no impact on the main narrative, nor do interactions actually carry any weight from party member to party member (in terms of noticing who you might be dating or talking with, or even mentioning things you discussed one on one in the main plot). Let me dig a bit deeper and explain why this makes the cast feel shallow. After each segment of each party members dungeon, their story is not touched on and they receive minimal characterization / growth outside of these social links. Because these social links are so shallow and you have the potential to miss out on many of them, Many characters, especially those who you don't focus on - end up feeling lifeless, one-dimensional, and even plain boring. And because many of the social links are so poorly constructed, most of the time the interactions have worthless events occurring, and the ones that do have meaningful events are never again re-established or integrated into the main plot, dropping it as if their story was complete. This isolates characters in a massive way, making it seem like the MC's harem rather than a band of collective humans consciously engaging in their own day to day lives. The time constraints make me feel like im playing atelier; they don't bring qualities into the game that add to my experience, but only restrict it. A player should be able to experience all the social links if one is going to want the full experience, its ridiculous to have it be tied to some system around the calendar restrictions. To make things worse, many of the character-archetypes used here simply destroy the dialogue interaction as they're so overbearingly simpleminded and one-dimentional that the conversations rarely evolve beyond their initial introductory personality. We've had such great stories and casts in the two persona two titles, Nocturne, the DDS and all the SMT's, and the cast in persona 3. The disconnect is severe here as the tone captured in a lot of the social links with the major characters aren't felt in the main narrative, they feel two different kind of ways which makes the experience feel quite hollow. Its especially noticeable with characters like Chie/ Teddie. Its moreso noticable here than with P3 because the characters aren't dynamic on their own; their dialogue or meaningful moments outside of S-links are minimal, especially after their initial entry. Many of these characters had potential before they met and teamed up with the MC. once they did, they fell into the background and were never built upon again. Their dialogue amounted to filler or jokes, or friendship, yeah! (or whatever the Slinks had for them) Characters like Kanji and Naoto had the base to be really deep and intricate characters, only to take a major backseat in plot events once their chapters were complete. S Links really damage these characters. Dojimas character is an absolute joke. Nanako is a literal advertisement. Mikasa version 2.0. Teddie's entire dialogue is puns and the side we see in his slink is never brought over into the mainline plot. There are some good S links - but many of them are filler side stories.To better improve on this Slink system if they don't plan to remove it would be to have meaningful plot events occur in them in relation to the party, and not isolate members or make restrictions on them. Make them mini-skits, similar to Tales, or mini QTE's or the mini-events Final Fantasy had. Don't center them around the protagonist and isolate events to the social links only. This whole system could be used in a much better way in terms of narrative. This school and homework/ job + life sim is a poor format to tell a story, especially when you stuff all your characterization in the poorly designed s links. Rise's dialogue is so mediocre that you can predict how every interaction will go with her. She includes Senpai in every other line of her dialogue, and if its not there you can bet she's figuring out a way to use it again. Her and Marie's lines are beyond uninspired and thoughtless, and their characterization is ridiculous frankly. Teddie's link story and dialogue are also terrible; they went nowhere with a character who could've been more than just comedic relief. Most of the females here offered minimal to the narrative. A positive I found was the dating elements here aren't as excessively unbelievable as they are in P5, yet the girls and their personalities and dialogue are so much worse that it doesn't matter if its more believable; If the characters are poorly written and built upon, the game is going to finish poorly and feel extremely unfulfilling. Add on a highly repetitive dungeon experience with tedious school life in between and its no wonder I'm never playing this game again. There's no characters to love, no investment to be had, and with a plot so mainstream and predictable, wheres the incentive here? Persona 4 Golden does filler, lots of filler, and it does it well. That's another positive I suppose. That leads me to the major complaint I had with this title; the ending plot scenarios and final arc's of plot twists. The only character that really gets some mention in key events is whoever you end up dating, and even then there really isn't any push or pull or interaction from your other party members in relation to the MC's relationship, nor is there any other real romance outside of the MC. There's implications, but it dies as does the growth of the cast.That's not what I was truly referring to though, forgive me. The Final Arc of the story reveals a massive deus-ex that literally makes the story reminiscent of the issues I had with Final Fantasy 9 and its ass-pull ending. Thanks Marie. The antagonists here had little to no depth (unless you partook of key social links) which once again lean to the fact that this format causes the main plot to suffer. Everyone's experience is going to feel vastly different unless you beat this game numerous times and complete everything over and over. The format in itself is flawed. You shouldn't have to play an RPG more than once to understand the depth of the characters and the story. That means your format isn't good at executing a narrative in one go. I shouldn't have to replay your story over and over to get all of the characterization. That's the job of you the writer to express across the game in one coherent narrative. The whole story feels like a life sim emphasizing the power of friendship, and while fantasy does have room to be creative, elements of realism maintained in the universe help keep the plot honest and consistent, and I felt at times the plot lost sight of that realism, especially near the end when scenarios just started popping up to fit the direction the narrative was going. The compartmentalization of the story which resulted in large segments of dungeon crawling and large segments of school sim really made the plot feel like it progressed at a snails pace, and it was truly a letdown when the final plot twist revealed itself before the final dungeon. It was like a slap in the face because you already knew where this game was going, but it still wished to toss you into some dungeons because why not. This is how nearly each dungeon before that felt, especially with how all of the story segments before and after them played out in a similarly repetitive fashion. This plot could've been much better if dialogue and characterization were the focal-point instead of these life sim aspects/ tropes / friendship. Comparing the ending to P2 and P3, this game feels like a bastardization of the series in comparison. P2 had some of the best female characters in the series. P3 managed to hold a better pace and structure, but tartarus and the dating elements did it no favors. Aside from the poorly constructed antagonists and protagonists, the NPC's were also rather shallow. Again, I can't say enough how much of a free pass persona gets for its world building. This is why I was so harsh on P5 and its reviews of 90s. There's games getting mid 70s doing dialogue, story, characters, and combat better. So maybe we need to get a different rating system, who knows. Its vastly inferior compared to the trails series in that regard -- with a game of this format, where its time restrictions are so taxing and emphasize actual day to day progression, you would think there would be a lot more depth to the NPC's and shop owners you encounter on a daily basis. You would think your quests would actually build your world in a way more than just Hey im looking for this item.... or making your date lunch. Im not advocating Bonding Links in Cold Steel as an improvement either, don't get me wrong. Both of those systems (Slinks and Bonding Events) do storytelling no favors in any medium and honestly would be better off gone. Not saying that series is perfect, but they've mastered world building, attention to detail in terms of NPC work and antagonist design; something persona really has trouble grasping, especially in these later titles. There's some NPC improvement, and its there, and its certainly better than FF15 or anything final fantasy has done in their recent titles for sure, but for the budget and time these games have -- its still not good enough, and neither are the branching dialogue-tree choices. If you're going to do these S links they need to tie into the plot more. there needs to be more than just slice of life events. It needs to have growth, stakes. Just because FF15 is poor in the NPC and Story department doesn't mean P5 is getting a free pass from me, or P4G. The music really accentuated the atmosphere and fit well here. Its not my style of music, but I certainly appreciated many of the songs especially some of the final themes. There's a wide variety of tracks in this title, and I feel they did a good job capturing the city and school life feel with the music. Not my favorite OST in the franchise, but its certainly catchy. This may seem harsh, but frankly I was disappointed with persona 4 golden. Everyone always claims this to be the best JRPG on Vita and I went in hyped. The combat was certainly impressive, and I enjoyed getting to handle everyone unlike P3 FES, yet the cast was vastly inferior as was the overall atmosphere of the game. This game is very hard for me to give a score because when I began this game, it was a 10/10 experience for me. As I began to see the repetition of each dungeon and how each plot progression point went exactly the same with little to no creativity within the narrative itself, and the poor downward spiral the end of the story took, I lost all desire to ever touch this game again. This game has a lot of nice aspects, but the main story itself is just mediocre at best and I can't give it a good grade for telling a poor quality story with such shallow characters. 4 / 10 Missed Opportunity This game could've been one of the best JRPG's stories of all time. Instead we have a conjoined mess of a school infused dating riddled with randomly generated dungeon crawling..

author: TLHunter312
review_title: Atlus delivers yet again - Persona 4 Golden
review_text: Overall rating: 9/10 Introduction: With Persona 4 Golden Atlus has struck gold again (pun intended). I ended up liking this game far more than I thought I would, in fact, there are parts of it I like more than both Persona 3 and 5. This game takes a lot of what made Persona 3 bad and improves it, a ton, mostly. I did 100% this game and got every achievement, which required 2 playthroughs. That took me 124 hours, and 4 minutes to do. This is while skipping most things during my second playthrough on New Game Plus. There is so much I love about this game much like there is for Persona 3 FES and Persona 5 Royal. Enough introductions, onto the review. Story and Themes 9/10: So Persona 4's story is a slight step down from Persona 3's incredible story. However, this is still super good. It much like the other persona games begins with our protagonist, Yu Narukami, going somewhere to stay for a while. This time in Inaba, which is based on Fuefuki, Japan, a tiny rural town. Things aren't peaceful for long though because all of the sudden a woman goes missing, then shows up dead. This leads to our protagonist and a couple of acquaintances investigating after our protagonist discovers he can somehow enter TVs. I'll let you find out what happens after this, but it's quite the journey and things are rarely as they seem. This game dives heavily into the themes of "accept yourself, identity, and seeking the truth no matter how painful it may be" and I really enjoy that personally because I'm somebody that even now is still learning to accept themselves and because of this, there are parts that hit close to home, specifically with the fifth party member that joins your team. I can really relate to him in many ways. The other theme of identity also plays a major role in most of the social links. Specifically two of my favorite party members, who both struggle with their identity and accepting who or what they are. Lastly, the theme of seeking truth plays perhaps the biggest role out of the three as it heavily affects multiple choices you can make in the story, multiple of which can lead you to a bad ending. The story eventually comes to a climax, but it keeps the tension going even after that and it gets crazy when you finally piece together some important information that I will not spoil. Even after that Golden extends the game a decent bit and keeps things fun and interesting. I'm not totally sure if it's my favorite story in the 3 - 5 trilogy but it definitely stands out a lot. Overall I really enjoyed it. The Investigation Team 9/10 : Where Persona 3 had the most mature cast, Persona 4's main team is probably the least mature. The cast of Persona 3 was very diverse, but Persona 4 does keep it more simple, which in multiple ways works to its advantage. SEES is quite a large group and not everybody is a social link, however every member of the Investigation Team is, and this works to the benefit of the game. Each character is unique and has their own quirks and a side they don't want to admit exists. However, as you do each of their social links you learn to care about each of them. My favorites for this game being the Fortune and Emperor arcanas. However, I will say most of their arcs aren't all that great. In Persona 3 each member of SEES has a pretty clear arc, in Persona 4 that's not the case, however, this is mostly because each character arc is locked behind a social link. One of the biggest advantages this game has over the others though is that this team feels very real, they all struggle with real issues that we can all pretty much relate to, with one exception, they also all feel like they hang out outside of the times you get together to take on shadows and explore dungeons. Persona 3 is good with this, and Persona 5 does it a bit, but it feels more real in Persona 4. You really get the feeling that they're all friends with each other and not just because they all have a common goal in mind. All in all, while I would argue parts of the team aren't handled as well as SEES it also does a lot of things better. Villain 9/10 : Persona 4 is a murder mystery and as a massive fan of those types of stories (when done well) they also do rely on a strong villain, and Persona 4 nails it with its villain. I really can't say much without getting into spoiler territory but the way they handle the villain is excellent, it's executed nearly perfectly. I would argue that without Persona 5 having multiple villains and if they just stuck to the villain in the Royal postgame, this game would be as good as Persona 5 Royal in terms of villains, but because Persona 5 does have multiple villains and a few standouts, I do still have to give that game the edge, however, the culprit in this game is good enough on their own for me to consider them one of the best parts of this game. Music 8.5/10: Persona 4's music may not entirely vibe with me, but I love it nonetheless. This game has so many great songs, a handful that I don't like as much as others, but I can't deny that they're good songs regardless. But some of the songs that I do love in this game, I really really love. The music in this game is much more upbeat for the most part, while Persona 3 had some funky get hyped songs as well as some sad songs, the soundtrack of this game feels much happier and lighter, while also having a few of those hard-hitting sadder songs. The soundtrack is diverse and definitely has a few surprises, though I will admit there is one song that is used and it feels weird and off-putting, however, this song is also tied to a character so it makes more sense, and while I would go more in-depth, I can't spoil the game. My favorites from this game being: Heaven, I'll Face Myself, Never More, Snowflakes, and The Fog. Each Persona game really has its own identity when it comes to music and Persona 4 is no different, this one feels much more upbeat and happy, which is in line with the lighter tone of the game. Social Links & Setting 8/10: I combined these two because they do go hand-in-hand and I like them both very equally. Persona 3 doesn't do social links as well in my opinion, but it has multiple standouts, but what Persona 3 did wrong with its links, Persona 4 fixed. Most prominently for me was that I didn't really care about some. Not only that but the only people that were voiced were the SEES social links. This to me really does matter because during the big moment when you gain power from your social links, having none of them be voiced does have less impact, Persona 4 fixes this. Unlike Persona 3 there was only one I didn't care for, the Hermit arcana. Some of these are also quite emotional, with one dealing with the fact that she believes she's Death, another struggling with the loss of a loved one, a couple struggling with self-acceptance, and so on. These people have very real issues and flaws and feel like real people. While Persona 3 had the Moon as my least favorite, a character that does have an arc more or less, Persona 4's least favorite was one that doesn't even have dialogue while also being a chore to complete. Persona 4 does an excellent job with its social links and I love it for that. The game also fixes one of Persona 3's flaws by making it so you have the choice to romance a social link or not rather than locking you into a romance with them regardless, the romance is also handled much better than in the previous game, it also does play a role and affects dialogue at certain key moments in the game. The setting plays a big role in not just being where everything takes place but it also plays a big role in the story, but the social links. As mentioned already it's a very tiny town where rumors spread fast and everybody knows each other. I personally love the small-town setting, it does make for some interesting consequences in the story when things go awry. My favorite social links for this game are in no order: Hanged Man, Fortune, Hierophant, Justice, Jester, and Emperor. Gameplay and TV world 8/10: Wow, I nearly forgot what it's like to play a Persona game with enjoyable dungeons and gameplay. Atlus made several improvements with the gameplay in Persona 4 and I can't quite put all of them into words, it just feels so much better to play than Persona 3. What I can say is that the combined floors of the dungeons this time around are only a fraction of how many floors there are in Tartarus. The gameplay in this game is faster and not only that but it's way more balanced. Enemies this time around are fairer and don't go for instakill moves as often as some of the enemies in Persona 3 did. There are also significantly fewer mini-bosses, but they are more memorable and are fun. Onto the dungeons themselves. These while being fairly basic are a lot of fun, they all look very unique and have a unique song to accompany them rather than a song that's remixed several times. The look of each dungeon is also very significant because of the ruler, similar to a palace in Persona 5.
