I really don't have any complaints aside from the fact that sometimes it's just a bit too basic, just floors, nothing too crazy like avoiding traps or something like that. Persona 5 yet again fixes this issue. The TV world also plays a big role in the story and is very significant for many reasons that you will learn about while playing the game. Similarities to Jojo's Bizarre Adventures Part 4: Diamond is Unbreakable: I know this is weird to mention in a review about Persona 4 Golden but hear me out. If you've watched Jojo Part 4 before playing this game like I did you will notice a lot of similarities, and it's something that actually makes me appreciate this game more. Now there are only some similarities that I can say without spoiling. First off, I'm not complaining. Both start with a person from the city visiting family, both feature a tale about a serial killer that leaves victims in a way where the cause of death is unknown, both feature forming a team to solve the case, both teams mostly consist of teenagers with weird powers, both take place in a small town, both are very similar in tone, both have openings that share several similarities (though P4G came first in 2012 since Part 4 wasn't adapted into anime form until 2016). It's really funny truth be told, but I love it personally, especially since Jojo part 4 is my favorite part. Of course, there are more similarities throughout the series but Persona 4 Golden seems the most similar, again there are more similarities between Part 4 and P4G but those are the ones I can list without spoiling more than the first couple of hours. Final thoughts: While writing this review I realized I love this game more than I realized, there's a lot to love here, from the music, the cast, the tone, the villain, the setting, the social links, and even the gameplay. I'm so glad I finally got around to playing this game. While the story isn't as good as Persona 3's, it's still very good and it's without a doubt the easiest one to get into in the series, with that hook at the start and everything that follows it's a game that's more than worth your time. It's yet another game in the series that I believe everyone should experience and it improves on everything I had a problem with Persona 3 and is even better than Persona 5 in multiple ways. As I mentioned at the start, Atlus struck gold(en) and while this was the last game for me in the 3 - 5 trilogy of games I can't wait to see what they do with Persona 6, I have a lot of hopes for that game, but I know regardless, it will be a good game as they've proven to me, 3 times now.

author: MSAddict
review_title: The definitive rerelease!
review_text: Persona 4 probably wouldn’t like me very much. If Persona 4 was my friend, I’d be the guy who at parties always pressured him into juggling steak knives or something, because “Man it’s so cool, you HAVE to see this.” I’d always go on and on about how cool his juggling abilities were, and he’d probably just roll his eyes and go along with it, but he’d rant about me to his other friends. Persona 4 is a game that came out in December of 2008, nearly four and a half years ago. Given the trend of Atlus to rerelease Persona games on Sony’s portable systems in the past five years, no one was really surprised about Persona 4 Golden being announced in August on 2011. As opposed to Persona 3, and Persona 2: Innocent Sin, Golden was released on Sony’s new showgirl, the Vita. The Vita lends itself well to Golden. The portability is certainly a plus, and the extra power behind the handheld makes it a much smoother game than any Persona game in the past. While loading times do still occur, they’re nowhere near the level of the PS2 era or the PSP remakes. Persona 4 is a game that honestly still stands up well today, so a remake—even one with some pretty cool extra features—seems frivolous to me. “Isn’t this time you could be spending on Persona 5, Atlus? What about localizing Eternal Punishment, huh?” But with my recent acquisition of a Vita, and my PS2 having been condemned by the demons of console failure, it felt like a good time to pick it up and see if it was a great as I remembered. Short enough to say it was. The game is still paced extremely well for a JRPG, and the freedom to either enhance your relationships with your friends or head straight for the dungeons in one that still feels like a natural inclusion to me. The combat is turn based, but engaging and varied enough that it doesn’t feel overly tedious. The writing is still clever, and all very Politically Correct, making it a definite “buy” for any Social Justice bloggers who haven’t yet played it. The voice acting is well done, or at least as well as can be expected, a whole host of new lines have been recorded, and several characters voices have been completely redone for the better. Several new animated cutscenes reminiscent of the anime series were made for the game, adding a nice “cinematic” effect to the game at times. For those unfamiliar with the Persona series (specifically 3 and 4), allow me to break it down for you. You are an unnamed teenager in Japan. You move to a new town to find that all sorts of crazy stuff is going down, notably people are dying left and right and no one knows why. You are inexplicably given the power to summon demons and gods from various pagan mythologies and must use them to save the world from vaguely implied destruction. Simultaneously, you must become the most popular boy in school, by helping out your classmates with their silly problems, befriending old ladies, evil nurses, and psychotic foxes, and occasionally getting all lovey-dovey with your female allies. That’s the gist of it anyway. It actually involves a lot of dungeon crawling and test-taking. The series might best be described as a very well written visual novel with a dungeon crawler tacked on. Which doesn’t sound appealing, sure. And to a lot of people, it’s not. Persona 4 is a game anyone looking for a good example of good writing in a game should look towards though. From the storyline, to the characters, if you’re writing a RPG, you should have played Persona 4 already. The characters are all very real, and your choices in responses to them can have some very real effects on them, both in story and gameplay. So what has Golden changed? Not much really, and this is where my sole complaints come from. The game has a new coat of polish, sure. The mechanics all flow better, a whole additional month of play is now included in the game, certain characters have been rebalanced, everyone has new abilities, and new costumes and blah de blah de bleeeh. Despite the game’s new prom dress, it’s still the same girl it was five years ago. I’d say it fixed all of Persona 4’s problems, but Persona 4 didn’t really have any problems! Persona 4 is still an excellent game, and while the Vita version is certainly more of the aforementioned excellence, and definitely a good game, if you’ve played the original and don’t want to shell out 250$ for a Vita then you’re not missing out on much! So, if you haven’t played Persona 4, should you play Golden? Yes. Is Golden the definitive version of Persona 4? Yes again. Should they have made Golden in the first place? Also yes. Persona 4 Golden is by all means an excellent game. And I really enjoyed playing and probably will continue to enjoy playing it. But if you have already played Persona 4 and you aren’t a die-hard SMT: Persona fan, than it’s probably not worth shelling out the tidy sum you’ll need for the console and the game. In the end, Golden is still a spectacular game, and one that I’d recommend to just about anyone. At least anyone who didn’t see her juggle those steak knives at old man PS2’s party four years ago as they all flew and stabbed Final Fantasy XI in the face.

author: ar1speedboy
review_title: Everyday's great at your Junes!
review_text: Persona 4 Golden, is without a doubt, the very BEST game I have ever played. If you've played Persona 3 then you know what you're getting, but if you haven't, even if you have never played an RPG before in your life, it might be a good idea to take a break from Call of Duty, Assassin's Creed and Grand Theft Auto to play something that will inevitably become one of the best (and if not THE best) game you have ever played. What is Persona 4 Golden? What is it about? Persona 4 Golden is a JRPG (Japanese Role Playing Game) and a HD remake of the PS2 classic, Persona 4. As well as providing shiny new graphics, the game also adds a lot of new content. There are new Social Links (keep reading to find out what they are), new dungeons (again, keep reading) and more events, story content and gameplay refinements. Persona 4 Golden puts you in control of the protagonist (you can name him, but we'll just call him Hero). Hero is going to live with his uncle and cousin in the rural town of Inaba. Soon after arrival he meets people who would soon become his greatest friends, and soon after that a murder takes place in Inaba. It soon goes on to become a serial murder case, and Hero learns that only he and his friends, with their new Persona powers can stop the murders and bring whoever is doing them to justice. Gameplay In P4G there are two main parts that make up the gameplay: Social Links and dungeons. In case you don't know, dungeons are common elements in RPGs where the player fights enemies in order to lever up. In P4G, the dungeons take the form of a randomised, multi-floored labyrinth, and at the top of the labyrinth lies a boss. You must take Hero and his friends to the dungeons to level up to increase your stats, your friends stats and your Persona's stats (if you don't know what Persona's are, they are basically this games version of Pokémon). Levelling up is crucial to your success in the game. If you don't level up enough, you will make the game impossible to win. You defeat enemies in turn based battles. The battles are fun with a lot of strategy, and offer infinite entertainments for both the beginners and the hardcore players. Social Links are your friendship with other people, put on a scale of 1 to 10. When you are not exploring dungeons you are either studying for school, going fishing, taking a part time job, eating out or hanging around with your friends. The more you hang out with your friends the deeper your friendship becomes, and your Social Links increase. The stronger your Social Links, the more powerful your Persona ability, and the stronger you will be when fighting your way through the next dungeon. The characters you meet have been written very well, and they are both realistic and very interesting. You will find yourself growing attached to them, and when your 70 hour journey is over, it's not the dungeons you will miss, it's the characters. Overall, both elements of the gameplay fit together perfectly, and both are very interesting and certainly very enjoyable. Cosmetics The graphics in this game are beautiful. This game does not try to look realistic or lifelike, instead it relies on an anime art style and it looks gorgeous. I can't imagine it any different, and the HD visuals added in Golden make it all the more stunning. The soundtrack is even better than the graphics. The music in this game literally has no flaws. It never gets annoying, never really gets repetitive and is not so overly catchy that you cannot get it out of your head when you need to focus on something else (*cough*Persona 3*cough*). It also plays very well on your emotions. I never really cry or smile when playing a video game, but the way this soundtrack manipulates you into feeling whatever it wants you to feel is incredible. Replay Value/Lasting Appeal Most games only seem to last about 12 hours before you finish them for good, but not this one. This game takes 70 hours to complete a single playthrough and if you decide to play it again it very easily goes into the 100s. I have sunk over 200 hours into this game and expect at least 300 before I am finished with it. This games actually requires more that one playthrough to unlock all the content, and the truth is there is so much content here that it is impossible to get it all in one playthrough. I am starting my fifth and I am still not done. As for why anyone would put so much time into one game is simple, it's fun, addicting and you also get very attached to the characters, making you sad when it's over and making you miss them as if they were real people (no, I'm not making this up). Final Conclusion Pros: - Great story - Great characters - Fun and varied dungeons - Gorgeous graphics - Brilliant soundtrack - Addictive Cons: - Ummm..... Rating: 10/10 If you haven't played the original Persona 4, then this is a must have, and is easily worth buying a Vita for. If you have already got a Vita and don't have this game, then what are you waiting for?!

author: netman70
review_title: Persona 4 Golden, the Best Game I have Ever Played.
review_text: Persona 4 Golden, where do I start with this amazing game? Let's do some background first. Persona 4 Golden for Playstation Vita is a remake of the critically acclaimed game Persona 4 for the Playstation 2, which was released five years before Golden. Persona 4 Golden has a wealth of new content, such as a new character, a new boss fight, tons of new demons to fuse, a new dungeon, new social links to explore, and so much more. This is absolutely the definitive version of the masterpiece that is Persona 4. Story: 10 In this game, the basic plot is that there have been some strange happenings in relation to a rumor going around school about a mysterious Midnight Channel that is supposed to be able to show you the face of your soulmate. Upon trying this, you and your friends realize that this is more than just a harmless rumor, and something must be done to stop whatever is going on. Gameplay: 9 The game plays like a true turn based RPG in battles, and a third person dungeon crawler outside of battle. Encounters are not random, as you can see the enemies in the dungeons before you get into a fight with them, which can be used for extra training or avoiding battles depending on what the situation calls for. The only reason this gets a nine instead of a ten is the fact that the difficulty at times could potentially turn off players who are either new to these kind of games or games where grinding is almost a necessity. Instant kills don't help either. Graphics: 10 This game, long story short, looks absolutely beautiful. It takes full advantage of the Vita's OLED screens and everything from the town you reside in, to the dungeons you fight in, to the battles you fight, all look amazing. Cutscenes are also tons of fun to watch and look absolutely great. Some of the best graphics I have seen on a handheld in a very long time. Sound/Music: 10 One of the improvements from Persona 4 to Persona 4 Golden is the amount of voice acting. In many handheld remakes of console games you may see a drop in the amount of voice acting, but in Persona 4 Golden they actually upped the voice acting by a time and a half. This means you get way more voiced dialogue by voice actors who really know how to do their job well. I always found myself listening to entire conversations, and not just reading the text and moving on with the story. The music is also extremely well done, with a lot of catchy tunes that will stick in your head from the game's less serious moments, and the battle themes are well done as well, and do a great job of setting the tone for a big or serious boss battle. Environment: 10 Outside of dungeons, one of the areas this game excels in is creating a kind of life simulator, where you can build bonds with friends and various people around town by improving your social link with them. You can have a girlfriend, and do various activities such as studying or part time jobs to either work on personal skills, or earn money, or even both in some cases. Replay Value: 9 Another great thing is that this game practically requires more than one playthrough in order to experience all of the content it has to offer. If you're looking for a timesink, look no further as this game can easily eat away over a hundred hours like it was nothing. Replay value takes a one point hit here because I know there will be people who don't view a second playthrough as the most fun thing in the world, while there are others who will be more than ready to make their second trip to the town of Inaba to do everything (and more) all over again. Final Score: 10/10 This game truly has it all, from a great story that keeps you guessing, to awesome character interactions and developments, along with a great battle system and an environment that draws you in and makes you want to keep playing and playing. If you haven't tried this game already, get your hands on a copy asap. You won't regret it for a second.

author: Bkstunt_31
review_title: The inevitable upgrade is here and it is royal indeed!
review_text: Persona 5 came out in the West in 2017 and oh man, did I enjoy it. It took the series’ traditional JRPG gameplay and just improved it in so many ways, all the while adding style galore and a jazzy soundtrack. But as they say… What have you done for me lately? In true Persona fashion, we are getting an update to Persona 5, called Persona 5 Royal . We saw the same treatment with Persona 3 and Persona 4 , so this update was pretty much guaranteed. If you're wondering what the changes are or even if Persona 5 is worth your time. you are in the right place, my friends! Let's look into everything Persona 5 Royal offers! An expanded tale, but still a wild ride! (Story) As you may know, Persona 5 puts you in the role of an unnamed High School student. He's a silent protagonist as well, as the game clearly believes in you taking over the character. You are sent to live with a family friend in Tokyo after trying to stop a drunk (but prominent) businessman from forcing himself on a woman late at night. Despite trying to do the right thing, the man ends up charging you with assault and you are expelled from your old school as a result. Well... this is a good start! Thankfully, you are given a second chance to attend high school in Tokyo, Shujin Academy, and are now the new kid in school. The new school comes with you being labeled a troublemaker, though, and you are even on probation. Even your new guardian isn't exactly happy with the situation, forcing you to live in an attic above his coffee shop. Being a Persona game, though, soon after moving to a new city and school, our protagonist gets drawn into the Velvet Room and discovers that he has the ability to enter corrupt individual's Mind Palaces and force them to change by stealing their heart. This is a crazy power, to be sure, and of course, you'll soon meet another corrupt adult at your new school: a gym teacher abusing his power and sexually harassing various female students. As you can imagine, your character will soon make use of his power to fight back against corrupt adults. The game's premise is wild, but right in-line with previous Persona games. Still, Persona 5 's subject matter is a bit more touchy with suicide and sexual assault being some of the first subjects your characters deal with. Fighting back against corruption is definitely the theme of the game. The story takes place over a school year with you playing through almost every single day, and as a result, you'll meet a wide variety of allies who join or help you out in some way. Getting to know these allies and bonding with them is one of the game's highlights for sure. Royal keeps the main story of Persona 5 mostly intact, which is understandable as it’s a very long game. Royal really just makes it longer by adding two new Confidants that you can spend time with and re-working a third confidant completely. The game also adds a new Palace (dungeon) and dozens of new cutscenes throughout. These new confidants are really just giving us more of what made the original title great, as the core story experience remains intact. You'll focus on the main plot every month or so, but in the meantime you are literally just an ordinary high-school student. So, most days you'll go to class and will then have to choose what to do with your time afterwards, and this is still what makes the story shine. How (and with who) you spend your time is going to directly impact your experience with the game, both with the story and gameplay. Between these choices and the wild main plot, the story is definitely a memorable one. Life is more than battles! (Game Play) If you’ve played any of Persona games before, you know they are really a mixed bag of gameplay. You have your normal JRPG here, of course, but Persona is also part Life Sim, which is what truly makes the series unique as both of these systems really have you always improving yourself in some way. What makes Persona 5 stand out is that nearly everything you do in your "normal high-schooler life" affects the gameplay. Hanging out with teammates can lead to them (or you) learning new skills. Hanging out with that back alley doctor can net you new healing supplies. Hanging out with an aspiring politician can improve your speaking skills with enemies. Everything you do feels like a step forward and really makes the gameplay fulfilling. The actual gameplay is fairly standard. You will explore new dungeons with every person you target, fighting enemies who are walking around and guarding against intruders (which would be you, as these targets see you as thieves). This lets you pick your battles, which is always nice in a JRPG, as well as ambush your enemies. These enemies are just placeholders, though. When you get into actual fights, you’ll see the monsters you’re fighting. All of your normal JRPG actions are here. Attack, defend, use items, or use your Persona abilities. Everyone of your party members has their own Persona with their own abilities and you can choose to manually control them or let the AI do the work. Your character, however, can host multiple Personas which gives you a much deeper (and more strategic) wealth of options. The game highly encourages strategy. Each Persona (and enemy) is strong or weak to different types of attacks. Going up against a boss who likes to use Ice attacks with a Persona who is weak to that is just asking for a bad time! On the other hand, if you hit an enemy’s weakness, you will get a One More action, which is pretty much a free turn. Hit everyone’s weakness and you can do a massive party attack. It pays to be strategic! The game also lets your main character recruit enemy Personas through negotiation (which is… interesting) and even lets you fuse Personas together to create new ones. Each Persona levels up as well, and fusing lower-leveled ones for higher-leveled ones is pretty much mandatory to keep up with things. Persona 5 Royal , of course, changes things drastically from the main game. The first thing I noticed is that every palace (main story dungeon) has been re-designed. Early on in the game you’ll acquire a grappling hook that is a key to most of the palace changes (but man, is it stylish!). Each palace also has three Will Seeds that are generally hidden and, when collected, give you a powerful accessory. You also have dozens of new Personas throughout the game, which is just fantastic, of course, as well as two new Arcana that Personas can be categorized into. Revamped Palaces and dozens of new Personas are sure great, but they also revamped the Mementos dungeon as well. They added a new character here, Jose, who has you gather flowers in Mementos in exchange for items. He can also change Mementos as well, giving you options on more experience, items or gold. All of that makes Persona 5 Royal good, but there are a lot of other changes as well. You can, of course, spend time with our two new Confidants to get game-altering abilities but Royal also addresses one of my biggest complaints of the main game: how often Morgana (one of your teammates) makes you go to bed! Royal gives you much more freedom in the early parts of the game and it is heavenly. This combined with the new Confidants and the game’s expanded story means you’re guaranteed to spend more time with Royal overall (which is exactly what returning players wanted). Nothing like a little cooperation! (Graphics) One thing Royal definitely didn’t need to change was the game’s graphics. I maintain to this day that Persona 5 (and Royal, of course) are some of the most stylish games you’ll ever play. Not only are animations beautiful, but even the menus are just downright gorgeous. The game loves to show off! It helps that the game overall goes for the more animated look instead of hyper-realistic (your 3D character models are human-proportioned, but drawn in anime style), as it looks fantastic and, as we all know, will hold up fantastically over time. The original title improved upon the usual Persona dungeons by custom-making each which was a huge improvement in the series. Royal has all of the same dungeons (and more), but as I mentioned, it has also mixed things up and the dungeons really are bigger and better now. Royal also introduces a new area to explore, Kichijoji, that features new shops and a darts/billiards club to hang out in. One other new addition that I loved were the new Showtime attacks. As you play through the game, your teammates will meet with each other and come up with tag-team moves that you can use in dungeons. These moves are powerful, sure, but they also come with some awesome animations as well. This game looks just as good as you would expect and will look good for years to come, I'm sure. Adding onto an already great soundtrack. (Audio) Another great reason to revisit Royal (other than all those changes up above) is the music. To this day I still listen to the Persona 5 soundtrack. It’s that good, with a funky music which often combines jazz, punk and pop together to just be downright catchy (check out “Wake Up, Get Up, Get Out There”, “Rivers in the Desert" and "Beneath the Mask" for a good track selection). Of course, Persona 5 Royal has added several new songs to the game, including a new main theme song and a new battle theme. And… they… are… great! They bring back vocalist Lyn Inaizumi and she knocks it out of the park once again. Outside of the soundtrack, the voice acting throughout the game is solid and enjoyable with everyone sounding great (including the two new Confidants, who do an amazing job). I should note that if you don't care for the English voice actors, you can switch over to the Japanese voice-overs (which used to be DLC in the original game). Overall, the audio here is better than ever and if you enjoyed the original soundtrack you'll love this one as well. Get ready for a huge JRPG time sink. (Re-Playability) The game’s re-playability is still likely its weakest point, but to be fair, Persona 5 is a huge game. You’re definitely getting your money’s worth here, as this is a 100+ hour JRPG and now, thanks to the additions of Royal , it’s even longer. I was also thrilled that Royal has a completely new (and revamped) Trophy List, which, of course, gives you challenges throughout the game and a reason to play New Game+ as some of the trophies require that. New Game+ also carries over things, like your social stats, Persona compendium and items which make a second playthrough much easier. I will also add that overall, Royal is much easier than the main Persona 5 (with the exception of a few specific boss battles, which is weird). This goes for both the main game and the trophy list, as many trophies are just plain easier to get in Royal. Take that for what it's worth. Overall: 10/10 In the end, Persona 5 Royal is basically a remixed ultimate version of Persona 5 , following in the footsteps of Persona 4 Golden and Persona 3 FES . Fans of the series should rest assured that it’s a worthy addition to the series and is, without a doubt, the way to play Persona 5 from here on out. Virtually everything you loved about the original game is not only in-place here, but improved upon. If you haven’t given Persona 5 a chance yet, but enjoy JRPGs… boy, do I have a game for you! Have fun and keep playing!

author: carlde21
review_title: The best thieves ever, striking fear in the hearts of the most evil and corrupt!
review_text: Persona 5 Royal, developed by Atlus, is a critically acclaimed JRPG, one of the best ever released. It's jam-packed with content and a compelling story that takes players on an unforgettable journey through the darker recesses of society. With its vibrant art style, intricate battle system, and engaging characters, this game solidifies itself as an absolute must-play for fans of the series, RPG fanatics, and even newcomers to the genre. I think it's safe to say that most adults have taken at least one history class at some point in their lives. Have you ever wondered how world events might have changed had a horrible person not come to power? Scenes of Farnsworth, from Futurama, are etched in my memory. Fans of the show might remember Farnsworth taking out Hitler from his time machine in the season 7 episode " The Late Philip J. Fry". It is an interesting thought exercise, how might our world look if something like that had been possible? The Persona series, especially 5, takes a deep dive into ideas like that and subjects such as psychology, science, religion, faith, and philosophy. Taking place in a typical high school, the story is centered around a group of teens who form the mysterious "Phantom Thieves" to try and improve the world. I can sense the groans already. Teenagers in a typical high school setting might not sound appealing, at all, and for the most part, I wouldn't fault someone for feeling that way. I enjoyed my University years infinitely more and life only got more interesting from there. I gladly left the drama behind the day I graduated high school, so what appeal does a game featuring high school have? That's a question I asked and why I stayed away from this game for so long but after seeing it on a steep discount I took a risk and I am glad I did. Yes, there are still some cheesy melodramatic moments but overall, this is a fascinating game with an intriguing story to tell and deep character development. There are about two dozen secondary characters that have a significant role in the game as well. In fact, one of the secondary characters runs a site to gauge public opinion on the Phantom Thieves, giving you insight into how the rest of Japan views your group, the approval rating showing during many of the loading screens. Trust me, it fluctuates like crazy! What the Phantom Thieves do in this alternate reality, known as the metaverse, has a direct impact on the real world but, like Superman, their true identity must never be found out. Have you ever been to a masquerade ball? Even if you haven't, you've likely heard of them, and that is the premise of the metaverse where a large chunk of the plot takes place. Ren, or Joker as he is more commonly referred to, is the main character and finds a mysterious app on his phone. This app allows the Phantom Thieves to enter a distorted version of reality where their appearance is altered as well as to not be detected by the person they are trying to create a change of heart for. Joker is the head of the mysterious group that includes other teens who have also happened to find the app on their phones. After entering this bizarre world, almost like a fever dream, and viewing the twisted versions of a teacher's heart and mind the enigma of the metaverse deepens. The metaverse is fascinating because a person's deep thoughts form into some tangible, viewable world that can be explored, known as a palace. All of the things we hide from the world are on full display, sometimes in very disturbing ways. Many of the seven deadly sins are represented through the palaces as well, such as avarice, lust, and pride. At the center of each palace is a treasure, the thing that person values the most. Stealing this treasure in the metaverse changes the heart of that person in the real world too, eventually leading to some form of redemption for some of the worst characters in the game. Think of it as some guilty conscious being buried away and the Phantom Thieves work to unearth it. There are 8 palaces in the game plus an optional 9th if certain criteria are met. Many themes are explored throughout the game such as the dichotomy between conforming and rebelling, as well as freedom, discovering your true self, and the consequences of one's actions. Those in charge of writing the story for this game deserve high praise as the pacing of the game is superb with frequent surprise twists and turns. While each palace focuses on one prominent figure in society, there are also mementos that take place in one gigantic dungeon that slowly opens up more at different junctures in the game. Mementos tend to focus on changing the hearts of less-known individuals and represent the current, general public perception. From what I could tell each floor was randomly generated and included tons of items and flowers to collect. Flowers can be collected to exchange for items and boost experience or money earned, or the frequency and quality of items dropped by enemies, but I believe those changes only took effect within the mementos. Be aware that once you leave mementos all flowers are lost forever so spend them all before leaving, they don't carry over to future visits. Exchanging flowers can be done anytime Jose shows up, but he shows up at random and sometimes you have to go 10 or more floors before he decides to appear on a floor. But you can simply wait by the stairs and go up and down until he appears. I wouldn't recommend diving into walkthroughs for this game, as tempting as it sounds. Granted this is a complex game with all sorts of people to talk to and things to do. At times it can get downright overwhelming as far as figuring out how to manage your time. This is because time is constantly moving forward, whether you like it or not. It doesn't help that there is that damn cat telling you that you can't go out at night or need to sleep rather than do even one, of probably many things you have in mind to do. So it might be tempting to seek help online to figure out how to best maximize your time. For the most part, I played this blind and I am glad I did. Other than googling "What confidants should I prioritize" and learning about three in particular, I simply used my best judgment. As a bonus, and as luck would have it when googling what confidants to focus on, I found out who I should focus on without even having to click on a specific link! While I suggest newcomers take the same route and play blind, I would recommend, at the very least, finding out those three specific people to seek out and form bonds with as one leads to the optional 3rd term and two others lead to the best ending. The third term adds so much to the game and has some of the best moments in this 100+ hour epic and it would be a huge loss to miss out on it. I got about 12 confidants to max rank and an additional 6 to at least rank 8. There are about two dozen confidants in total. Confidants , by the way, are specific characters you can form bonds with during your free time. By hanging out with them and giving good responses, you gain points that go towards increasing your rank with them. These ranks go until 10 and as you move through the ranks, many benefits are unlocked that make battles easier and flow better. Keep in mind that the weather and time of year have an impact on what you do and who you can see and characters change their pattern and where they hang out depending on several factors. These ranks also allow for more potent personas to be created, however, you can't create a persona of a higher level than Jokers, unless there are some stat boosts added after the new persona is created, which happens quite often, actually. For those familiar with other Persona games, Igor makes his return here and the story surrounding him in this game is fascinating, to say the least, with a lot of ups and downs and even a few unexpected things thrown in towards the end. This is a story-driven game with a ton of dialog. While there are 9 dungeons, plus mementos, a large portion of the game is spent talking to others. But unlike other games that drone on and on, such as some of the Trails games, it never gets too boring in Persona 5 and helps a great deal in becoming immersed in the world. Hours can speed by when you are between two palaces. I've had 5-hour sessions where all I did is run around Tokyo talking to people or looking for ways to get my social ranks up. There are 5 social stats: Knowledge, Guts, Proficiency, Kindness, and Charm which all can go up to level 5 very slowly, but surely as you progress through the year. I got all 5 up to rank 5, by the skin of my teeth, with about a week to go in term 3, knowledge being the last to go up to 5. Never have I had so much fun doing mundane things such as washing laundry, studying, or reading a book. Trying to explain to friends who haven't played this game that doing those things, and thus increasing social stats, is a fundamental aspect of the game is a hard sell, but it really is interesting. For instance, reading books, studying, or responding to questions in class increases knowledge. Yes, Joker does have to go to class but Atlus has somehow made these ho-hum tasks engrossing and I learned a number of things through the questions teachers ask him. It even got to the point where I couldn't wait to finish the palaces so I could continue to work on bonds and social stats or, heck, even play a game of darts. In most RPGs it is the opposite for me, get through the talking as soon as possible so I can go on my next mission or dungeon. It isn't that the palaces were bad, some were enjoyable, especially the first four. But somewhere around the 5th palace things started to drag a little. The 5th Palace is probably the hardest, longest one in the game punctuated by one of the more frustrating bosses I have ever had to face in any main story of any RPG. The time limit is one thing, but before even getting to the point where you can touch the jerk he sends five waves of enemies, each wave having four enemies, that have to be beaten in two turns. This proved to be incredibly difficult even on normal and other than my Google search for confidants to focus on, this was the only other time I looked up information on how to tackle an aspect of the game. Trust me, the solution is counter-intuitive, to say the least! This is one example, possibly the only one, that I can point to as poor game design. The boss wasn't entertaining, period. The next three palaces were a walk in the park comparatively, and I didn't have another serious challenge until the very last boss at the end of term 3, so the balance in this game was somewhat erratic. Other than that, palaces are indeed long but are rewarding with plenty of save points spread throughout. Yes, the quality of life addition of being able to save anywhere would have been nice, but rarely did I feel stressed by a save point being too far away. None of the palaces are straightforward Point A to Point B experiences and require a lot of backtracking and carefully checking your surroundings to see if you can climb a ledge, use the grappling hook (L1) to reach a distant area, or climb through a vent. This is where the third eye comes into play. It is a godsend at all times and my finger was practically glued to the R1 button. I tend to have a poor memory so people like me might struggle at times regarding how to progress, but it is never over the top. One thing I loved about the palaces was the ability to sneak attack enemies. It is, generally speaking, very easy to ambush enemies in this game. Almost too easy. Ambushing enemies can help in causing a great deal of damage to be done before they can do a thing. If you get enemies down to a certain HP low point, the ability to talk to personas is presented. You can ask them to join you (get a mask, and thus a new persona to summon), get money, or get an item. Sometimes they will refuse all of that in which case you can do an all-out attack where all four party members join together to pummel the enemy. Otherwise, this is an excellent way to get tons of money quickly, especially if you get a specific confidant who helps you to hold up enemies for even more money. Negotiating with enemies to convince them to join you is straightforward and negotiations in Persona 1, Innocent Sin, or, believe it or not, the SNES SMT games were more difficult because they felt less predictable and more challenging. I never failed to negotiate in Perona 5, but often did in the other games mentioned. It was made too easy in this game, partially because Morgana tells you exactly how to do it, which I didn't appreciate as it took some of the mystery out of talking to demons. What I did appreciate were some of the tips Morgana gave for a few of the harder bosses as all bosses are not straightforward and require careful thinking to exploit their weak spots and eventually defeat them. Nearly every foe and even a few of the bosses have clear weak points which you can learn from trial and error, or via a confidant who sometimes discloses what enemies are weak and strong against at the start of the battle. Otherwise, you just have to go for it and experiment. Thankfully, once exposed, everything is displayed in the future by simply analyzing opponents. I suppose it is hard to have a happy medium between disliking negotiating tips and appreciating tips given for bosses or even enemies from Morgana and might be a little hypocritical of me. Persona 5 Royal is stylistic and a visual feast for the eyes. The game boasts a stunning, vibrant aesthetic that helps in becoming further absorbed in the game. The beautifully animated cutscenes and meticulously designed environments breathe life into the world. This is probably the most stylistic game I have ever played, RPG or not. As much as the art style helped to create an engrossing atmosphere filled with enigmatic vibes, I wasn't a huge fan of the music as, in some respects, some tracks worked against these specific vibes. There were some melancholic tracks and the main theme of the last palace (the 9th) were exceptional examples of the music working towards the mood of the game. On the other hand, the battle theme feels so out of place and it is easy to get tired of having to listen to it so many times in the 100+ hours it takes to beat all three terms. I much preferred the battle theme from Revelations: Persona and an updated version of that track would have been a stronger fit in Persona 5. I turned down the music of one of the more upbeat Palace tracks and listened to Deva Yuga, from Persona 1 as that track is much superior in my view. An updated version of that would have worked well with Persona 5. I really loved the off-kilter, sometimes creepy tracks of the first game, the moans, groans and taunts of your characters toward demons were more intimidating in 1 than in 5. The tracks tended to be too upbeat for me in this game. Personal preferences aside regarding the music, Persona 5 Royal is an amazing game that exceeds any high standards set by just about any other excellent game in the roleplaying genre. Its engaging storyline, complex characters, and refined gameplay mechanics make it a true masterpiece in gaming. Prepare to be captivated by its stylish presentation, immersed in its thought-provoking themes, and enriched by its diverse cast of characters. Persona 5 Royal is a must-play for anyone seeking an extraordinary gaming experience.

author: Blk_Mage_Ctype
review_title: BEWARE: The Phantom Thieves have stolen my heart... You could be next!
review_text: Introduction: I first played Persona 5 many years ago on PS4, enjoyed it very much and came close to finishing it, but unfortunately I had a lot of things going on at the time, so I had to put it aside. Alas, the console broke down before I could return to it, and I had moved away from PlayStation hardware in favor of PC gaming. Fortunately, the improved Persona 5 Royal version eventually went multiplatform, thus enabling me to play the very best version on the most powerful hardware available. Visual Presentation: Being originally developed for the PlayStation 3 hardware, Persona 5 was never a game which featured cutting-edge visuals, but nevertheless the game's stylized artistic direction manages to make Persona 5 a visually interesting game. Persona 5 features colorful graphics set in the distinctive style of Japanese Anime with a combination of fully animated 3D models as well as 2D animated portraits for each of the major characters, complete with both in-game rendered 3D and 2D anime cutscenes. As a result, P5R looks like a combination of a Visual Novel and a 3D Japanese Role-playing Game, which is likewise reflected in the gameplay, but we'll get more into that later. Audio Presentation: Persona 5 Royal features multiple musical tracks, consisting of both orchestral melodies as well as complete songs, each with English language lyrics. The music sounds good and the songs are extremely catchy, provided that you can appreciate Jazzy tunes, lounge music, and Japanese Pop. The in-game dialog is available in your choice of either Japanese or English, with all critical, plot-significant dialog and story sequences featuring full voice acting. The English Dub is best described as adequate, the performances aren't outstanding, but they suit the characters well and the lines are well spoken. I haven't sampled the Japanese Dub, but I'm unqualified to comment on it regardless because I don't speak the language. Gameplay Mechanics and Features: Persona 5 Royal is a combination of a traditional Turn-based JRPG, Dungeon Crawler, and a Life Sim/Visual Novel in which you must balance a daily schedule of attending High School, spending time speaking with friends to strengthen your bonds with them, exploring dungeons and engaging in traditional turn based combat with enemies. As you would expect from the aforementioned combination of genres, the game is extremely dialog heavy, including sequences in which you must answer questions in class, engage in conversation with friends, and carefully choose your responses from a multiple choice dialog tree in order to answer questions correctly as well as get closer to your friends. You also have a variety of stats directly associated with social interaction — Knowledge, Guts, Proficiency, Kindness, Charm — which directly effect your ability to express yourself. These stats are increased by engaging in various daily activities as well as interacting with particular individuals, and are fortunately in most cases gained passively from average everyday activities, so you don't have to invest too much time into increasing them. Interacting with your friends increases the Rank of your bond with them, granting various perks in combat and allows you to fuse more powerful Personas to equip yourself with. The JRPG portion of the game is likewise exactly what you would expect from the genre. You explore dungeons, (Palaces) engage in turn-based combat with enemies (Shadows) with a variety of techniques at your disposal, earn Experience Points to Level Up along with money to buy equipment, and open treasure chests to gain loot in the form of various items. The only variation to the standard JRPG formula lies in the eponymous Personas, Mythological Entities which are equipped to you similarly to weapons, granting you magical abilities. Personas level up passively along with you when equipped, but have their own separate stats. Those who have played various Monster Taming RPGs will be familiar with the basics here, but it isn't difficult for newcomers to learn through progression. Altogether, the combination of genres compliment each other and makes for an engaging, multifaceted gameplay experience which can seem deceptively overwhelming at first but quickly becomes second nature in practice. Story: In Persona 5 Royal you take on the role of a teenage boy who has been moved away from his home out in the country to live with a family friend in the city after he became involved in a confrontation with a drunken man who was attempting to force a young woman into his car, with the man injuring himself in the process and the boy arrested then charged with assault. The boy arrives in the city only to find that his undeserved reputation as a juvenile delinquent has followed him there, with his new guardian addressing him as an unwelcome guest, his teachers at school likewise dismissing him as a delinquent, and his classmates avoiding him while exchanging rumors regarding the details of his arrest. Shortly after his arrival, he discovers a mysterious App has appeared on his Phone which seems to restore itself no matter how many times he deletes it. One day on his way to school the App is inadvertently activated during a conversation with another ostracized student, transporting them into another world in which the School has been replaced by a Palace ruled by the School's abusive P.E. Instructor, with the two being locked up in the dungeon by the guards. They escape their cells with the help of a mysterious feline creature named Morgana, but are quickly caught by the guards on their way out of the palace, leading to the boy awakening to his Persona — his "other self" — granting him the power to defeat the palace guards and escape. The next day they return to the Palace where they are informed by Morgana that it exists within the mind of its ruler as a cognitive manifestation of his distorted desires, and that by stealing his treasure they can change his heart, thus putting an end to his abusive behavior. From there the trio forms a team known as The Phantom Thieves of Hearts, setting out to use their powers to reform society by changing the hearts of various corrupt authority figures, recruiting new allies along the way as they are drawn ever deeper into an insidious plot to seize control of Japan by manipulating the masses. Performance: Being a port of a game which was originally developed for the PlayStation 3, Persona 5 Royal doesn't require a particularly powerful PC to run. I encountered no performance issues whatsoever over the course of my 171 hour long playthrough and the game ran flawlessly at Max Settings on my PC. Your experience may vary based on the specs of your PC, but I can safely say that there are no bugs, glitches, or performance issues to speak of regardless. Final Verdict: Persona 5 Royal is an excellent game featuring many hours of content between the deep, engrossing story and entertaining assortment of gameplay mechanics. I came just short of a 100% run, missing only a single Confidant, yet completing the story and side quests in their entirety, closing out the game by earning 100% of the Achievements. My playthrough lasted 171 hours, thus making it by far the longest of any single player game I have ever played in 35 years of gaming. I enjoyed the game thoroughly and am left with nothing bad to say about it whatsoever. I highly recommend it to anyone seeking an immersive JRPG to occupy their time.

author: ivory_soul
review_title: A fantastic story with great characters, but 100+ hours is too long
review_text: I really like the Persona and Shin Megami Tensei series, but they are insanely long and challenging. These are hardcore JRPGs not meant for casual players. Most won't have the stamina needed to sit through 150+ hour games and the PlayStation trophy data shows that. Less than half of all Persona 5 players finished the game. Thankfully, for people like me, Atlus put me in an extra easy mode called Safety that let me finish my first-ever Persona game. I tried the third and fourth games several times and just couldn't do it. While I eventually did well in battles, the games were too long. The story in Persona 5 is fantastic and there are plenty of great things about this game, but a few key issues may drive most players away even more casual JRPG fans. The story is insanely deep and detailed. There are plenty of mysteries and twists and turns that kept me trucking on because I wanted to see what happened next. The characters are compelling, well-written, and very likable, however, you still need to like anime to enjoy the characters in this game. There are some typical anime tropes that leak in, but I think people who play JRPGs are already aware of this. Your character is Joker, a teenage boy wrongfully convicted of assaulting a high-profile individual for just trying to save a woman from harassment on the street. You end up living with someone who volunteered to take in a convict and watch over you so you can get rehabilitated. This game plays just like previous Persona games with a time limit, days going by, social rankings, and acquiring personas. The game will introduce things to you throughout the entire game, and I mean throughout. 40 hours in I was still getting tutorial messages. The game is an incredibly slow burn. I didn't get to do any battling until the fifth or sixth hour. This was all story and world-building, introducing the idea of personas, your purpose, and your back story, and showing you how to go about the day-to-day. The game is mostly dialog, to be honest. Out of the 80 hours, it took me to finish the game maybe 25 of that was actually exploring the dungeons and fighting. There is a lot of character-building and slice-of-life stuff in here. You also have a time limit to finish every palace which is the main dungeon in the game. When you're not battling you are living your everyday life. You need to go to school and the day is broken up into sections such as early morning which is reserved for dialog you hear on the train going to school, talking to friends at the train station, etc. Morning and afternoon are reserved for things happening at school during the week or random quizzes that you can answer to increase your social stats. These stats are knowledge, proficiency, charm, kindness, and guts. These are needed to finish confidant arcs and max out that persona category so you can get stat boosts when using that type of persona. These stats can be increased by doing certain activities like watching movies, playing games, doing chores, and other everyday activities. It's important to use your downtime for increasing these stats as the game is balanced by not just level grinding, but having these extra stats for each persona type. After school time is reserved for doing things around the city such as said activities and getting together to enter Momentos which is a secondary dungeon with a few dozen levels that you need to descend to complete requests from people. In the end, it's required to descend fully for the final dungeon, but before that it's optional. I recommend doing these late-game so you can just barrel through the levels by the end. The evening is reserved for nighttime activities and jobs even to earn more money. After the activity, the evening is done you advance to the next day and do this all over. Some days are interrupted by story elements, scripted scenes, and other events. It's important to hang out with confidants when you get texts from them to advance their persona ranking. These are where the side stories for each character are held. They can be long-cut scenes too. Usually, you get 30 odd days between each major palace to fill the time. This time period can take hours to finish. When you do actually battle Persona is based on finding the weaknesses of enemies. This can be both good and bad. If you find the weakness you get one more turn. This can be elemental or physical. The downside is that the entire game can be over if you don't find these quickly. It's trial and error as to finding the weakness and some just don't have one. You waste precious turns trying to figure this out and it can make some boss fights grueling. You can save within these palaces and return to the real world to buy items and increase your persona rankings more, but if you don't find the treasure and beat the boss by the deadline it's game over. I've always hated this about the series and it makes the game more difficult and frustrating than it needs to be. You can capture personas by talking to them when they're weak in battle. If successful they will join your ranks. It's important to keep a good variety of personas leveled up and acquire new ones with better skills. You can fuse and itemize them in the Velvet Room as well as sacrifice weaker ones to strengthen others. While you can use multiple personas your party members are stuck with one. Every few levels they will gain new abilities for their personas and you have a limited number of slots so it's important to keep them balanced. Inside these palaces, you can acquire items, treasures to sell, and powerful equipment that you can buy in the airsoft shop. These palaces are huge with multiple levels and can take hours to complete. I played the game on safety difficulty so I could beat each palace in a single sitting, but if you need to level grind and fuse personas you could take the entire time limit. Each palace is a different theme and they look cool, but the weak puzzles and labyrinthine halls of some of them are really annoying. Enemies walk around in real-time and because you are thieves you can get behind cover and dash around them stealthily or take them head on. Some palaces are a really confusing mess and I found some just went on for too long. Those are your two main parts of the game. Battling in Momentos or palaces and living your everyday life to increase social stats and play mini-games. I personally don't like the trial and error of exploiting weaknesses to win each fight. The graphics are decent, while stylistically they look great with lots of flash and color, but technically it looks like a typical JRPG and borderline last generation and not too much of a step up from the PS3 version. While it seems there is a lot to do in the game there actually isn't. You're so focused on visiting confidants and maxing out social stats in the real world that it feels like a chore after a while. You have to realize there are nearly 250 in-game days you have to get through on top of the palaces and momentos. The game just feels like it never ends. 80 hours to finish safety difficulties and it can take 150-200 hours for higher difficulties. I had to dedicate every free minute I had over the last three weeks to finishing this game and not playing any other games in between. I wish there was a warning at the beginning of the game letting players know how long the game can take on average or even put it somewhere on an official source of info for the game. I have played and bought many JRPGs not realizing just how long they take to beat. Overall, I don't want to talk too much about the story because I can easily spoil something. The Phantom Thieves and trying to change the hearts of criminals is a great story. It can be very dark at times talking bout child exploitation, abuse, murder, money laundering, and many other crimes. It's a dark game and I felt it had a very memorable story, but it takes way too long to tell it. Many will balk at the trial and error of weakness exploitation to win battles, insane amounts of grinding, and the constant need to micro-manage your personas to get a well-balanced always leveled-up arsenal might seem like too much. That doesn't include dozens upon dozens of hours of reading dialog and watching cut scenes. I recommend this only to the hardest-core of JRPG fans. This game is not to be taken lightly. While I complain about some of these things fans of this genre embrace it and that's okay, but for only around 40% of players to have finished the game says something about the length.

author: P1Falchion
review_title: The Phantom Thieves are back
review_text: Persona is a series I got into in 2014. I remember when I saw the trailer for Persona Q I was hooked so before the release of that game, I decided to play through both Persona 3 and 4 in preparation for that game. Both Persona 3 and 4 are games I fell in love with because of its characters, story, music, and gameplay. As time passed every once and a while we would get information on Persona 5 and my anticipation towards that game was at 11 and I couldn’t wait to play another fantastic Persona game. So in 2017 when that game came out I marathoned through that game and my experience was mainly great but towards the end of the game, I started to think something was wrong. Something about this game was keeping me from loving the game and after the credits rolled I felt underwhelmed. I say all this because with Persona 5 Royal I knew there were going to be new story moments and I was worried that I would feel disappointed again and for a while, it seemed like my feeling was going to stay the same. However, after clearing the new story section and I reached the end credits of the game I was delighted and at the same time sad but in the best way. These are the emotions I had when I cleared Persona 3 and 4 and I was so happy that Persona 5 Royal was finally able to give me those feelings I was looking for back in 2017. Persona 5 Royal story starts with the Phantom Thieves taking part in a heist at a Casino. The protagonist Joker, is trying to escape from the Casino and as he was about to make his escape the police were able to catch him and the police tell him that he was sold out by a team member. Afterward, he is taken to an interrogation room where the police drug him, beat him and make him sign a false confession statement. Before he could be taken away a prosecutor named Sae Niijima asks to interrogate him and now she wants to hear everything from him as to how he was able to change the hearts of people. After that, the game cuts to when the protagonist arrived in Tokyo and the rest afterward is the story of how we got to the point where he ended up being captured. The protagonist can be named whatever you want him to be called but when he becomes a Phantom Thief his codename is Joker. A cutscene shows that he was trying to protect a woman who was being harassed by a man and afterward the man is seen injured and he tells the police that the boy was the one who assaulted him. The protagonist, as a result, is on probation and he ends up moves away from home and he now lives at a cafe called Cafe Leblanc. His guardian is the owner of Cafe Leblanc Sojiro Sakura. Sojiro tells him that he will be going to Shujin Academy and he will be living in his cafe for the year. He also warns Joker that if he does anything that would get him in trouble he will report him to the police and he would go to prison. On the first day of school, the protagonist meets a student from Shujin named Ryuji and as the two try to reach the school they notice it looks like a castle for some reason. They go in and they are greeted by knights who then take them both to a dungeon and it's at that moment they meet the ruler of the castle. The ruler is a teacher named Kamoshida but he’s completely different from the teacher they know. Eventually, Ryuji finds a way for the protagonist to escape but he refuses to leave Ryuji behind which triggers a voice that tells the protagonist if he truly wishes to rebel against then to stand up to Kamoshida. After the protagonist confronts Kamoshida he awakens to his Persona which allows him to fight back against the shadows trying to kill him and Ryuji. And just like that, the adventure of the Phantom Thieves begins. The story behind the dungeons is pretty much you are entering a world of people’s perception of a particular area. So at the beginning of the game, you infiltrate the Palace of a teacher who views the school as a Castle. This is how Palaces work throughout the whole game so every time you visit a new palace you will be in a completely different environment. As you make your way through these Palaces the goal is to get to the treasure which represents a person’s most negative desire. The Phantom Thieves want to steal these treasures because once they steal them in the real world it would make it so terrible people would confess their wrongdoings. Before the Phantom Thieves can steal their treasure, they must send a calling card saying they will steal their treasure for the treasure to take a physical form. Once you send the calling card you go back into the Palace and you attempt to steal the Treasure. Once you make your way back to the treasure you'll get into a boss fight and after the boss fight, the treasure is yours and days later the Phantom Thieves' target confess their crimes. This is pretty the structure of Persona 5 and after you complete a Palace it will be a while before you get to another Palace. While infiltrating palaces are the main objectives in this game that won't be the only thing you will be doing. Another important location is Mementos which is everyone’s Palace. There will be times when you are requested to change the hearts of people and whenever you need to change their hearts you go to Momentos and you find and defeat their shadow and like that you complete the quest and you get a small reward for doing so. Once you get your Persona you are thrown into battle and for newcomers, this will be pretty easy to get into. Personas have certain skills as well as their strengths and weaknesses. For example the Persona you start with is Arsene and his strengths are Curse skills and his weakness is Light and Ice skills. When you fight an enemy you use the skills of the Persona you have to figure out enemies' weaknesses. Every time you gain a party member each character has a unique Persona and like that your strategies for battles open up as you are trying to figure out when you want to utilize certain party members. Once you get to the point in the game where you have multiple party members you have access to the All-Out Attack. When you hit enemies with their weaknesses they are stunned you can perform an All-Out Attack which has all your party members attack at the same time. There is a lot of options that open once you have a full party. For example, there is this skill called a Baton Pass which means when you attack an enemy with their weakness you can execute another attack or you can pass your extra turn to another party member and if you do that they get an attack boost. After you have all your party members you will have plenty of options when it comes to what type of Persona you want in battle. One advantage the protagonist has compared to the rest of your party is he can use multiple Persona, which means you have more skills at your disposal. There are a couple of ways to get more Persona, one way is if you knock down all the enemies in battle you can talk to them and convince them to join you. The way to do that is you talk to them and get them to like you and after you do that you can use them in battle. There will even be times when you are battling an enemy they may want to give up and you can ask them to join you and like that you have another Persona. Getting Personas in battles is all well and good but you can have stronger Persona if you play your cards right. This is where the Velvet Room comes to play. The Velvet Room is the area where you can fuse the Personas you gain from dungeons and you can make them stronger by fusing them with other Personas you have. The Velvet Room has a lot of uses not just for fusing Persona and as you play the game you gain more to do in the Velvet Room. At one point you can sacrifice Personas you don't need to a Persona you want to make stronger. Or you can itemize them and you can acquire rare weapons, armor, or skills. Being a Phantom Thief is great and all but there is one more important aspect of the game which is playing the role of a high school student. You will be going to school and at that time you will do your best to be the best student you can be and at the same time, you will try and develop a relationship with the characters you meet. These people you start forming a relationship with are your confidants and they are important for many reasons. One is that every time you develop a bond with someone you learn a useful skill from them that can be useful when you are infiltrating a Palace or exploring Momentos. You can get skills like escape easily from battles, negotiate easily with enemies, switch party members mid-battle, etc. There are many useful tools you can gain from developing a relationship with not only your fellow Phantom Thieve members but, with other characters you meet throughout the game. The confidants you meet are one of my favorite parts of Persona in general because this when you learn about characters and their stories and for the most part a lot of these characters have great stories and are part of the reason why so many people love the Persona series. The gameplay is a lot of fun whether it be infiltrating a Palace, bonding with your confidants, fusing Personas, or doing small mini-games like playing darts with your friends there is a lot to keep you busy. This game has a style like no other game I have played. Everything about this game has such a cool, slick, popping style that helps show off Persona 5 personality. Just looking at the menu for Persona 5 you know you are getting a stylish game. The game looks fantastic from all the new animations included during battles. If this is your first time experiencing Persona 5 the Palaces have so much personality and each feels so unique and as a result, you never feel like there is a dull moment. The music for Persona 5 was already one of the best soundtracks I have ever heard but now a lot of the new tracks included have elevated the soundtrack even more which I didn’t even think was possible. I mentioned that Persona 5 was not a game I loved the first time I played it and the main reason why I didn’t like it as much was that I felt Persona 5 lacked its personality in terms of the story. I felt like the story was following the beats of past Persona games only Persona 5 didn’t execute them as well as they could have. But the reason why now with Royal I’ve had a change of heart was because of the new story segment that was added in the game. That story was what I was looking for in Persona 5 something that made it stand out on its own in the story department and after completing the game I felt genuine sadness and happiness when the game concluded. Thankfully my issue with Persona 5 story shouldn’t be an issue for newcomers of the series so the only other element of the game I still have a small issue with the game is in regards to its length. This is a pretty long game and even with all the knowledge, I knew about the game it still took me 100+ hours to beat. I think this game could’ve been shorter but again this is a minor issue and I’m pretty sure people will love the world of Persona 5 so much that it won't be an issue for others. Unfortunately, the area of the game I’m still not a fan of is Momentos. Exploring Momentos is still a pretty boring experience and thankfully in Persona 5 Royal they added more tracks to Momentos so it doesn’t feel too boring but good music can only do so much sometimes and in this case, Momentos could not be saved. Persona 5 Royal is one of the best RPGs you can play from this generation. If you love RPGs this is a game you don't want to skip. Persona 5 Royal’s cast of characters is fantastic and seeing each character's story is great to see. The Palaces you explore are always exciting moments to get to especially if this is your first time experiencing this game. One of the best parts of the game is when you are about the steal someone's heart and Life Will Change plays in the background which is one of the most invigorating themes in the game and it's fitting given you are pulling off a heist. The soundtrack of Persona 5 Royal is easily one of the best soundtracks ever for a video game. And the new added story and characters are great additions to this game. Persona 5 was a game I didn't love back in 2017 but with all of the added content to this game Atlus stole my heart and I can’t wait for later down the line to play through this game again.

author: TLHunter312
review_title: The game that stole my heart - Persona 5 Royal
review_text: Overall rating: 10/10 Introduction: If you've been keeping up with my past Persona reviews you'll know that Persona 5 was my first game in the series, followed by Royal shortly after, and now with it fresh in my mind after finally finishing my Joker-only run I'm finally ready to do a review on it. I have a lot to say so this will be longer than my reviews on Persona 4 Golden and Persona 3 FES. I'll be referring to the game as 5 Royal, keep in mind a couple of things were introduced in Royal, those being Kichijoji, persona traits, and the post-game but I'm counting it as part of Royal since Royal is the definitive version of 5. Now then, onto the review. Gameplay 10/10: Wow, talk about a huge step up from the previous two games. Persona 5 Royal steps things up quite a bit from the previous games by turning up the combat speed quite a bit. While it is still turn-based it's without a doubt faster-paced thanks to the changes to the combat system. It's also extremely engaging and requires your full focus for just about every fight no matter how insignificant it may seem. The game has also introduced guns as a weapon you can use allowing even more possibilities with combat as well as making things easier, along with guns there are also two new elements, Nuke and Psy. If that wasn't enough for you, there's also a new system introduced called "negotiations" which lets you speak to a potential Persona to get it on your side and join you. But wait, there's still more Persona 5 Royal both introduce a myriad of new moves and accessories to use, some of the best can only be obtained through beating some of the game's most challenging bosses. You thought I was done, didn't you? Well, guess what, Persona 5/Royal has introduced even more features, such as sacrificing your personas to get skill cards, accessories, weapons, and armor as well as the Fusion Alarm, which may appear after defeating an enemy and allows provides you benefits to everything you can possibly do in the Velvet Room aside from summoning or registering your Personas. Now that's a lot I know, but you'll figure things out fairly quickly. Persona 5/Royal also allows you to customize your Personas to a crazy degree allowing for almost infinite possibilities. Exclusive to Royal as well is something that adds even more customization to your personas, called "traits" special attributes, and buffs that add a lot to builds, and while there are a handful of exclusives nearly every one is possible to get on every persona. Do you want a Pixie that has Megidolaon and wipes out enemies with ease? It's possible. What about a healer Yoshitsune? It's possible. Those are just a couple of crazy ideas. Every battle in this game is different and no two battles are the same even after 3 playthroughs of Royal and 1 of the base version of 5 that still rings true. Aside from that a lot of the combat should feel familiar if you've played the previous two games so you should know what to expect. There's also a bunch of new personas to the series as well as DLC that lets you get some really interesting personas including ones that had only appeared in Persona 4 Arena and Persona 4 Ultimax previously, all of these DLC personas have their signature move and a special stronger variant exclusive to Joker known as "Picaro". I know some of that is a lot to take in, but there's a lot that Persona 5 Royal does, and even when you're in the moment during a boss fight you know what each of your personas can do and what they specialize in. Another cool thing is that outfits in this game change the music and there's only a handful that don't. There are numerous outfits, but a few examples are: SEES Uniform, Yasogami High uniform, Featherman outfit, and the Ultramarine outfit (Velvet Attendant clothing). Music 10/10: I was conflicted on whether or not to give music a 10/10 but I ultimately decided to do so because Persona 5 Royal has my favorite music in the series and while Lotus Juice or Shihoko Hirata aren't doing the vocals anymore, we do have Lyn Inaizumi who gives the 5 series of games an identity of their own and brings a great new flare to the series, on top of that the music is expertly composed by Shoji Meguro as well as Toshiki Konishi, Kenichi Tsuchiya, Atsushi Kitajoh, and Ryota Kozuka. However, Lotus Juice is still behind the scenes and did the lyrics for multiple songs in Royal, my favorite being Take Over, my favorite battle theme in the whole series. The music is extremely diverse, more so than it was in the previous two games. You have a mix of everything in this game, happy, sad, depressing, chill, motivating, intense, and even 8-bit for a few of the retro games you can play to increase your social stats. There isn't a single song in the soundtrack that I feel is a weak link, I think they all work extremely well and while I'm not a fan of all of them there are many standouts for me. One of which is without a doubt my favorite song in the whole series and one of my favorite songs, Life Will Change (with vocals). It's a song that without spoilers plays at key moments, originally with the vocals, then instrumental and once you hit a key point in the story the lyrics come back in full force and it's unforgettable. If I had to describe a feel to the music, I would say it's "jazz that makes you want to get up and dance with the music." With some other stuff thrown in of course. Whether the songs have vocals, or not the soundtrack is one of a kind much like the rest of the series, this game has undoubtedly my favorite soundtrack in the series! My favorite songs in Royal were: Take Over, Life Will Change, Ark, Rivers in The Desert, Will Power, Gentle Madman, Swear To My Bones, Our Beginning, I Beleive, Keep Your Faith, Throw Away Your Mask, Out of Kindness, Hoshi to Bokura To (piano version), Beneath The Mask -rain-, and Butterfly Kiss. Palaces 9.5/10: Palaces are 5 Royal's version of the story dungeons. If you were bored by the lack of verticality and were sick of just running in straight lines or random rooms hoping to reach the end of an area during story segments of the game in the previous games, boy do I have good news for you. Now, there are some spoiler-y parts to Palaces, but nothing I can't talk about, but if you want to go in blind, stop reading here and buy the game, or skip this section entirely. Palaces are the warped desires of a person made manifest in the Metaverse, each one is unique and no two palaces are the same and none are repeated either. Along with these palaces are puzzles, boss fights, and lots of loot, and unique to Royal, will seeds. Weird bean things that resemble a skull and are part of the Palace ruler's distortion given physical form and somewhat related to the palace ruler. Searching these out and getting all 3 will give you a unique accessory that provides a buff, and when taken to a certain character in Mementos, this games Tartarus will be modified to be even better. There are 3 in every palace aside from the last 2 during the base game and I highly recommend seeking these out because it's worth your time and they will help you out.
